name: CNTK
baseline: TensorFlow (tensorflow-gpu 1.2.1 as a Keras 2.0.6 backend)
workload: Keras backend comparison (Keras 2.0.6, cntk 2.0 versus tensorflow-gpu 1.2.1, Theano 0.9.0) on one GTX 1080 Ti: average training seconds per epoch for bidirectional LSTM on IMDb, text-generation LSTM, MLP and CNN on MNIST, FastText on IMDb and CNN on CIFAR-10.
claimed_speedup: szilard benchm-dl keras_backend.md (GTX 1080 Ti, 2017): text-generation LSTM 3.3x faster than the TensorFlow backend; bidirectional LSTM 2.6x on a later-fixed buggy go_backwards path (Keras 2.0.5/2.0.6); slower than TensorFlow on CNNs (up to 1.7x).
compiler_and_flags: No compile flags (Python stack): Ubuntu 16.04, CUDA 8.0 + cuDNN 5.1, Keras 2.0.6, tensorflow-gpu 1.2.1, cntk 2.0 (szilard/benchm-dl versions.txt).
hardware: Local machine with a GeForce GTX 1080 Ti Founder's Edition (CPU model not stated); the page also has M60 (Azure NV6), Titan X (Maxwell) and K80 columns, the K80 numbers copied from Max Woolf's blog.
tradeoffs: Deep-learning toolkit with C++ core, Python, C# and BrainScript front ends; the repository was archived by Microsoft on 2026-02-17, the last main release is 2.7 and the README says there are no plans for new features and points users to ONNX and ONNX Runtime. The measured path is the Keras CNTK backend, not native CNTK scripts.
caveats: Third-party 2017-era numbers on old software (TensorFlow 1.2.1, CUDA 8, cuDNN 5.1, CNTK 2.0), one GPU model per column, no variance reported, CPU not stated; the page says only that it was inspired by Max Woolf's benchmark, and its K80 column is copied from Max Woolf's blog; minimaxir/keras-cntk-benchmark (MIT, 26 stars) holds keras_cntk_benchmark.py but its README states no CPU model or versions, and benchm-dl (70 stars) itself holds no Keras-backend scripts (only cnn-mnist/). The win is confined to LSTM/RNN and small dense models; TensorFlow is faster on both CNN tests (MNIST CNN 4.7 versus 5.0 s per epoch, CIFAR-10 CNN 14.2 versus 24.2 s on the 1080 Ti), and on the K80 column FastText also favours TensorFlow (58.3 versus 69.5 s); the Keras Python layer sits between the benchmark and both engines. Accuracy is comparable across backends. The repository was archived by Microsoft on 2026-02-17 (read-only); the last code commit is 2020-03-31 and the README calls 2.7 (2019) the last main release. The HKBU dlbench study (arXiv 1608.07249, claims 5-10x over Torch and TensorFlow on CPU LSTMs) was seen only as a search snippet because arxiv.org and dlbench.comp.hkbu.edu.hk are blocked here, so its numbers are not recorded; the hclhkbu/dlbench repo README (MIT, 170 stars) has the harness but no results. CNTK's own README makes no speed claim against other frameworks. [retier] Keras 2.0.7 fixed the CNTK go_backwards bug behind the bidirectional row; neither backend used cuDNN LSTM; TF path ran tf.while_loop swap_memory=True; scripts and CPU unstated; repo archived 2026-02-17; Keras dropped CNTK after 2.3.1.

name: MXNet
baseline: TensorFlow and PyTorch (TensorFlow 2.3 and PyTorch 1.6.0 from framework examples; NGC TensorFlow 1.15.2 and NGC PyTorch 1.5.0a0 containers)
workload: OneFlow DLPerf report v1.0 (Oct 2020): ResNet-50 v1.5 training throughput in images/s, FP32 batch size 128 per GPU, 1 to 32 Tesla V100 GPUs; also BERT-base pretraining sentences/s.
claimed_speedup: ResNet-50 v1.5 FP32 bsz 128, 1 GPU: upstream MXNet 1.6.0 (gluon-cv) 384.19 img/s vs PyTorch 1.6.0 348.62 and TensorFlow 2.3 321.80 (1.10x and 1.19x, derived from page data); NVIDIA NGC MXNet 392.24 vs NGC PyTorch 367.29 and NGC TensorFlow 1.15 362.44. 32 GPUs FP32: NGC MXNet 11331.93 vs NGC PyTorch 10917.09 (1.04x) and NGC TensorFlow 1.x 9514.64 (1.19x), derived from page data; upstream MXNet 9579.74 is behind PyTorch 10021.29 and only 1.02x over TensorFlow 2.3 9418.44. AMP bsz 256, 32 GPUs: NGC MXNet 30713.68 vs NGC TensorFlow 1.x with XLA 29171.69 and NGC PyTorch 22551.16, but upstream MXNet 10565.55 is far behind TensorFlow 2.3 19314.31. BERT-base FP32 bsz max, 32 GPUs: MXNet without clip_by_global_norm (bsz 64) 4340.89 sentences/s vs NGC TensorFlow 1.x 3089.74 and NGC PyTorch 3039.3 (both bsz 48, with gradient clipping); the TensorFlow 2.3 figure 2244.38 (bsz 64) is in the DLPerf README summary table, not in the report.
compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt framework builds, no compile flags stated: NGC 20.03 containers (nvcr.io/nvidia/mxnet:20.03-py3 with MXNet 1.6.0, DALI and Horovod; tensorflow:20.03-tf1-py3 with 1.15.2; pytorch:20.03-py3 with 1.5.0a0), CUDA 10.2 and driver 440.33.01; upstream rows use MXNet 1.6.0 with gluon-cv, TensorFlow 2.3.0 and PyTorch 1.6.0 examples.
hardware: 4 nodes, each 8x Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB, Intel Xeon Gold 5118 @ 2.30GHz, 384 GB RAM, InfiniBand 100 Gb/s, Ubuntu 16.04.4
tradeoffs: Archived on GitHub 2023-11-17 (read-only); bindings for Python, R, Julia, Scala, Go, JavaScript and more; hybridization between imperative and symbolic execution. Benefits shown depend on NVIDIA's tuned NGC container (DALI, Horovod).
caveats: The benchmark is run by OneFlow, a competing framework, from public scripts in Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf; OneFlow beats MXNet in every row quoted. All frameworks call cuDNN and cuBLAS for the convolutions and GEMMs, so the gaps measure framework overhead, input pipelines (NGC rows use DALI) and distributed communication, not kernels. The MXNet margin is small and not consistent: upstream MXNet 1.6.0 gluon-cv is slower than PyTorch 1.6.0 on 8 GPUs (2556.03 vs 2632.93 img/s) and on 32 GPUs (9579.74 vs 10021.29), and beats TensorFlow 2.3 by only 1.02x there (9418.44). With AMP, upstream MXNet is roughly half the speed of TensorFlow 2.3 and NGC PyTorch (10565.55 vs 19314.31 and 22551.16 img/s on 32 GPUs; 2908.88 vs 6898.00 on 8 GPUs). The large NGC MXNet figures come from NVIDIA's tuned DeepLearningExamples container with DALI and Horovod, not upstream MXNet. The BERT rows are not like-for-like: MXNet's gluon-nlp script has no clip_by_global_norm, which the report says raises throughput and may lower accuracy, and it ran at bsz 64 against bsz 48 for the NGC baselines; OneFlow run the same way (W/O clip) is faster than MXNet. The DLPerf README summary shows NGC MXNet 32-GPU FP32 as 11233.92 while the report shows 11331.93. Versions are from 2020 (TensorFlow 2.3, PyTorch 1.6), so current TensorFlow and PyTorch 2.x numbers have moved. An older NeurIPS 2019 PyTorch paper table (MXNet 218, PyTorch 212, TensorFlow 200 img/s, seen only as a search snippet; arXiv and NeurIPS blocked) points the same way. The repository was renamed apache/mxnet and archived (read-only) on 2023-11-17; Apache MXNet was retired to the Attic.

name: PyTorch
baseline: TensorFlow
workload: u39kun/deep-learning-benchmark: forward-pass (eval) and forward+backward (train) time per batch for VGG16, ResNet152 and DenseNet161, 224x224x3 images, batch size 16, FP32 and FP16, on several NVIDIA GPUs using NGC containers.
claimed_speedup: Titan V FP32, PyTorch 0.3.0 vs TensorFlow 1.4.0: vgg16 train 108.8 ms vs 157.2 ms (1.44x), resnet152 train 180.2 ms vs 269.8 ms (1.50x). RTX 2080 Ti FP32, PyTorch 1.0.0 vs TensorFlow 1.12.0: resnet152 train 142.5 ms vs 191.0 ms (1.34x), resnet152 eval 41.8 ms vs 43.6 ms; ratios derived from page data. TensorFlow 1.12.0 is faster on vgg16 train (90.8 ms vs 95.5 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt NGC docker images, no build flags: nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:17.12 (0.3.0) and :19.01-py3 (1.0.0), nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorflow:17.12 (1.4.0) and :19.01-py3 (1.12.0); CUDA 9.0.176, cuDNN 7.0.0.5, driver 387.34, or CUDA 10.0.130 with cuDNN 7.4.2.24 for the 2080 Ti rows.
hardware: NVIDIA Titan V, GTX 1080 Ti, Tesla V100 (AWS p3) and RTX 2080 Ti; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Eager-mode Python front end over a C++/CUDA core (ATen, autograd); needs GPU memory and a CUDA or ROCm stack for the GPU speedups.
caveats: The benchmark is a small community repo (u39kun, not project-authored) with 2017-2019 framework versions (PyTorch 0.3.0 and 1.0.0 against TensorFlow 1.4 to 1.12 graph mode), so it says little about TensorFlow 2.x with XLA or PyTorch 2.x. Both frameworks call cuDNN for the convolutions, so the gaps measure framework overhead and kernel selection, not new kernels. The harness is not symmetric: the TensorFlow training step fetches every gradient tensor back to the host through sess.run(self.grad) (a device-to-host copy the PyTorch loop does not do) and builds the graph with phase_train=False, while the PyTorch loop also computes a gradient for the input image (requires_grad=True) and enables cudnn.benchmark autotuning; the size of these effects was not measured. The win is mixed: TensorFlow 1.12 is faster on vgg16 training on the 2080 Ti (90.8 vs 95.5 ms FP32, 58.6 vs 68.1 ms FP16); on the V100, TensorFlow 1.5.0 beats PyTorch 0.3.0 on vgg16 (eval 24.0 vs 26.2 ms, train 71.7 vs 83.5 ms) while PyTorch wins resnet152 train (136.5 vs 199.8 ms); on the 1080 Ti vgg16 train is 131.3 (TensorFlow) vs 131.9 ms; eval times are mostly within about 4% (Titan V FP32 vgg16 eval 31.3 vs 31.8 ms). Results are batch size 16 only, synthetic inputs, 20 timed iterations after 20 warm-ups. A second independent source, Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf report v1.0 (Oct 2020, 4x8 V100 GPUs, ResNet-50 v1.5 FP32, bsz 128), has PyTorch 1.6.0 10021.29 img/s vs TensorFlow 2.3 9418.44 (1.06x, derived from page data) and NGC PyTorch 10917.09 vs NGC TensorFlow 1.x 9514.64, but with AMP NGC PyTorch 22551.16 loses to NGC TensorFlow 1.x both with XLA (29171.69) and without (24734.22), and on BERT-base NGC TensorFlow wins the FP32 bsz-max row (3089.74 vs 3039.3) and the AMP bsz-64 row with XLA (9409.2 vs 9331.72); that report was read at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf/HEAD/reports/dlperf_benchmark_test_report_v1.md. The PyTorch NeurIPS 2019 paper table (MXNet 218, PyTorch 212, TensorFlow 200 img/s ResNet-50, seen only as a search snippet) was not readable because arXiv and NeurIPS are blocked.

name: TensorFlow
baseline: PyTorch (NGC PyTorch 1.5.0a0+8f84ded, container nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:20.03-py3)
workload: Training throughput of ResNet-50 v1.5 (images/sec, automatic mixed precision) and BERT-base pretraining (sentences/sec, AMP) on 1 to 32 Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB GPUs (4 nodes x 8) using NVIDIA DeepLearningExamples scripts; the TensorFlow side is NGC TensorFlow 1.15.2 (nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorflow:20.03-tf1-py3) with XLA, and stock TensorFlow 2.3.0 with tensorflow/models scripts.
claimed_speedup: DLPerf ResNet-50 v1.5 AMP: NGC TensorFlow 1.x with XLA 1198.55 vs NGC PyTorch 802.9 img/s on 1 GPU (1.49x) and 8588.45 vs 6154.66 on 8 GPUs (1.40x); with DLPerf's static-loss-scale PyTorch run the lead is 1.45x/1.33x; NVIDIA READMEs: 1099.55 (1217.90 with XLA) vs 856.52 img/s on 1 V100.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (prebuilt NVIDIA NGC containers 20.03 for TensorFlow 1.15.2 and PyTorch 1.5.0a0; TensorFlow 2.3.0 and PyTorch 1.6.0 installed separately); CUDA 10.2, driver 440.33.01; XLA and AMP enabled per run as listed in the report.
hardware: 4 nodes, each 8x Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB, Intel Xeon Gold 5118 @ 2.30GHz, 384 GB RAM, InfiniBand 100 Gb/s EDR, Ubuntu 16.04.4
tradeoffs: XLA and AMP need extra configuration, and the TensorFlow 1.x XLA run used a smaller per-GPU batch (224) than PyTorch (256) to avoid out-of-memory; TensorFlow 1.x is end-of-life, TensorFlow 2.x is the maintained line.
caveats: Mixed evidence, not a clean win. The suite is run by OneFlow (a competing framework that tops every table) and published in October 2020, so the numbers are six years old. The wins come from NVIDIA's NGC build of TensorFlow 1.15.2 with XLA plus AMP, not the stock tensorflow/tensorflow v2.3.0 tree, and are against NVIDIA's NGC PyTorch examples; XLA itself now lives in openxla/xla. Without XLA, NGC TensorFlow BERT AMP is far slower than NGC PyTorch (183.25 vs 444.51 sentences/s on 1 GPU, 5189.07 vs 9331.72 on 32 GPUs at bsz=64; about 2.4x and 1.8x, derived from page data). Stock TensorFlow 2.3.0 BERT is slower than NGC PyTorch in both precisions (DLPerf README: FP32 2244.38 at bsz=64 vs 3039.3 at bsz=48; AMP 4168.79 at bsz=96 vs 10349.12 at bsz=96 on 32 GPUs, about 2.5x, derived from page data). In FP32 PyTorch is faster almost everywhere: ResNet-50 bsz=128 NGC TensorFlow 362.44/2721.98/5099.42/9514.64 vs NGC PyTorch 367.29/2887.65/5716.79/10917.09 img/s, TensorFlow 2.3.0 9418.44 vs PyTorch 1.6.0 10021.29 on 32 GPUs; BERT FP32 bsz=32 NGC PyTorch leads at every scale, and at bsz=max TensorFlow leads only on 32 GPUs (3089.74 vs 3039.30). The stock PyTorch examples were not run with AMP. The ResNet AMP comparison pits TensorFlow at bsz=224 (OOM at 256) against PyTorch at 256. XLA vs no-XLA gains inside TensorFlow are TensorFlow-vs-TensorFlow and are not counted as a win over PyTorch. PyTorch is also listed (wave 12) with older numbers showing it 1.3-1.5x faster than TensorFlow 1.4-1.12 on other workloads, so the two entries carry opposite claims. Tier B, not A, because compiler and build flags of the containers are not stated and batch sizes differ between some compared rows. Google's own XLA blog post was not opened. [retier] GPU JPEG decode (DALI nvJPEG) for TF vs CPU decode for PyTorch; static vs dynamic loss scaling; different throughput definitions; wins only with the NGC build plus XLA and AMP; PyTorch faster in FP32; 2020 numbers; opposite claim to the pytorch/pytorch entry.

name: Flashlight
baseline: PyTorch 1.8 and TensorFlow 2.4
workload: Wall-clock seconds for 100 iterations of forward plus backward passes including data loading, on six large networks (AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet-50, a BERT-like transformer, an ASR transformer, ViT), on 1 GPU and 8 GPUs with data-parallel gradient synchronization.

name: DLR-FT wasm-interpreter
baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift), Wasmer (Cranelift) startup
workload: wasmi-benchmarks startup suite: compile + instantiate of 7 modules from tiny to huge, geometric mean of per-case ratios against the fastest runtime for each case.
claimed_speedup: wasmi-benchmarks startup geomean x10.95 (relative to the fastest) against Wasmtime Cranelift x1634.19 and Wasmi v2 lazy-translation x10.66 (recomputed from data/amd-epyc-7763/criterion.json); about 149x over single-threaded Cranelift (derived). Execution geomean x122.00 against WAMR x17.07 (third slowest of 23).
compiler_and_flags: wasmi-benchmarks (github.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks) Cargo.toml [profile.bench] lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, run as 'cargo criterion --bench criterion --all-features ... startup/' (criterion 0.8.2; sample_size 10, 2 s measurement, 1 s warm-up). Rust toolchain: .github/workflows/startup.yml uses dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable with no rust-toolchain file, so the rustc version is not recorded; the C/C++ runtimes are built with gcc-15/g++-15 (.github/actions/install-dependencies). Runtime versions are pinned only by the Cargo.lock at HEAD (wasmtime 47.0.3, wasmer 7.2.1); the plots repo does not record which suite commit produced them.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (plot title and data/amd-epyc-7763 directory). This is the CPU of GitHub's ubuntu-latest runners and the suite's startup.yml workflow runs there, so the data probably come from a shared CI VM (not confirmed). The plots repo also holds Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, Intel i7700 and Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C data, not read here.
tradeoffs: In-place interpretation of WebAssembly 2.0 with no intermediate representation, no_std, aimed at avionics; no GC proposal planned.
caveats: The suite is maintained and run by the Wasmi author, so it is third-party for every runtime except Wasmi. Ratios were read from the SVG text labels and checked against the raw criterion data, which reproduce the startup geomeans exactly. The measured crate is dlr-wasm-interpreter 0.2.0 (current crates.io release). Startup is decode + validate + instantiate of 7 modules (erc20 to ffmpeg); the win is an in-place interpreter versus optimizing JITs, which is expected. Against other interpreters it is not the fastest: Wasmi v2 lazy-translation (also validates eagerly) is x10.66, Wasmi v2 lazy x1.37 and Wasm3 lazy x2.77, and V8 starts faster on the two largest modules (ffmpeg 35.5 ms vs 127.1 ms, spidermonkey 10.9 ms vs 32.9 ms). Startup-only win: execution geomean on the same CPU (plot geomean-execute.svg) is x122.00, about 7 times slower than WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07 (derived from page data), over 20 of 21 cases (no tail calls); the committed criterion.json gives a different execute geomean (98.25), so the execute plot came from another run. Data probably from a shared GitHub Actions VM. The project's own README gives no performance numbers. [retier] Startup-only win over optimizing JITs in the wasmi-benchmarks suite; the suite builds wasmtime 47.0.3 with default-features=false and no parallel compilation, so the Cranelift startup column is single-threaded and the gap is overstated against a default multi-core Wasmtime. V8 is faster on ffmpeg and spidermonkey. 0.2.0 preallocates a 1.5 MB stack on every invoke (issue #413 panics on nRF52840); unreleased HEAD cuts default stacks to 208 values and 208 frames; soundness issues #406 and #412 open. rustc version unrecorded, no suite commit named. Rust, not C++.

name: evm.zig (evmz, Zig EVM execution engine)
baseline: evmone (v0.23.0, baseline and advanced interpreters) and revm (=43.0.2 raw interpreter, Interpreter::run_plain)
workload: VM-core 'compare' lane over the evm-bench-style fixtures (arithmetic loop, MSTORE loop, keccak loop, ten-thousand-hashes, SLOAD and SSTORE loops, LOG0/LOG4 with 0 and 32 byte data, ERC20 mint, transfer and approval+transfer, snailtracer): deployed runtime bytecode called repeatedly through each engine's interpreter-level path with analysis prepared outside the timed window, fixed Osaka spec, median of 100-run medians, lower time is better.
claimed_speedup: README (Apple M1 Max, ReleaseFast, 2026-08-13), evmz versus evmone-base versus revm-int: Arithmetic loop 0.104 / 0.109 / 0.501 ms, Storage SSTORE loop 0.162 / 0.854 / 0.875 ms, ERC20 transfer 3.761 / 6.247 / 6.084 ms, Snailtracer 19.965 / 59.804 / 37.990 ms. bench/README.md ratios (base/evmz and revm/evmz): SSTORE 5.27x and 5.40x, SLOAD 3.97x and 2.34x, snailtracer 3.00x and 1.90x, ERC20 transfer 1.66x and 1.62x, Arithmetic 1.05x and 4.82x. evmz is slower than evmone-base on MSTORE loop (0.125 vs 0.084 ms, 0.67x), LOG0 32-byte (0.057 vs 0.033 ms, 0.58x), LOG0 0-byte (0.69x), LOG4 0-byte (0.80x) and ten-thousand-hashes (0.86x). AMD EPYC Genoa (KVM guest pinned to one CPU) rows are near parity with evmone-base: ERC20 transfer 7.686 vs 7.447 ms (0.97x), arithmetic 0.151 vs 0.145 ms (0.96x), keccak loop 4.597 vs 4.584 ms (1.00x), snailtracer 33.347 vs 57.983 ms (1.74x), SSTORE 0.595 vs 0.838 ms (1.41x), and ahead of revm on every row (1.08x to 3.08x).
compiler_and_flags: Zig >= 0.16.0 (bench/build.zig.zon), zig build bench-compare -Dbench-optimize=ReleaseFast -Dbench-support-min=osaka -Dbench-support-max=osaka -Dnative-keccak=xkcp -- --spec osaka --num-runs 100 --warmup-ms 100 (five repeats, median of the five per-run medians); evmz modules built with omit_frame_pointer; evmone v0.23.0 with intx 0.15.0 compiled inside the Zig build by Zig's bundled clang from a hand-listed source set with -std=c++20 -fomit-frame-pointer -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti (not evmone's own CMake Release build); revm =43.0.2 built with cargo --release, RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native -C force-frame-pointers=no, CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=fat, CODEGEN_UNITS=1 (Rust toolchain version not pinned for the sidecar).
hardware: Apple M1 Max, macOS arm64 (headline snapshot, 2026-08-13); AMD EPYC Genoa, Linux x86-64, KVM guest pinned to one CPU (earlier snapshot).
tradeoffs: Tail-call-dispatch interpreter in Zig with fork rules, tracing and single-step selected at compile time (separate binaries), zero-alloc pooled executor, optional XKCP Keccak and native crypto libraries (blst, mcl, libsecp256k1) as lazy dependencies, zkVM guest builds (ZisK, SP1, OpenVM). The headline numbers enable the optional XKCP Keccak provider ('maximum-performance configuration'). Pre-1.0 (version 0.0.0), builds need a very recent Zig (0.16).
caveats: Comparison is VM-core only: interpreter execute() with analysis prepared outside the timed window, no transaction validation, journal or database, so it is not a whole-client comparison (the repo says the executor lane is deliberately later). Correctness check in all three runners is limited to a success status (evmz result status, evmone EVMC_SUCCESS in bench/evmone/vm_loop.cpp, revm InterpreterAction::Return with is_ok() in bench/revm/src/main.rs); bench/src/compare.zig only collects timings and host call counts and does not assert that return data, gas used or logs match across engines. The README headline table shows the four rows where evmz wins; the full M1 table also has rows where evmone-baseline is faster (MSTORE loop 0.67x, LOG0 0-byte 0.69x, LOG0 32-byte 0.58x, LOG4 0-byte 0.80x, ten-thousand-hashes 0.86x), and on the AMD snapshot evmz is within about 7% of evmone-base on 9 of 14 rows (ratios 0.94x to 1.07x, derived from page data) and slower on the LOG0 rows (0.73x, 0.75x). The AMD snapshot is older, run in a KVM guest pinned to one CPU, and names only the EPYC Genoa family, not a model. The M1 snapshot enables evmz's optional XKCP Keccak provider while evmone uses its bundled keccak.c, so the keccak-heavy rows partly compare hash implementations. The evmone baseline is compiled by Zig's clang from a hand-picked source list and flag set rather than evmone's CMake Release build, and revm's sidecar has no pinned Rust version. Revm is timed through its raw interpreter (Interpreter::run_plain), not a transaction path. The project is pre-release (version 0.0.0, unaudited) and contains CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md (AI-assisted development); first-party numbers only, 3 stars. Not the cryptuon/zig-evm project, which is rejected for a hard-coded table. [retier] VM-core only, first-party, 3 stars; the harness checks only success status with no cross-engine output or gas check. Storage rows (SLOAD 3.97x, SSTORE 5.27x, part of ERC20) measure mock hosts: evmone's std::map host with two EVMC callbacks per access against evmz's fused AutoHashMap host; the arithmetic loop is at parity (1.05x) and evmone-base is faster on 5 of 14 M1 rows. Measured against evmone commit 786c96f1 (0.23.0-dev) and revm 41.0.0 (2026-08-13), with evmone built at -O2 by Zig's clang rather than its CMake build and XKCP Keccak on the evmz side only; PR #65 bumped the baselines without re-measuring. EVMC adapter removed (#33). Not the rejected cryptuon/zig-evm.

name: Fizzy
baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift), Wasmer (Cranelift) startup
workload: wasmi-benchmarks startup suite: compile + instantiate of 7 modules from tiny to huge, geometric mean of per-case ratios against the fastest runtime for each case.
claimed_speedup: Startup (compile plus instantiate) geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test (lower is better), AMD EPYC 7763: Fizzy x17.83 vs WAMR fast-interpreter x56.73, V8 x33.27, Wasmer (Cranelift) x1484.15, Wasmtime (Cranelift) x1634.19 (about 3.2x lower than WAMR fast-interp, derived from page data). Fizzy is below WAMR fast-interp on all five CPU data sets (Apple M2 Pro 18.69 vs 49.35, Apple M4 Pro 17.20 vs 43.90, Intel i7-7700 17.63 vs 61.71, Xeon Platinum 8573C 11.21 vs 44.15) and below V8 on four of them, but not on Apple M2 Pro (Fizzy 18.69 vs V8 16.97).
compiler_and_flags: Built by the wasmi-benchmarks harness through Robin Freyler's fizzyx 0.1.1 crate: fizzyx-sys build.rs runs Fizzy's CMake via the Rust cmake crate with FIZZY_TESTING=OFF, FIZZY_WASI=OFF and a force-included compat_shim.hpp; Rust harness profile.bench lto=fat, codegen-units=1. C++ compiler, version and CMake build type are not stated. Fizzy's own README performance setup: CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (-O3), LTO, latest GCC or Clang, libstdc++, no -march=native.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (named in the plot title; the plots repo also holds data for Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, an Intel i7700 and Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, not read here)
tradeoffs: WebAssembly 1.0 only; supports no GC, SIMD or newer proposals. Built for deterministic blockchain use (metering, canonical floating point).
caveats: Startup-only win: on the same suite Fizzy's execution geomean is x45.63 vs WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07, Wasm3 (eager) x16.51 and V8 x1.05 on EPYC 7763 (about 2.7x slower than WAMR fast-interp, derived from page data), so it is not faster than any category baseline at running code. Per-test startup on EPYC: V8 is faster than Fizzy on ffmpeg (35.46 ms vs 215.36 ms), spidermonkey (10.94 ms vs 52.31 ms) and pulldown-cmark (2.30 ms vs 2.72 ms); Fizzy wins on bz2, coremark, argon2 and erc20. Lazy-validating interpreters are far faster at startup (Wasm3 lazy x2.77, Wasmi v2 lazy x1.37). The WAMR comparison is against its fast-interpreter mode, which precompiles at load. Suite is maintained by the author of the competing Wasmi runtime and the Fizzy bindings (fizzyx) are his; plots are regenerated in place (last EPYC update 2026-08-25, values as of 2026-10-06). Fizzy implements WebAssembly 1.0 (MVP) only. Latest commit (2025-11-10) is a README merge; the last code change was 2023-03-03. Fizzy's own CHANGELOG (v0.5.0 detailed results, hardware not stated) shows execution about 5.1x faster than WABT 1.0.19 interpreter (508%) but only 1.7x faster than WABT 1.0.12 (167%), while wasm3 0.4.7 took 26% of Fizzy's execution time and 27% of its instantiation time. Fizzy failed in Frank Denis's libsodium 2021-Q1 run (needs WASI poll_oneoff).

name: PolkaVM
baseline: Wasmtime (cranelift); the same table also lists Wasmtime winch, Wasmer singlepass, Wasm3, Wasmi, wazero, CKB VM and Solana RBPF
workload: Three guest programs (pinky, a cycle-accurate NES emulator running a homebrew game; prime-sieve; minimal) built for PolkaVM's RISC-V RV32EM ISA and for WebAssembly for the other VMs; one-shot time including compilation and initialization, steady-state execution time, and compile time.
claimed_speedup: One-shot (compile + init + run) on pinky: PolkaVM 64-bit recompiler 55.408 ms vs Wasmtime (cranelift) 116.002 ms and Wasmer (singlepass) 137.832 ms (about 2.1x and 2.5x, derived from page data). prime-sieve: 14.390 ms vs Wasmtime cranelift 125.107 ms, Wasmtime winch 54.295 ms, Wasmer singlepass 57.379 ms (about 8.7x, 3.8x, 4.0x, derived from page data). minimal: 113.743 us vs Wasmtime cranelift 935.241 us (about 8.2x) but only 1.13x ahead of Wasmer singlepass 128.467 us (derived from page data). Compile time on pinky: 167.553 us vs Wasmtime cranelift 62.212 ms (about 370x); prime-sieve 442.354 us vs 76.662 ms (about 173x) (derived from page data). Steady-state execution is not faster: pinky 6.422 ms vs Wasmtime cranelift 5.776 ms; prime-sieve 2.104 ms vs 2.161 ms (parity); minimal 4.852 us vs 0.252 us per call (PolkaVM about 19x slower, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: At the benchmarked commit 190ea5ac: benchtool built with Rust 1.82.0 (tools/benchtool/rust-toolchain.toml; the workspace root pinned 1.75.0, and the 1.86.0 in the record is today's HEAD), cargo --release with lto = true, codegen-units = 1, debug = true; guest programs built with nightly-2024-11-01 (guest-programs/rust-toolchain.toml) by guest-programs/build-benchmarks.sh, Wasm guests with RUSTFLAGS '-C target-cpu=mvp -C target-feature=-sign-ext'; benchtool pins wasmtime 26.0.1 (default features off: cranelift, winch, runtime, so no parallel compilation and no cache), wasmer 5.0.0 (singlepass), wasmi 0.39.1, and a Go shim on wazero v1.8.1; 02-run-benchmarks.rb disables turbo boost, sets the performance governor and pins the run to CPUs 1-2 with a cgroup; criterion sample_size 10, mean estimate reported.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X 32-Core, x86_64 Linux; results from commit 190ea5ac, timestamp 2024-11-24
tradeoffs: Guests must be compiled for PolkaVM's own RV32EM RISC-V ISA, not WebAssembly; no floating point or SIMD by design; Rust host API (no C API seen in the workspace); sandboxing and gas metering are built in; the interpreter fallback is far slower (pinky 1.689 s one-shot vs 55.408 ms recompiler); README says the project is unfinished and a heavy work in progress.
caveats: Numbers date from November 2024 (commit 190ea5ac; Wasmtime 26, Wasmer 5), long before current Wasmtime releases. This is a first-party suite: the PolkaVM author chose the workloads. The VMs execute different binaries (RISC-V for PolkaVM, Wasm for the rest), and the Wasm guests were built for the MVP target with sign-ext disabled. The win is in one-shot and compile time. Wasmtime cranelift is faster or equal in steady-state execution on pinky and prime-sieve, and about 19x faster per call on the minimal program, because PolkaVM's recompiler has a high fixed per-call cost from running in a separate sandbox process. Part of the compile-time gap is that Wasmtime cranelift optimizes while PolkaVM's recompiler is single-pass (README: guaranteed single-pass O(n) compilation). Wasmtime was built without parallel compilation. The README says the project is unfinished and should not be used in production.

name: risechain/pevm (parallel EVM on revm)
baseline: sequential revm (pevm's own execute_revm_sequential path)
workload: Criterion (100 samples) wall time to execute one whole Ethereum block with state preloaded in memory: 85 real mainnet blocks from Frontier to Cancun, plus three mocked 1-Gigagas blocks (raw transfers, ERC20 transfers, Uniswap swaps); sequential revm versus pevm's Block-STM style parallel executor.
claimed_speedup: Benches README (Graviton3 c7g.8xlarge): mocked 1-Gigagas blocks, Uniswap Swaps 413.42 ms sequential vs 18.707 ms parallel (22.1x), ERC20 Transfers 246.43 vs 60.817 ms (4.05x), Raw Transfers 159.08 vs 56.425 ms (2.82x). Mainnet: 'We are currently ~2.02 times faster than sequential execution on average', max speed-up x4.32 (block 7279999, 4.54 vs 1.05 ms), max slow-down x0.89. Derived from page data over the 85 mainnet rows: 63 blocks more than 5% faster, 18 within 5% of 1.0, 4 slower (0.89x to 0.93x); per-block mean ratio 1.96x, geometric mean 1.78x, ratio of summed times 2.04x. Top-level README repeats 2x average and 22x on the Uniswap gigagas block for the legacy Block-STM design.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --features global-alloc --bench mainnet, and JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_MALLOC_CONF="thp:always,metadata_thp:always" cargo bench --features global-alloc --bench gigagas. Bench profile inherits the workspace release profile: codegen-units=1, lto=fat at the time the tables were written (November 2024); strip=true and panic=abort were added later (PR #443, 2024-12-16), and Cargo ignores panic for bench targets anyway. Global allocator: snmalloc on aarch64 and rpmalloc elsewhere for mainnet, jemalloc with THP for gigagas. Concurrency: min(available_parallelism, 12 on ARM / 8 on x86) for mainnet; gigagas uses available_parallelism (32 on the stated machine). rustc version not stated (no rust-toolchain file; edition 2024 at HEAD).
hardware: AWS c7g.8xlarge, Graviton3, 32 vCPUs @ 2.6 GHz
tradeoffs: Parallel executor that still delegates VM execution to revm (an inline parallel-aware EVM is only a TODO). Speedup depends on block parallelism; falls back to sequential execution when a block self-destructs then redeploys a contract, and the concurrency level is hard-coded (8 on x86, 12 on ARM) with the README noting it ideally needs auto-tuning. Needs cmake to build snmalloc. Repo warns it is a work in progress and not production ready.
caveats: Numbers are first-party and stale: crates/pevm/benches/README.md was last changed for results on 2024-11-05/2024-11-20 (later edit 2024-12-16 only touched profiling commands), so they reflect the November 2024 code and revm version; the gigagas section says CANCUN spec while the current gigagas.rs runs SpecId::OSAKA. No rustc version anywhere. Baseline is revm run sequentially inside pevm's own harness (pevm.execute with force_sequential, i.e. execute_revm_sequential, which wraps storage in a CacheDB, commits state.clone() per transaction and builds pevm-format state transitions), not an independent geth, evmone or reth run. Pevm::execute itself falls back to sequential for blocks under 4,000,000 gas or with fewer transactions than the concurrency level, which is why 18 mainnet rows read 1.0x. Chain state is preloaded into memory (authors argue disk-backed state would favor parallel execution, unmeasured). The 22x figure is a synthetic mocked block of independent Uniswap swaps (README says it does not represent real-world blocks). The README describes the measured design as 'Legacy'; the new architecture (inline EVM, shreds, sparse trie) is still TODO, and the repo is marked work in progress, not production ready. Parallel Go (Polygon, Sei) being slower than sequential Rust/C++ is asserted with no numbers. [retier] First-party harness on Graviton3 with the baseline being the risechain/revm fork (rev 7345c07) run sequentially inside pevm's own code; tables from November 2024 code (82fd0f1) where every transaction was validated (NeedValidation bitflag 0), fixed by PR #508 in 2026-05 with the maintainer reporting the fixed code slower and no new numbers. The sequential arm deep-clones state per transaction and frees its CacheDB inside the timed call while the parallel arm drops asynchronously. Per-block geomean 1.78x, summed-time ratio 2.04x (derived from page data); the 22x comes from a synthetic Uniswap block whose transactions are independent by construction (SpecId::LATEST). Open correctness issue #518 (EIP-7702 re-delegation divergence); unkeyed FxHash location keys; no rustc version.

name: Stitch (makepad)
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter and Wasmtime Pulley (execution); Wasmtime Cranelift (startup)
workload: wasmi-benchmarks execution suite: 22 cases, geometric mean of per-case ratios against the fastest runtime for each case.
claimed_speedup: wasmi-benchmarks (AMD EPYC 7763, run by the Wasmi author): execution geomean over 18 common cases has the Robbepop/stitch v0.1-dev fork about 1.05-1.10x faster than wasm3 and Wasm3-class interpreters; over Stitch's own 20 cases 1.10x vs WAMR fast-interp and 1.035x vs wasm3; Wasmi v2 is 1.26x faster than Stitch (derived from the per-case SVGs). First-party README table: old Wasmi 0.31.2 baseline, wasm3 runner commented out.
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release in coremark/ (Rust release profile; rustc version not stated). Harness pins wasmi 0.31.2 and wasmtime 20.0.1; the wasm3 runner (wasm3 crate 0.3.1) is commented out in coremark/Cargo.toml and coremark/src/main.rs at HEAD.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (named in the plot title; the plots repo also holds data for Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, an Intel i7700 and Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, not read here)
tradeoffs: Relies on LLVM sibling-call optimization (not guaranteed) and a 64-bit target only; about 15k lines of code with significant unsafe and no external audit (README).
caveats: Only a single CoreMark workload; the edge over wasm3 is within a few percent on Mac and negative on Linux, and Wasmtime's JIT is 4-8x faster than Stitch, so it does not beat any JIT baseline in the category. The Wasmi baseline is the old 0.31.2 stack interpreter (open issue #2 asks for an update since Wasmi 0.32+ is much faster); the wasm3 runner is commented out of the published harness. Open correctness issues #3 and #4 (filed by the Wasmi author, July 2025 and June 2026): live locals and registers are not preserved on entering block/if/loop, so some modules return wrong results (example returns 0 instead of 42); unfixed upstream. Relies on LLVM sibling-call optimisation with no guarantee; 64-bit only; no SIMD or WASI; large amount of unaudited unsafe code (README). Independent wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks plots (Aug 2026; criterion, profile.bench lto=fat, codegen-units=1) measure a bug-fixed fork (Robbepop/stitch branch v0.1-dev, shown as 'Stitch (lazy)'): geomean execute time relative to the fastest runtime is Stitch 15.73 vs Wasm3 (eager) 16.51 on AMD EPYC 7763, 11.94 vs 12.64 on Apple M2 Pro, 9.70 vs 10.71 on Apple M4 Pro (about 1.05-1.10x faster than Wasm3, derived from page data), but Wasmi v2 (eager) is faster than Stitch on all three (12.40, 8.83, 8.06). The record's claim about rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark was not checked by the verifier. [retier] The wasm3 runner is commented out of the first-party harness and its baseline is Wasmi 0.31.2. Open wrong-result bugs in upstream (issues #3, #4); the measured Robbepop/stitch v0.1-dev fork fixes them, raises the 128 KiB function-body limit still capped in upstream src/config.rs (likely cause of the FFmpeg issue #1), and fixes memory.grow, grow_with_stack and operand pops; crates.io still ships 0.1.0 (2024-05-13). wasmi-benchmarks builds wasmtime without parallel compilation, so startup gaps against Wasmtime are overstated. Rust, not C++.

name: tinywasm
baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift, Winch, Pulley), Wasmer (Cranelift, Singlepass) and WAMR fast-interpreter startup
workload: wasmi-benchmarks startup suite: compile + instantiate of 7 modules from tiny to huge, geometric mean of per-case ratios against the fastest runtime for each case.
claimed_speedup: Startup geomean on AMD EPYC 7763 relative to the per-case fastest runtime (lower is better): Tinywasm x37.19 versus Wasmtime (Pulley) x1777.72, Wasmtime (Cranelift) x1634.19, Wasmer (Cranelift) x1484.15, Wasmtime (Winch) x298.15, Wasmer (Singlepass) x162.12 and WAMR fast-interpreter x56.73; V8 is x33.27 and Wasmi v2 (lazy) x1.37. About 44x lower than Wasmtime Cranelift and 1.5x lower than WAMR (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: wasmi-benchmarks Cargo.toml [profile.bench]: lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1 (cargo criterion --bench criterion uses it; a separate [profile.ci] with thin LTO is not used by the workflows). Rust toolchain unpinned: no rust-toolchain file, CI workflows (.github/workflows/startup.yml, execute.yml) install dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable; C/C++ runtimes are built by their wrapper crates with the system compiler, version unstated. Tinywasm 0.10.0 is built with default features, without the nightly-tail-calls feature its README recommends for maximum performance.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (named in the plot title; the plots repo also holds data for Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, an Intel i7700 and Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, not read here)
tradeoffs: Safe Rust (except an optional simd-x86 feature), no_std, passes the WebAssembly 3.0 core test suite; can serialize to .twasm for faster loading.
caveats: The suite is maintained and run by the Wasmi author (Robbepop), so it is third-party for Tinywasm but run by a competitor. Ratios were read from the text labels of the rendered SVG; the plots repo records no runtime versions, toolchain or run date beyond its commit 'update AMD EPYC 7763 plots' (2026-08-25). The EPYC 7763 is the CPU of GitHub's ubuntu-latest runners, so the run probably came from the workflow_dispatch CI jobs on a shared VM, but the plots repo does not say so. The suite pins tinywasm 0.10.0 with default features (no nightly-tail-calls); tinywasm 0.11.0 shipped 2026-09-19. Startup-only win, as expected of an interpreter against compiling JITs, and no better than V8 (x33.27). Execution geomean on the same CPU (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg) is x40.50, slower than Wasmtime (Pulley) x27.92, WAMR x17.07, Wasm3 (eager) x16.51 and Wasmi v2 (eager) x12.40. The README itself points users wanting better performance to wasmi, wasm3, wazero, wasmer or wasmtime. In the independent Apple Silicon report (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark/HEAD/docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md, tinywasm 0.11.0 with nightly-tail-calls) tinywasm execution geomean is 3.20 vs Pulley 2.09 and WAMR 1.63 on M4 E-cores (2.98 vs 1.68 and 1.38 on A12), and it fails the legacy-exceptions modules. Last commit on the default branch main is 2026-09-22; the next branch was updated 2026-10-03. name: wasm3
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter (iwasm); Wasmtime Pulley interpreter; WasmEdge interpreter
workload: Interpreter-only comparison on the 17 Wasm cases every runtime runs (xmrsplayer audio, AssemblyScript graphql, audio DSP, MVP kernels), CPU time per call, N=10 per platform, Apple M4 Max E-cores and iPhone XS Max (A12) E-cores.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime (lower is better), M4 Max E-cores: wasm3 1.01, WAMR fast-interp 1.63, Wasmtime Pulley 2.09, WasmEdge interpreter 8.42; A12 E-cores: wasm3 1.04, WAMR 1.38, Pulley 1.68, WasmEdge 9.28. About 1.6x faster than WAMR fast-interp and 2.1x faster than Pulley on the M4 (derived from page data). Page text: 'wasm3 is the fastest interpreter on nearly every case it runs'.
compiler_and_flags: wasm3 v0.9.0 built with -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions, Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0), no WASI sources; WAMR cmake Release -O3 FAST_INTERP only (AOT/JIT/FAST_JIT off); Pulley rust nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS --cfg=pulley_tail_calls, fat LTO
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (MacBook Pro, macOS 27.0); iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores (iOS 18.7.10)
tradeoffs: Pure interpreter with no JIT or AOT tier: far slower than compiling runtimes. In the wasmi-benchmarks suite (AMD EPYC 7763, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg) execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test is wasm3 16.51x vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15x and V8 1.05x. Very cheap startup: same suite startup geomean wasm3 lazy 2.77x vs WAMR fast-interp 56.73x, V8 33.27x, Wasmer Cranelift 1484.15x, Wasmtime Cranelift 1634.19x. Of the Wasm 3.0 features the benchmark tested it supports only tail calls and extended-const. Maintainer states the project is in a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: Result is interpreter versus interpreter: wasm3 is not faster than JIT/AOT Wasmtime, Wasmer or V8 (its own docs/Performance.md CoreMark table, 2019-2020 on an i5-8250U and labelled historical by the project, has wasmtime 0.8.0 and Wasmer Cranelift 4.0x faster and wasm-micro-runtime 8.1x slower; in the wasmi-benchmarks suite on an AMD EPYC 7763 its execute geomean is 16.51 vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15 and V8 1.05, and behind Silverfir-nano's interpreter 9.02 and Wasmi v2 12.40). The 17-case geomean covers only MVP/scalar code: wasm3 cannot run the SIMD-canonical builds, exceptions, GC, typed references, memory64 or multi-memory, and WAMR leads on the SIMD rows. Instantiation is its weak spot: extended-const modules cost it 116-122x Pulley's time on the M4 (62-85x on the A12). The benchmark author built WAMR with 29 carried patches, WasmEdge with 26 and Pulley from a fork branch with 9 extra commits, while wasm3 v0.9.0 ran unpatched. Only Apple Silicon E-cores measured. Independent libsodium 2021-Q1 run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2021-Q1/README.md): 'wamr was slower than wasm3 on every single test', native about 30x faster than wasm3 and about 46x faster than WAMR. The README still declares a minimal maintenance phase, though September 2026 commits add atomics and an exception-handling API.

name: wasmz
baseline: Wasmtime Pulley interpreter and WAMR fast interpreter
workload: Interpreter-only comparison of 7 runtimes on Apple Silicon E-cores: 17 shared cases, CPU time per call.
claimed_speedup: CPU time per call relative to the fastest runtime, geometric mean over 17 cases, N=10: Apple M4 Max E-cores wasmz 1.59 vs WAMR 1.63 and Pulley 2.09 (about 1.3x faster than Pulley, derived from page data); iPhone XS (A12) E-cores wasmz 1.63 vs Pulley 1.68 but WAMR 1.38.
compiler_and_flags: wasmz dev built with 'make release' (Zig ReleaseFast); wasm3 at submodule commit 79d412e built with cmake (its CMakeLists defaults to Release, -O3); WAMR at submodule commit 11eb206 built with cmake -DWAMR_BUILD_INTERP=1 -DWAMR_BUILD_AOT=0 -DWAMR_BUILD_FAST_JIT=0 -DWAMR_BUILD_JIT=0 -DWAMR_BUILD_SIMD=0; wasmi at commit 9f6ff82 built with cargo build --release -p wasmi_cli (all in bench/build.sh). Compiler versions (Zig, gcc, rustc) are not stated in the report.
hardware: MacBook Pro Apple M4 Max (E-cores) and iPhone XS Max (Apple A12 Bionic, E-cores)
tradeoffs: Zig library with C API and Rust bindings; GC, SIMD, exceptions and threads claimed.
caveats: First-party numbers from a 2026-04-16 dev build; CPU model and compiler versions not stated. The wasm3 used is v0.5.1 (submodule commit 79d412e); the independent harness used v0.9.0. Timings are whole-process wall time via hyperfine, so start-up is included and wasmz's lazy (on first call) compilation favours it on the 19 MB esbuild module; WAMR is excluded from esbuild. The harness does not check program output. Many miscompilation fixes landed after the benchmark (August 2026 commits such as 'keep operand-stack reads of a local independent of later writes' and 'only rename a label slot onto the temporary that a branch consumes'), so the numbers were measured on code later fixed for correctness bugs. The QuickJS and esbuild memory rows measure the sh -c wrapper (1.8 MB for every runtime), so those RSS figures are invalid. The independent harness rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark (docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md, wasmz v0.1.4) puts wasmz behind wasm3 (geomean 1.59 vs 1.01 on M4 Max E-cores). It is roughly level with WAMR fast-interp there (1.63) but behind it on iPhone XS A12 (1.63 vs 1.38), and ahead of wasmtime Pulley (2.09). The same harness reports six failing rows for wasmz: wrong results on extconst_init and extconst_init.mvp, traps on graphql_as and callref_dispatch, and segfaults on v128 ops in sieve and crc32. It also notes that wasmz never collects GC structs and does not support multi-memory or multi-value results through its C API. Treat the win over WAMR and wasm3 as unconfirmed. Zig library with a C API (libwasmz plus wasmz.h), so callable from C++.

name: wazy
baseline: wazero (the Go runtime it descends from; the repo's three-way benchmark arms against wasmtime-go exist but the README states no wasmtime numbers)
workload: benchmarks/vs-wazero in the repo: instantiate a 37 KB TinyGo module, host calls, compile, compiled and interpreted execution kernels, memory.fill and interruptible loops, run against a pinned wazero; plus a 6.5 MB Rust document-converter module (go-anydoc) run as a single instantiate.
claimed_speedup: README (Apple M4 unless noted): Instantiate 9.1x (1.724 us vs 15.74 us, 37 KB TinyGo module). Interruptible loops with WithCloseOnContextDone 9.8x vs wazero@main (docs/performance.md: 160 us vs 2074 us on a 100k-iteration loop, fibonacci 6.56 ms vs 76.0 ms, i9-12900HK). memory.fill 1.68x geomean (7.1x at 15 bytes, parity at 64 KiB). Compiled execution: string_manipulation -18%, reverse_array -14%, base64 -12%, fibonacci a wash. Host calls a tie (47.8 ns vs 48.3 ns). Cumulative geomean -17.8% time and -22.9% B/op across internal/integration_test/bench vs the wazero fork point. docs/performance.md adds BenchmarkConstAddrLoads 1.62 us vs 5.10 us (about 3.1x). 6.5 MB Rust module (go-anydoc) vs wazero v1.12.0: 4.9x compiled and 1.7x interpreted on a 5 MB docx body; the README says most of the 4.9x is the cost of WithCloseOnContextDone on wazero and about 1.3x remains with the option off (M5 Pro run). go-anydoc's own README: about 1.8x faster than wazero v1.12.0 interpreted, with 59 vs 40.5 million allocations on a 7.6 MB PDF.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 (Go 1.26.1 on the go-anydoc third-party run, CGO_ENABLED=0); benchstat over interleaved A/B runs with upstream wazero as a control; commands: cd benchmarks/vs-wazero && go test -run='^$' -bench=. -benchmem -count=10. That module links wasmtime-go v34 and therefore needs cgo for every arm (docs/performance.md), so the head-to-head was not a CGO_ENABLED=0 build. The wazero pin is ambiguous: the benchmark README says fork point c0f3a4ec6411, docs/performance.md says f4779551afb4, and go.mod pins v1.12.1-0.20260904184217-6edbb8c01a5f; some figures were taken against wazero@main or wazero HEAD.
hardware: Apple M4 (native arm64) for the head-to-head and cumulative numbers; core-pinned Intel i9-12900HK for memory.grow and interruptible-loop numbers; a third-party run on Apple M5 Pro (18-core), macOS 26.5
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no CGO; has a compiled mode and an interpreter mode (the README benchmarks both and the CLI has an -interpreter flag); adds Component Model, WASI 0.2 and the WASI 0.3 async ABI that wazero lacks; the host-call win comes from deleting reflection-based registration (the API broke compatibility with wazero once). Not callable from C++ directly.
caveats: The baseline is wazero, not Wasmtime, Wasmer, WAMR or V8. docs/performance.md shows wazy behind Wasmtime Cranelift: about 16% behind on Case3/fibonacci, and 0.75 s vs 0.37 s (about 2x behind) on the 7.5 MB PDF run of the 6.5 MB module, where wazero took 3.4 s. It is ahead only on dynaddr (1.18x) and at parity on dispatch, and wazy omits the Spectre index clamping that Wasmtime does by default. The README itself says its largest figures (9.8x, 4.9x) come mostly from what WithCloseOnContextDone costs wazero, and that the raw code-generator gap is about 30% on the large module. The host-call and fibonacci results are ties. The README's Instantiate figure (9.1x, 3.3 KB heap per instance) comes from an engineering-log sweep on the pooled linear-memory path. On 2026-09-20 two correctness and isolation fixes landed on that path (commit ed4381b8 'stop recycling a memory a closed module can still reach', commit 0f363441 'stop racing api.Memory readers when a module closes'). The figure was not re-measured after them, and the wazero pin it ran against is not recorded. The project is a young single-author hard fork of wazero (not a GitHub fork) with 44 stars. [retier] Independent go-anydoc bench (wazy v0.3.0 vs wazero v1.12.0, Go 1.26.1, M5 Pro) gives about 1.8x interpreted, but the 4.9x/9.8x headlines are mostly WithCloseOnContextDone cost on wazero (codegen gap about 1.3x) and Wasmtime Cranelift is about 2x faster (docs/performance.md: about 16% behind on fibonacci, about 2x on a 6.5 MB module; cold compile 1.2 s and 517 MB RSS). The 9.1x instantiate figure was measured on the pooled-memory path before the 2026-09-20 isolation fixes ed4381b8 (#74) and 0f363441 (#69), with a harness that skips _start and closes each instance at once so the pool always hits; the last tag v0.3.0 lacks those fixes and #75 (api.Memory racing Module.Close) is open. The wazero pin is ambiguous (3 values) and the vs-wazero module needs cgo. Go wazero fork; off-baseline.

name: WebAssembly Micro Runtime (WAMR)
baseline: Wasmtime Pulley interpreter (A-tier numbers); Wasmtime, Wasmer and V8 JIT/AOT (libsodium suite)
workload: Interpreter-only comparison on the 17 Wasm cases every runtime runs (audio, graphql, DSP, MVP kernels), CPU time per call, N=10 per platform, Apple M4 Max E-cores and iPhone XS Max E-cores; WAMR configured as fast interpreter only.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time per call relative to the fastest runtime over the 17 cases all seven runtimes run (lower is better): M4 Max E-cores WAMR fast-interp 1.63 vs Wasmtime Pulley 2.09 and WasmEdge interpreter 8.42; iPhone XS (A12) E-cores 1.38 vs 1.68 and 9.28. About 1.28x faster than Pulley on the M4 and 1.22x on the A12 (derived from page data). Per case on M4 (CPU ms per call): bulk_memory 10.41 vs 22.14, call_indirect 18.48 vs 31.53, convolution 3.928 vs 5.883, sieve 0.5128 vs 0.7082. The harness repo's earlier docs/cross-runtime-pulley-vs-wamr.md (iPhone 12, 2026-05-15, Pulley with the author's phase-3 fusion patches) has WAMR 1.37-1.86x faster on call_indirect, xmrsplayer, graphql (AssemblyScript) and the vtable suite.
compiler_and_flags: WAMR main (WAMR-2.4.1-364, b70d708d, 2026-09-21) with 29 local patches, cmake Release -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12, INTERP=1 FAST_INTERP=1 AOT=0 JIT=0 FAST_JIT=0 SIMD=1 RELAXED_SIMD=1 BULK_MEMORY=1 TAIL_CALL=1 etc., WAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1; Pulley from wasmtime v49 fork (9 extra commits), rust nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS --cfg=pulley_tail_calls -C target-cpu=apple-a12, fat LTO, 1 CGU; Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0).
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (MacBook Pro, macOS 27.0); iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores (iOS 18.7.10)
tradeoffs: Configurable runtime (classic and fast interpreter, AOT via wamrc, Fast JIT, LLVM JIT); README lists small text sizes on cortex-m4f (about 58.9K fast interpreter, 56.3K classic interpreter, 29.4K AOT runtime). The fast interpreter is slower than wasm3 (1.63x vs 1.01x in the cited doc).
caveats: WAMR is itself a category baseline; listed for its measured wins over Wasmtime's Pulley interpreter and, in AOT mode, over JIT runtimes. The win is interpreter versus interpreter, not versus Wasmtime's native Cranelift JIT. Pulley is not ahead everywhere: it beats WAMR on fib (1.13 vs 1.38 relative on M4), fib_tail, tailcall_fsm and extconst_init. In the same harness WAMR is slower than wasm3 (1.63 vs 1.01 geomean) and level with wasmz (1.59 on M4, 1.63 on A12). The benchmarked WAMR is unreleased main (the latest release, 2.4.5, lacks 364 of those commits) carrying 29 patches by the benchmark author (legacy EH, relaxed SIMD, PROT_NONE linear memory), and the Pulley side is a fork with 9 extra commits (including call_indirect argument bundling). Only Apple Silicon E-cores measured. AOT evidence (derived from page data, reproduced by the verifier): in jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2022-12 libsodium CSVs (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2022-12/res/iwasm.csv with wasmtime.csv, wasmer-cranelift.csv, wasmer-llvm.csv, node.csv, native.csv) the iwasm geomean time over the 61 tests common to all six files is 0.665x Wasmtime, 0.688x Wasmer Cranelift, 0.794x Wasmer LLVM and 0.588x Node/V8, and 2.30x native; the CSVs do not say iwasm ran in AOT mode (inferred from magnitude; CPU and flags not in the repo, and no README for that run). In the wasmi-benchmarks suite (AMD EPYC 7763, execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test, date not stated) WAMR fast-interp is 17.07 vs Pulley 27.92, but behind Wasm3 16.51, Wasmz 15.89, Wasmi v2 12.40 and Silverfir-nano's interpreter 9.02. WAMR wiki (https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/wiki/Performance, i7-7700, GCC 7.5.0 -O3, 2020-09-01) compares only against wasm3 and native.

name: zwasm
baseline: wasmtime 43.0.1; wasmer 5.0.4; wazero 1.11.0; WasmEdge 0.16.1 (interpreter)
workload: End-to-end wall time of '<runtime> run <module>' (spawn, instantiate, execute WASI _start) with hyperfine on short TinyGo and ClojureWasm guests, plus peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l.
claimed_speedup: Startup-bound short workloads (mean ms): tinygo/fib zwasm-aot 2.0, interp 2.3, jit 2.8 vs wasmtime 7.2, wazero 7.1, wasmer 12.0, WasmEdge 16.5. Peak RSS on tinygo/fib: zwasm-aot 2.1 MB, jit 3.2, interp 2.7 vs wazero 8.7, wasmtime 13.3, WasmEdge 23.7, wasmer 27.5 ('4-12x less').
compiler_and_flags: zwasm built with Zig 0.16.0 (pinned in flake.nix) via zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; comparators wasmtime 43.0.1, wazero 1.11.0, wasmer 5.0.4, WasmEdge 0.16.1 pinned in flake.nix devShells.bench; hyperfine 5 runs plus 3 warmup; peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (Mac aarch64), one host
tradeoffs: Single-pass JIT, interpreter and AOT backends with Wasm 3.0 and WASI 0.2/0.3; small footprint and fast startup traded for peak throughput.
caveats: The win is cold-start latency and memory footprint only. The same doc shows the optimizing JITs ahead on sustained compute: wasmtime/wasmer/wazero beat zwasm-jit/aot by about 1.5-3.9x (shootout/fib2 zwasm-jit 1077 ms vs wasmtime 700 ms; matrix 343 vs 88 ms; base64 781 vs 57 ms, about 13.7x). The startup rows time a whole process (spawn + instantiate + run) on sub-10 ms guests, so they measure startup, not execution; the zwasm-aot row excludes its one-off compile step while comparator rows include their JIT compile, and the doc does not say whether wasmtime/wasmer compilation caches were on. Single host (Apple M4 Pro, macOS); wasmer only on aarch64-darwin. The independent harness at rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark (docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md, zwasm v2.7.0 with the JIT compiled out) puts zwasm's interpreter at a geomean 8.47x the fastest runtime's CPU time on M4 Max E-cores (wasm3 1.01, WAMR 1.63, WasmEdge 8.42). A fork's README (andypeng2015/zwasm) says the 'majority match or beat wasmtime' on 29 benchmarks, which the canonical benchmarks doc does not support. github.com/clojurewasm/zwasm (used by the rebecker harness) appears to be the project's earlier home. v1 line (frozen at v1.11.1) is MIT; v2 is Apache-2.0. Embeddable from C/C++ via the standard wasm-c-api.

name: evmone
baseline: go-ethereum (geth) built-in EVM interpreter
workload: Execution of five EVM contract benchmarks (erc20.approval-transfer, erc20.mint, erc20.transfer, snailtracer, ten-thousand-hashes) through the evm-bench runners.
claimed_speedup: evm-bench README table: sum of benchmark times evmone 66ms vs geth 235ms (README prints geth as 3.561x relative to evmone 1.000x); snailtracer 43ms vs 163ms; erc20.transfer 8.6ms vs 24.6ms; ten-thousand-hashes 2.4ms vs 13.2ms.
compiler_and_flags: evm-bench evmone runner: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (compiler not named), evmone 0.9.1 pulled via CPM; geth runner: `go run`, Go 1.19 module, go-ethereum v1.10.25
stars_or_usage: 979 stars; EVMC module usable as a geth plugin
tradeoffs: C++20 required. Exposes the EVMC API, uses intx for 256-bit arithmetic and ethash for Keccak. Two interpreters: Baseline (default, minimal JUMPDEST analysis) and Advanced (indirect call threading, expensive upfront bytecode analysis). Using it inside geth needs a geth build with EVMC support. ecrecover is implemented directly by evmone with degraded performance (README).
caveats: Evidence is the independent third-party evm-bench suite (ziyadedher/evm-bench, GPL-3.0, 225 stars, last commit 2024-03-19, renovate dependency bumps only). Its README states no hardware or compiler; the runners pin evmone 0.9.1 (Baseline interpreter, the default) and go-ethereum v1.10.25, both 2022 releases, so the table is several versions old. Each runner times only the contract call (deployment excluded), 5 runs per benchmark. The evmone runner executes against evmc::MockedHost (in-memory hash-map storage, fresh per run), while the geth runner goes through geth's full StateDB with access-list preparation and snapshot/revert on an in-memory database, so the storage-heavy erc20 rows charge geth for a state layer the evmone side mocks away; the compute-bound snailtracer row (43ms vs 163ms, about 3.8x derived from page data) is the fairest interpreter-to-interpreter comparison. Results are not cross-checked between runners beyond a success status. evmone's own geth-vs-evmone HackMD report (notes.ethereum.org, blocked here) was seen only as a search snippet: geomean evmone/Baseline 784M gas/s vs Geth 161M gas/s. The repo CHANGELOG has only self-comparisons (v0.9.0: Baseline 26% faster than 0.8.0 and 18% faster than Advanced on a 4.0 GHz Intel Haswell with Clang 15). The ipsilon/evmone repo was formerly ethereum/evmone. [retier] Independent evm-bench (ziyadedher/evm-bench, 2022 versions evmone 0.9.1 Baseline interpreter and go-ethereum v1.10.25, EVMC 10.0.0 London) with no CPU or compiler named; evmone runs on the evmc MockedHost while geth runs on a full StateDB, so the erc20 ratios are inflated and even snailtracer (3.8x) copies 11-slot spheres and 19-slot triangles from storage per ray. src/run.rs rounds each run to whole milliseconds before averaging (about 20% quantisation on the 2.4 ms and 5 ms rows) and snailtracer runs once. Open EIP-7702 consensus bugs (#1447-#1449, #1728) and state-root divergence (#1727). An EVM, not a wasm runtime.

name: hxcpp (Haxe C++ backend and runtime)
baseline: NekoVM and HashLink (HL/JIT) Haxe targets; also compared with Haxe's JVM/Java and JavaScript (Node) targets
workload: tong's gist 'Haxe benchmarks' (one results file, three revisions, last active 2025-09-20) running the HashLink repository's other/benchs suite (Startup, Anonymous, BinaryTrees, Fib, FloatArray, IntArray, Mandelbrot, NBodies) compiled from the same Haxe source to each target (js, cpp, cs, hl, java, lua, neko, php, python; hlc and jvm in the 2025 rerun). In the upstream runner each program is re-launched until 1 s of total time accumulates (first run discarded), the output is checked against the expected @:result value, the per-target Startup time is subtracted, and the mean is truncated to 0.01 s. 2018 run plus a September 2025 rerun in a comment.
claimed_speedup: tong's gist run of the HashLink other/benchs suite: cpp total 0.7166 s vs HashLink 5.678 s (7.9x) and Neko 27.16 s (37.9x) in 2018 (derived from page data); Node (about 0.45-0.53 s once the double-counted js rows are summed once) and the JVM match or beat cpp, so hxcpp is not the fastest Haxe target overall.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the gist. The upstream HashLink runner (other/benchs/Benchs.hx) compiles each benchmark with haxe -cpp cpp -main <name> -dce full -D HXCPP_SILENT -D HXCPP_GC_GENERATIONAL and leaves C++ compilation to hxcpp's default toolchain; the gist's own runner, which adds cs, java, lua, php and python targets, is not included in the gist, so its flags are unconfirmed.
hardware: 2018 run: Intel Core i5-6600 @ 3.9 GHz, 15959 MB, Arch Linux x86_64, kernel 4.17.2. 2025 rerun: AMD Ryzen 7 7700 @ 5.39 GHz, 32 GB, Arch Linux, kernel 6.16.8.
stars_or_usage: 329 stars; the C++ target of the Haxe compiler (3,138 commits)
tradeoffs: hxcpp is the runtime support for the Haxe C++ backend: Haxe source is compiled to C++ and then built by the platform C++ compiler, so builds are slow (about 2 s per small program in the gist versus 0.1 to 0.2 s for neko, hl, js) and need a C++ toolchain; it ships its own garbage collector and runtime library and has the cppia scripting host. Output is native code, so it is the fastest Haxe target on most of these rows but the language semantics follow Haxe, not C++.
caveats: The measurements are an individual's gist, not an official suite, and neither Haxe nor hxcpp versions, the C++ compiler or its flags are given, so the run is below tier A (the benchmark sources are public in HaxeFoundation/hashlink other/benchs, but the gist holds only results and its runner was extended beyond the upstream hl/hlc/js/neko/cpp target list). The suite comes from the HashLink repository, i.e. from the baseline's own project. The 2025 rerun lists no totals and shows hlc (HashLink's own C output) failing the result check on every benchmark ('result 0 but expected ...') and lua erroring on BinaryTrees, so hxcpp is never compared with HashLink/C, the AOT path closest to it. Even against HashLink the win is not on every row: HL/JIT beat cpp on Anonymous in 2018 (0.29 s versus 0.38 s). Against the other baselines the win is not clear: in 2018 JavaScript beat cpp on Anonymous (0.02 versus 0.38) and Java on BinaryTrees and Mandelbrot (0.06 versus 0.08, 0.12 versus 0.13), the totals put C++ 0.72 s next to Java 0.81 and JavaScript 0.96, and in the 2025 rows JVM and Node are faster than cpp on several rows (Anonymous 0.03 and 0.02 versus 0.1, BinaryTrees 0.02 versus 0.05, Mandelbrot 0.07 versus 0.13; derived from page data). Times are truncated to 0.01 s after startup subtraction, so many cells are 0 or 0.01 and small ratios are unreliable. The official HaxeBenchmarks site benchs.haxe.org exists but was blocked (EGRESS_BLOCKED), and its GitHub repo HaxeBenchmarks/benchs.haxe.org holds the site code, not result data. hxcpp is an AOT C++ backend and runtime rather than a VM, so the comparison is AOT against interpreters and JITs. name: WasmEdge
baseline: Wasmtime, Wasmer (Cranelift, LLVM, Singlepass), V8 (Node.js) and wazero
workload: libsodium benchmark suite, 2022-12 run: 61 tests with results for every listed runtime plus native.
claimed_speedup: README: 'the fastest Wasm VM' (backed by its authors' 2021 IEEE Software paper, not opened). 2022-12 libsodium suite (derived from page data, geomean of per-test time ratios over the 61 tests that also have a native result): WasmEdge 0.97x the time of Wasmtime (1.03x faster), 1.00x Wasmer Cranelift, 0.86x Node/V8 (1.17x faster), 0.31x Wasmer Singlepass, 0.21x wazero; 1.16x slower than Wasmer LLVM; 3.35x native, against 2.30x native for WAMR iwasm and 2.36x for WABT wasm2c, so WasmEdge is mid-pack, not fastest. 2026 rerun (Frank Denis, 'Performance of WebAssembly runtimes in 2026', search snippet only): WasmEdge with --run-mode=aot 1.74x native vs Wasmtime 46.0.0 2.41x and Wasmer 7.1.0 2.08x without wide arithmetic (about 1.39x faster than Wasmtime, derived from snippet numbers).
hardware: AMD Zen 2 cloud instance at Scaleway, tests pinned to one core, each test run 200 times (search snippet of the blocked 00f.net 2023-01-04 post; not stated in the repo)
tradeoffs: Speed needs the LLVM-based AOT compiler step; the interpreter mode is among the slowest: geomean 8.42x the fastest on the M4 Max E-cores (REB doc) and 145.74x vs 1.15x for Wasmtime Cranelift on EPYC 7763 in the wasmi-benchmarks execute plot. Large dependency footprint.
caveats: Parity with Wasmtime and Wasmer Cranelift only: the 3% edge over Wasmtime on the 61 native-comparable tests reverses to WasmEdge 1.07x slower than Wasmtime (and 1.05x slower than Wasmer Cranelift) when the 8 short tests without a native result are included (hash3, onetimeauth, secretbox, secretbox2, shorthash, siphashx24, stream3, stream4, where WasmEdge takes 2-3x longer, likely fixed per-run overhead). Slower than Wasmer LLVM (1.16x), WAMR iwasm (1.46x) and wasm2c (1.42x) in the same 2022-12 data, contradicting the README's 'fastest' claim; the README claim rests on a 2021 IEEE Software paper by WasmEdge's own authors that I could not open (IEEE blocked). The CSVs do not say WasmEdge ran AOT (implied by 3.35x native; the 2026 post had to force --run-mode=aot). The 2026 numbers are snippet only (00f.net blocked) and no 2026 results repo exists (jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks holds only 2021-Q1 and 2022-12 and is archived). In interpreter mode WasmEdge is the slowest of seven interpreters, 8.42x the fastest geomean on M4 Max E-cores (rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md). Compiler and flags unknown.

name: Wasmer (LLVM backend)
baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift) and V8 (Node.js)
workload: Libsodium's built-in crypto benchmark suite (about 70 primitives such as AEAD, hashes, signatures, box) compiled once to WASI and run in each runtime, December 2022 edition, wasmer with its LLVM compiler backend.
claimed_speedup: Frank Denis libsodium CSVs (2022-12, 69 rows): wasmer-llvm 0.872x wasmtime's time and 0.747x node's (0.841x and 0.753x on rows at or above 5000 units); against WasmEdge 0.819x overall but 1.031x (slower) on rows at or above 5000 and 1.104x above 100000, so the WasmEdge win rests on about 18 tiny rows; 0.858x of wasmer-cranelift (about 1.17x, 0.902x on rows at or above 5000), not the README's 50%. WAMR iwasm (1.277x faster, wins 68 of 69) and wasm2c are faster in the same data (derived from page data).
license: MIT (repository); BUSL-1.1 for the LLVM and Singlepass compiler crates from Wasmer 6.0
tradeoffs: The LLVM backend compiles far slower than Cranelift and needs a matching LLVM install (LLVM 22 now); for startup-sensitive use the Cranelift or Singlepass backends are the practical choices. Wasmer is a runtime with its own WASIX layer, not a drop-in for the Wasmtime embedding API.
caveats: Ratios are derived from the raw per-benchmark CSVs (wasmer-llvm.csv, wasmtime.csv, node.csv; values are libsodium's per-iteration times from test/default/cmptest.h, lower is better) in the author's benchmark repo (ISC, archived 2026-08-19), geometric mean over 69 shared rows. The 2022-12 folder has no README; the matching post (00f.net, 2023-01-04, blocked here, snippet only) says the runs used a Zen 2 CPU pinned to one core with each test run 200 times, but no exact CPU model, runtime versions or flags are reachable. Compile time is not part of the measured numbers (LLVM compile is far slower). In the same dataset WAMR's iwasm, a listed baseline, beats wasmer-llvm: wasmer-llvm takes 1.277x iwasm's time (faster on 1 of 69) and 1.171x wasm2c's time (faster on 10 of 70) (derived from page data), and the 2023 post (snippet only) names iwasm the top runtime; so wasmer-llvm beats Wasmtime and V8 but not WAMR AOT on this workload. Snippets of the author's 2026 posts (blocked) say Wasmer was the best performer with WAVM, WAMR and Wasmtime close, and that wasm2c used 0.887x Wasmer's time and 0.814x Wasmtime's (Wasmer about 8% faster than Wasmtime, derived from snippet data); not checked on the page. The win is specific to the LLVM backend (wasmer-cranelift ties Wasmtime at 1.02x, singlepass is 3.12x slower) and to this crypto-heavy workload. Wasmer is itself a named baseline; this entry is evidence that its LLVM backend beats Wasmtime's default and V8 on steady-state throughput. name: AssemblyScript (TypeScript-like to Wasm compiler)
baseline: JavaScript on V8 (Node.js v18.7.0), same n-body source compiled with tsc
workload: n-body simulation from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game (5 bodies, f64) in AssemblyScript Wasm, the same source transpiled to JavaScript with tsc, and a Rust Wasm version, timed inside Node.
claimed_speedup: No valid numeric win: the n-body README figure (Wasm 1,606 ms vs JS 11,640 ms, about 7.2x) compares against a tsc build whose class fields start as undefined (useDefineForClassFields), a 7x penalty reproduced by the enricher; corrected, plain JavaScript is roughly equal. LeanyLabs micro-benchmarks have JS winning 4 of 6.
compiler_and_flags: asc from the 'latest' npm package (exact version not stated), asconfig target wasm: optimizeLevel 3, shrinkLevel 0, converge, noAssert, runtime stub; Node v18.7.0 run with --nowasm-bounds-checks --nowasm-stack-checks --noliftoff --expose-gc; Rust Wasm built with rustc 1.64.0-nightly
hardware: MacBook Pro (15-inch, 2019), macOS 12.5.0 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Strictly typed TypeScript subset (no any, closures and many dynamic features unsupported or limited); compiles through Binaryen to Wasm with its own GC runtime (stub, minimal or incremental); calls across the JS and Wasm boundary are costly so only compute-heavy kernels win; code must be written in a numeric style (unchecked(), f64) to approach the quoted speed.
caveats: The compiler repository itself carries no benchmark numbers (README and tests contain none) and the project's website could not be opened. The only first-party number is one n-body example in the separate AssemblyScript/examples repo: single workload, unspecified CPU model, asc version 'latest' (package.json devDependency), and Node started with --nowasm-bounds-checks --nowasm-stack-checks --noliftoff, which favours the Wasm side. The README says 'npm test [steps=1000000]' while tests/index.js defaults to 20000000 steps, and the table does not say whether it is the cold or warmed-up series. The JavaScript side is the AssemblyScript source transpiled by tsc (unchecked() calls stripped), not an idiomatic JS n-body, and its 11640 ms looks anomalous: AssemblyScript issue 1326 (June 2020, AssemblyScript 0.10.0, Node 14.4.0, Windows 10, 20,000,000 steps) measured the same sample at JavaScript 3.0 s and AssemblyScript 5.6 s, the opposite result. Independent micro-benchmarks (LeanyLabs/assemblyscript-benchmarks, 7 stars, i5-8250, assemblyscript ^0.18.4, Node version not stated) show JavaScript winning four of six cases. A 2020 Iowa State University master's creative component ('Benchmarking AssemblyScript for Faster Web Applications', Ostrich suite numerical kernels on Chrome and Firefox) reportedly finds 1.1x to 7.2x speedups over JavaScript (search snippet only; host blocked; not peer-reviewed). The baseline is JavaScript running on V8, not another Wasm runtime; the emscripten C++ baseline from the lead was not found for this project. [retier] The only first-party comparison used a crippled JavaScript baseline plus Wasm-favouring Node flags (--nowasm-bounds-checks --nowasm-stack-checks --noliftoff), the stub runtime and --noAssert with unchecked() reads; no CPU model, asc 'latest'. name: aWsm
baseline: Wasmer; WAVM; Lucet; Node.js with Emscripten; wasm3 on microcontrollers
workload: PolyBench/C slowdown over native C, on x86-64, aarch64 (Raspberry Pi) and Cortex-M4/M7, for an ahead-of-time Wasm-to-LLVM compiler with a small C runtime.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 average slowdown over native: Wasmer 149.8%, WAVM 28.1%, Node.js + Emscripten 84.0%, Lucet 92.8%, aWsm 13.4%. aarch64: aWsm 6.7%. Cortex-M7 40.2% and M4 24.9%, versus 'more than 10x' for the wasm3 interpreter on microcontrollers (links wasm3's Performance.md).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the cross-runtime comparison. The repo's code_benches/run.py (native vs aWsm only) builds native code with clang -O3 and Wasm with wasi-sdk/wasmception clang -O3 -flto, then compiles aWsm's LLVM bitcode with clang -O3.
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler through LLVM, so compile latency; the runtime is under 5K lines of C and the compiler under 3.5K lines of Rust; output is ELF objects; seven selectable memory-bounds-check mechanisms. Not a fit where interpreters or JIT are required.
caveats: README says 'these numbers are from May 2020'; hardware, compiler versions and flags are not given in the README. baseline: state-of-the-art sharded execution (paper's cost baseline); no sequential revm or pevm comparison found
workload: bench-sendeth: replay of native ETH and ERC-20 transfer workloads (zero contention 'none', hot-account 'hotn', and replayed real-trace generators) over a 2^30-account QMDB database with Merkleization every block, using revm for execution on one many-core node; the README claims throughput scaling and a cost comparison.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Over 1 million Merkleized EVM-Compatible transactions per second while maintaining state verifiability'; 'Near-linear throughput scaling up to 96 cores and beyond on a single machine'; '91% cheaper than sharded execution'. Search-result text of the paper (arXiv 2507.10757): over 1.1 million native ETH transfers per second and over half a million ERC-20 transfers per second on a single node. No timing of sequential revm or pevm on the same workload is given in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.85.0 (rust-toolchain.toml); benchmark run with cargo run --release through bench-sendeth/run.sh (which exports RUSTFLAGS=-Awarnings); release profile opt-level 3, thin LTO, codegen-units 16, panic=abort; revm 20.0.0 and alloy 0.11.1 per workspace Cargo.toml. Paper reproduction commands: run.sh --size full with --generator none, hotn (--contention-degree 0.1 --skew 100) or replay.
hardware: Repo states none. Third-party article snippet (OAK Research, not opened): one AWS server with 96 vCPUs, 786 GiB DRAM and six NVMe SSDs in RAID0 (22.5 TB).
tradeoffs: A transaction scheduler and pipeline (ParaLyze address estimation, ParaFramer with ParaBloom Bloom filters to group non-conflicting transactions into frames, ParaScheduler precedence graphs) rather than a new EVM interpreter: it runs revm and QMDB underneath, so gains come from parallel scheduling of independent transfers and are bounded by contention. Needs a very large machine (the benchmark initialises a database with billions of accounts, and the README's Docker setup asks for at least 256 GB of virtual disk and 32 GB of memory). Synthetic transfer workloads; the repo is described as ongoing research.
caveats: Not a faster-than-baseline claim in the sense of the listed baselines: neither the README nor bench-sendeth compares against sequential revm or pevm on a common workload (the only comparison in the README is '91% cheaper than sharded execution', a cost figure against an unnamed baseline, with the methodology in LayerZero Labs' own paper, which is blocked here: layerzero.network, arxiv.org and emergentmind.com returned EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the paper's numbers come from search-result text only). The workloads are plain ETH and ERC-20 transfers, which is far easier to parallelise than general contract code; the paper is 'Under submission' (not peer reviewed) and is written by the vendor. The repo holds a single 'Initial commit' dated 2025-06-26, so there is no development history to check, and the 96-vCPU machine is only known from a third-party article snippet. bench-sendeth writes a metrics JSON per run but no published result file is in the repo. FAFO is a transaction scheduler and parallel execution pipeline on revm plus QMDB, not a bytecode VM, so the bytecode-vms-and-wasm filing is a loose fit. pevm and revm are catalogued separately, and Block-STM style comparison, if any, is in the unopened paper. [retier] First-party TPS and '91% cheaper than sharded' claims only, no sequential revm or pevm baseline, vendor preprint unreachable here. The bench harness hands precomputed write sets to 99% of ERC-20 transactions and all ETH transfers, runs with nonce checks disabled, nonce 0, gas price 0 and no signatures, skips the beneficiary reward, never checks results, and hard-codes thread pools, so the numbers are an upper bound. Transfer-only workloads; single commit 2025-06-26, stale; a transaction scheduler rather than a VM (loose category fit); Cargo.toml says MIT only.
