name: JerryScript
baseline: Duktape
workload: V8 benchmark suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run on JerryScript ESNext, QuickJS, Duktape and Node.js; the issue reports one peak-memory figure per engine plus per-benchmark scores.
claimed_speedup: Issue #4386 lists 'peak memory consumption' (labelled KB) of 239,664 for JerryScript ESNext vs 582,240 for Duktape and 5,523,792 for QuickJS (JerryScript about 2.4x less than Duktape, derived from page data). On speed JerryScript loses on every test: V8 TotalScore 250 vs Duktape 487 and QuickJS 1,042 (higher is better), per test vs Duktape Richards 173 vs 223, DeltaBlue 180 vs 282, Crypto 182 vs 385, RayTrace 291 vs 617, EarleyBoyer 408 vs 686, RegExp 155 vs 221, Splay 365 vs 1296, NavierStokes 398 vs 1073, so about 1.9x slower than Duktape overall (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: JerryScript: python tools/build.py --clean --lto=OFF --jerry-debugger=ON --jerry-cmdline=ON (issue text also lists snapshot execution, 512KB stack limit, 64MB GC mark limit). Duktape: gcc -O3 -DDUK_CMDLINE_CONSOLE_SUPPORT duktape.c duk_cmdline.c duk_console.c -lm -lc -o duk. QuickJS: qjs combined.js. Compiler versions not stated.
tradeoffs: Footprint-first design: runs on devices with under 64 KB RAM and 200 KB flash, 258K binary on ARM Thumb-2, written in C99, snapshot support for precompiled bytecode. Full ECMAScript 5.1 compliance, about 70% of ECMAScript 2025 per README. The small footprint is bought with speed.
caveats: The only numeric comparison reachable is a third-party GitHub issue (#4386, opened 2020-12-29 by lygstate, still open with the discussion label, no replies), not project-authored. It shows JerryScript slower than Duktape on all eight V8 tests and much slower than QuickJS; the claim that holds is memory only (README: 'Heavily optimized for low memory consumption'). The peak-memory row is not credible as labelled: Node.js and Node.js Jitless share the identical 73,873,464 'KB' (about 70 GB) and QuickJS shows 5.5 GB, so the unit or method is wrong (as bytes the figures would be plausible), and no measurement method, hardware or compiler version is given. The JerryScript build used --system-allocator=ON (malloc instead of its compact heap), --cpointer-32bit=ON, --jerry-debugger=ON and --lto=OFF, so neither its memory nor its speed reflects a footprint-tuned build. Counter-evidence from the independent ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark CI (V8 v7 suite, 10/5/2026): JerryScript 3.0.0 completes only Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto and RayTrace (no total score) and is slower than Duktape 2.99.99 on all four on ubuntu (273/276/301/344 vs 288/315/783/584) and macos-arm64 (205/229/261/337 vs 538/632/1257/1032), and its executable is larger there (454.2K vs 370.4K on ubuntu); build configurations differ. Samsung's first-party slides (SunSpider 1.0.2 max RSS on Raspberry Pi 2, JerryScript 1.0 vs Duktape 1.5.1) report lower RSS for JerryScript, e.g. 3d-cube 35 vs 125 KB, 3d-raytrace 185 vs 339 KB, access-binary-trees 38 vs 160 KB, crypto-md5 142 vs 261 KB, but slideshare and summit.riot-os.org were blocked, so these come from a search snippet only. Last commit 2025-10-08 is one day inside the 12-month active window (the previous commit was 2025-06-03), so it turns stale on 2026-10-09. [retier] Memory win only, from third-party issue #4386 (no method; built with --system-allocator=ON, which the configuration docs call unsupported on 64-bit, architecture unstated; peak-memory units impossible, Node 73,873,464 'KB'). Slower than Duktape on all 8 V8 tests (250 vs 487); in the ahaoboy CI the stock build (tools/build.py, fixed 512 KB heap) scores nothing on EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay and NavierStokes, and 3.0.0 fails 4 of 8 tests. name: Lua-CSharp
baseline: NLua (C# binding to native Lua) and MoonSharp (Lua interpreter in C#)
workload: add.lua loop calling a host C# add(x, 1) function 25,001 times (for _ = 0, 25000), timed through DoString/DoFile so script compilation is included; time and managed allocation per invocation (sandbox/Benchmark/AddBenchmark.cs).
claimed_speedup: 8.05 ms vs NLua 36.45 ms and MoonSharp 19.87 ms (about 4.5x and 2.5x faster, derived from page data); allocation 31.3 KB vs NLua 12,306.5 KB and MoonSharp 13,887 KB.
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet 0.14.0 ShortRun job with 10 warmup and 10 measured iterations and MemoryDiagnoser, target net8.0 (sandbox/Benchmark/Benchmark.csproj); baselines MoonSharp 2.0.0 and NLua 1.7.3 NuGet packages; build configuration and runtime used for the chart not stated
tradeoffs: Pure managed C# implementation (works in AOT and Unity, no native dependency, no IL generation) but not every Lua standard library function is supported (see its Compatibility section); strings are UTF-16.

The workload measures host-call interop overhead (NLua marshals through reflection-registered methods into native Lua), not Lua execution speed, so it says nothing about Lua-CSharp's VM versus PUC Lua; the repo has an NBodyBenchmark with no published numbers. A .NET library, not callable from C++. First-party numbers. Asymmetric: Lua-CSharp uses a hand-written stack callback while NLua gets a MethodInfo reflection call (RegisterFunction) and MoonSharp an auto-converted Func; [IterationSetup] forces one invocation per iteration on 8-36 ms runs, below BenchmarkDotNet's recommended minimum. Issue #156 (Unity Mono): C# calling Lua ran 40 fps on 0.4.2 against NLua 170 and MoonSharp 315 (395 on an unofficial 0.5 build). name: LuaBridge3
baseline: Sol3 (sol2) and vanilla LuaBridge (C++ Lua binding overhead over the plain Lua C API)
workload: Per-operation binding overhead in nanoseconds across 34 cases (global and table get/set, chained table access, free, member, static and derived method calls, userdata properties, shared-pointer ownership, multi-return, lambda captures, optionals, converters), Google Benchmark, all three libraries on embedded Lua 5.4.8, each case in isolation.
claimed_speedup: README chart Images/benchmarks.png (ns per operation, lower is better, 34 cases): against Sol3, LuaBridge3 is faster on 20 of 30 shared cases (member function call 152.4 vs 356.9, derived method call 91.8 vs 260.5, c function 44.2 vs 116.2, static member function call 88.4 vs 212.1, shared ptr pass 61.7 vs 123.2, userdata property getter 86.4 vs 165.5, userdata variable write 79.7 vs 161.2), slower on 9 (table get 29.1 vs 17.9, table chained get 69.6 vs 28.0, table chained set 56.5 vs 26.8, table global string get 39.7 vs 11.9, table set 18.3 vs 17.2, multi return 49.7 vs 44.8, stateful function object 40.0 vs 37.4, c function through lua in c 40.4 vs 34.3, lua function in c 26.8 vs 25.7) and tied on optional failure (14.3). Against vanilla LuaBridge it is faster on 12 of 22 shared cases (table get 29.1 vs 57.1, optional success 26.8 vs 110.0, table chained get 69.6 vs 156.7) and slower on 10 (c function 44.2 vs 34.3, member function call 152.4 vs 148.7, static member function call 88.4 vs 60.9, lambda capture 45.1 vs 32.8, multi return lua 48.3 vs 33.0, return userdata 167.2 vs 142.0). The headline userdata variable access rows (70.2 vs Sol3 299.9 and vanilla 269.3) are not like-for-like: LuaBridge3's script does one read, the other two do two reads and a write. Win/loss counts derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build (Benchmarks/README.md), Google Benchmark v1.8.4, Lua 5.4.8 sources compiled into each executable; Sol3 built with SOL_ALL_SAFETIES_ON=1 and SOL_NO_EXCEPTIONS=1. No LTO flag is set in the CMake files despite the README's link-time-optimization wording; compiler and compiler version not stated.
tradeoffs: Dependency-free binding that works with PUC Lua, LuaJIT, Luau and Ravi; supports many C++17/20/23 std types, lambdas and multiple inheritance; works with or without exceptions.
caveats: First-party chart only, embedded as an image (Images/benchmarks.png); no hardware, compiler or compiler version stated. Harness is not like-for-like: (1) userdata variable access, access large and access last run 'return b.var' for LuaBridge3 but 'b.var = b.var + 1.0 return b.var' (two reads plus a write) for Sol3 and vanilla LuaBridge, so the largest claimed wins (70.2 vs 299.9 ns) compare one operation against three; (2) LuaBridge3 and vanilla cases invoke the Lua script with raw lua_getglobal + lua_pcall while every Sol3 script case goes through sol's lua["name"]() proxy lookup and call each iteration, adding C++-side overhead only to Sol3 (Sol3 c function 116.2 vs c function through lua in c 34.3, a gap of about 82 ns that LuaBridge3 does not show, 44.2 vs 40.4; rough inference derived from page data). On cases that use each library's own C++ API on both sides (table get/set, chained, global get, multi return, stateful function object), Sol3 is mostly faster. Vanilla LuaBridge beats LuaBridge3 on 10 of 22 shared cases, mostly call paths. Sol2 version is ambiguous: Benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt pins v3.3.0 while Benchmarks/README.md says v3.5.0, and vanilla LuaBridge is fetched from master. README says it 'competes directly with sol2', not that it beats it. Baseline (other binding libraries) is not in the category list (Lua, Duktape, QuickJS). Derived from vinniefalco/LuaBridge per README.
found_via: WebSearch: 'embeddable scripting language C++ faster than Lua benchmark github' (Lua binding results); README and benchmarks.png fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com

verification.notes: Numbers in the record match the chart, but the claim is overstated: the biggest wins (userdata variable access 70.2 vs 299.9/269.3 ns) time one property read for LuaBridge3 against a read-modify-write-read for Sol3 and vanilla, and every Sol3 script case pays an extra lua["name"]() proxy call that the LuaBridge3 harness avoids with raw lua_pcall. Keep at C with harness flaws documented; it is slower than vanilla LuaBridge on 10 of 22 shared cases and slower than Sol3 on most C++-side table cases.

name: Luau
baseline: PUC Lua 5.x interpreter (Lua 5.1 to 5.4)
workload: Interpreter dispatch loop, table library, string library and garbage collector sweep, as described in the project's performance guide.
claimed_speedup: borisbat/dasProfile (Luau 0.736 -O2 vs Lua 5.5.1, Clang 19): Luau faster on 12 of 16 kernels, geomean 1.51x on a Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE and 1.56x on an M1 Max (derived from page data); about 1.4x without the sha256 kernel and about 1.25x without float2string as well (see caveats). Loses integer loops: primes 0.151 s vs 0.059 s. Luau's own performance guide gives ratios only (table.sort about 4x, table insert/remove/move 3x, paged GC sweeper 2-3x).
compiler_and_flags: dasProfile: Clang 19, Luau built -O2, Lua 5.5.1 built with its upstream Makefile; rochus-keller AWFY: GCC 12.2.0 (the Luau guide tunes the interpreter for Clang and MSVC)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE and Apple M1 Max (dasProfile); AWFY run by rochus-keller on an i5-8350U
stars_or_usage: 5.9k stars; scripting layer of Roblox, also adopted in commercial games per README
tradeoffs: Derived from Lua 5.1 with its own type annotations and a sandboxing model (safeenv via luaL_sandbox) that the fastest paths rely on; API mostly Lua 5.1 compatible with caveats; interpreter-first design, JIT/native codegen is optional and not available everywhere.
caveats: First-party documentation page with ratios but no workload list, hardware, compiler flags or raw numbers, so tier C. The interpreter claim ('noticeably faster than Lua 5.x ... Lua 5.4 ... doesn't come close') has no number; the ~4x table.sort figure names no baseline; table insert/remove/move 3x is 'compared to un-tuned versions'; the 50+% table length gain is versus the default binary search computed from scratch. The repo has bench/ (bench.py with --compare for other VMs, micro_tests, gc) but no checked-in result tables. Several gains (fastcall builtins, imports) require the sandboxed pure global environment and are deoptimized by loadstring/getfenv/setfenv. Independent data point against a different baseline: rochus-keller/Are-we-fast-yet Luau/Results.pdf (14 Are-we-fast-yet benchmarks, i5-8350U, GCC 12.2.0, Luau commit 5836a9c, make config=release, 2025-10-25) gives geomean factors relative to LuaJIT 2.1 JIT of 2.39 for Luau default, 2.31 for -g0 -O2, 1.64 for -O2 --codegen, versus 2.32 for LuaJIT -joff; that is, the Luau interpreter is roughly at LuaJIT interpreter speed (about 3% slower), with no PUC Lua 5.x column. [retier] dasProfile is run by the Daslang lead (independent of Luau). Its Lua sha256 kernel fakes bit32 with loaded closures inside variadic select() wrappers while Luau calls bit32 builtins directly, so the 5.5x sha256 gap is mostly different code; float2string prints different strings. Luau has no integer type and loses integer loops. The rochus-keller Are-we-fast-yet Results.pdf (i5-8350U, GCC 12.2.0) puts the Luau interpreter level with LuaJIT -joff (geomean 2.39 vs 2.32) with no PUC Lua column. luau.org blocked here.

name: MuJS
baseline: goja (Go JavaScript interpreter); also Boa (Rust) and Jint (.NET) JavaScript interpreters in the same table
workload: V8 v7 benchmark suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run once per engine per daily GitHub Actions job through each engine's CLI; base.js times every benchmark in-process (one warm-up Measure, then at least 1 s and 32 runs), and Score is the geometric mean of the per-benchmark scores, higher is better.
claimed_speedup: V8 v7 overall Score, README snapshot 10/11/2026 (higher is better; MuJS reported as version 1.3.8): ubuntu MuJS 435 vs goja 365, Boa 279, Jint 246 (1.19x, 1.56x, 1.77x, derived from page data); macos-arm64 MuJS 522 vs goja 358, Boa 302, Jint 239 (1.46x, 1.73x, 2.18x, derived from page data); windows MuJS 339 vs goja 229, Jint 159 (1.48x, 2.13x, derived from page data; Boa has no score there). The same tables put MuJS below the category incumbents Duktape (682 / 842 / 371) and QuickJS (1522 / 1672 / 1105).

caveats: Nobody at the MuJS project claims this win; it is read off an automated third-party leaderboard (ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark, 59 stars, regenerated daily, one run per engine per day on shared GitHub Actions runners whose CPU model is not stated). The only engines MuJS beats are interpreters written in other languages (goja in Go, Boa in Rust, Jint in .NET, plus es5, quickjs-oxide, xst and ringo); the category incumbents Duktape (about 1.57x, 1.61x and 1.09x faster on ubuntu, macos-arm64 and windows, derived from page data) and QuickJS (about 3.2-3.5x faster) beat it on every platform, so MuJS is not faster than the usual C embeddable JavaScript engines. Score excludes process startup and CLI-wrapper overhead (base.js times in-process after a warm-up); only the Time(s) row includes it. The README rows align with the engine columns (MuJS's eight per-test values 310, 397, 241, 620, 534, 251, 818, 640 give the 435 Score as a geometric mean, derived from page data). name: Pallene
baseline: PUC-Rio Lua 5.4 interpreter (the Lua 5.4 bundled with Pallene in 2020); LuaJIT and C in the same post
workload: Independent blog: n-queens counter xdamcnt2 (N up to 12, non-recursive, code in github.com/eklausme/c) and an array-of-records float update loop (N=4000, S=1000), each in Pallene, Lua and C. Paper (snippet only): binarytrees, binsearch, centroid, conway, matmul, queen, sieve and others from the repo benchmarks directory.
claimed_speedup: Klausmeier blog (2020): n-queens Pallene 0.32 s (0.31 s with compiler optimization flags) vs Lua 5.4 3.92 s (about 12x, derived from page data; the post says 13x) and vs LuaJIT 0.58 s (about 1.8x, derived from page data), C -O3 0.2 s; array loop Pallene 0.14 s vs Lua 5.4 0.72 s (about 5x, derived from page data), but LuaJIT 0.07 s is 2x faster than Pallene there. Paper (SBLP 2018 / SCP 2020, search snippets only): around ten times faster than Lua on Sieve and Queens, comparable to LuaJIT; more than three times faster than LuaJIT and the Lua-C API on binary search; LuaJIT substantially faster only on Matmul (NaN-boxing gives 8-byte floats vs 16 bytes in Lua and Pallene).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.3.0 on Arch Linux 5.6.6; the C reference built with -march=native -O3; Pallene and Lua 5.4 build flags not stated (a second Pallene run 'with compiler optimization flags' does not name them)
hardware: AMD FX-8120 eight-core, 3.1 GHz max (blog); paper hardware unknown
tradeoffs: Statically typed, ahead-of-time compiled sister language of Lua (README); output is a C extension module, so a C compiler is needed at build time and the code is loaded through require; it is a companion for hot paths, not a replacement interpreter.
caveats: Independent numbers are from one 2020 blog post on two small programs with a 2020 Pallene (older syntax) and an AMD FX-8120; Pallene and Lua flags unstated. LuaJIT beats Pallene 2x on the array-of-records loop and, per the paper snippets, on Matmul. The peer-reviewed papers (inf.puc-rio.br, ScienceDirect, ReadKong mirror) and the 2020 PhD thesis are EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so paper numbers are snippet only. The README gives no figures and the repo benchmarks directory has code (benchmarks/run, benchlib.lua) but no results. Pallene is a Lua companion language compiled to C Lua modules, not a C/C++ library.

claimed_speedup: Between 0.60x and 1.19x of the C interpreter's time: faster on sort (0.250 s vs 0.418 s, 0.60x), loops (0.375 s vs 0.521 s, 0.72x), coroutines (0.158 s vs 0.192 s, 0.82x) and nbody (0.612 s vs 0.686 s, 0.89x); parity (1.00-1.03x) on binarytrees, closures, fannkuch, fib, tables; slower on json (1.15x), spectralnorm (1.19x) and strings (1.19x).

name: sol2
baseline: Other C++ Lua binding libraries (LuaBridge, OOLua, Kaguya, luwra, Selene, SWIG, tolua++ and others); floor is the plain Lua C API
workload: Per-operation overhead of binding layers over the Lua C API (member function call, userdata variable access, table get/set, multi-return and others) measured with nonius in the lua-bindings-shootout repo.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Fastest in the land (see: sol2 bar in graph)'; benchmarks page: sol 'seems to take the cake in most categories for speed'. The page has graphs only, no numeric table.
compiler_and_flags: All libraries compiled against a DLL build of Lua 5.3.3, no link-time optimization (per page); compiler and flags otherwise not stated
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 binding for Lua, LuaJIT and others; heavy template use means long compile times; its fast paths (c_call and disabled type checks) trade safety for speed.
caveats: Evidence is first-party graphs from 2018 (page dated May 17th, 2018) from the author's own lua-bindings-shootout (nonius, Lua 5.3.3 DLL per the docs page; shootout README lists plain C on Lua 5.3.4, sol2 v2.20.0 and sol3 'latest'); no numbers in text and no hardware, compiler or flags stated. Approximate values read off benchmark_results/member function call.png: plain_c about 115 ns, sol3 about 135, oolua about 145, sol2 about 150, luwra about 205, luabridge about 420, old sol about 425, toluapp about 590 (read from the image, not text). Third-party counter-evidence: satoren/lua_binding_benchmark result/result.csv (Intel Core i5-4460, GCC 5.3.1, CMake Release, units not stated, lower is better) puts sol2 v2.5.1 fastest among bindings on global table (338.4) and table chain (561.0, below plain API 596.5), but behind kaguya (1006.9), luacppinterface (1002.0) and the plain API (1086.6) on C++ object member call (sol2 1342.9), behind luwra on C function call (234.7 vs 254.8) and returning a class object (1253.3 vs 1314.4), and behind sol v1 on Lua function call (293.4 vs 330.0). A 2026 first-party chart in the LuaBridge3 README shows Sol3 slower than LuaBridge3 on most script-invoked cases (member function call 356.9 vs 152.4 ns) but faster on C++-side table get/set; that harness is biased against Sol3 (extra lua["name"]() call per iteration, unequal userdata access scripts). Binding-layer overhead, not script execution speed; every binding is slower than the plain Lua C API. Baseline (other binding libraries) is not in the category list (Lua, Duktape, QuickJS). Last commit 2025-03-07, so stale.

name: SWIG
baseline: SWIG's own default Python proxy-class wrappers (same tool, default code generation mode)
workload: Per-call overhead, in microseconds, of calling three member functions of a trivial C++ class Go from Python through SWIG-generated wrappers: callme0() with no arguments, callme4() with four ints, callme8() with eight doubles; default proxy classes vs the -fastproxy option vs the -builtin option.
claimed_speedup: Default 0.15 / 0.26 / 0.32 us; -fastproxy 0.09 / 0.16 / 0.20 us (about 1.6-1.7x lower, derived from page data); -builtin 0.07 / 0.14 / 0.17 us (about 1.9-2.1x lower, derived from page data). Manual text: '-builtin ... significant performance improvement in the wrapped code'.
tradeoffs: -fastproxy makes generated proxy classes less user-friendly (docstrings, annotations and default arguments are not visible) and is ignored for methods with %pythonprepend-style extra code; -builtin replaces proxy classes with built-in types and does not use the Python limited API. Both are Python-only options; the per-call numbers are for Python, other target languages have no comparable table.
caveats: The baseline is SWIG's own default proxy-class mode, not another binding tool: the manual makes no numeric comparison against SIP, pybind11, Boost.Python, nanobind or Cython, and two WebSearches for third-party SWIG call-overhead numbers found none (nanobind's and pybind11's benchmark pages do not include SWIG). The manual itself says the overhead is 'reduced slightly' with -fastproxy. No hardware, compiler, Python version, repeat count or harness is given for the table; no benchmark script was found for it (Examples/python/performance returns 404). Trade-offs from the same manual: -fastproxy (also turned on by -O) hides docstrings, Python annotations and default argument values in the generated proxy class unless -olddefs is added, it is silently ignored for methods that use %pythonprepend or similar additions, and -builtin and -fastproxy do not work with Py_LIMITED_API. Another table in the same manual shows the -threads option slowing the profiletest.i run (single threaded 9.6 s vs fully multithreaded 15.5 s, about 60% slower). LICENSE: the SWIG tool is GPL-3.0-or-later with portions under LICENSE-UNIVERSITIES; the Lib and Examples directories (the runtime code copied into generated wrappers) are under a permissive grant ('copy, modify, distribute ... without restriction'). The lead's statement that the generated output is not covered by the GPL was not independently verified here.

name: yklua (Yk JIT retrofitted into PUC Lua)
language: C (Lua interpreter) with the Rust Yk JIT
baseline: PUC-Rio Lua 5.5.0 (stock lua.org tarball, the version yklua is based on) built with -flto as an LTO baseline
workload: ykjit/yk-benchmarks nightly ReBench suite: 14 Are-We-Fast-Yet Lua benchmarks, 4 Computer Language Benchmarks Game programs (fannkuchredux, spectralnorm, knucleotide, binarytrees), 3 real-world programs (LuLPeg, HashIds, Heightmap) and the in-house BigLoop; 5 process invocations x 10 in-process iterations each, yklua vs stock Lua 5.5.0.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean execution-time ratio yklua/Lua of 0.513 (about 1.95x faster) over 22 benchmarks in the 2026-10-06 11:14 nightly run (index lists 0.504 to 0.519 for the last 10 runs). Per-benchmark mean iteration times from that run's data file (derived from page data): Mandelbrot(500) 370.2 ms vs 63.4 ms (5.84x), BigLoop 3.90x, spectralnorm 3.30x, Heightmap 3.18x, Sieve 3.01x, NBody 2.88x, fannkuchredux 2.33x, Queens 2.15x, Permute 2.08x, Bounce 1.99x, Towers 1.81x, LuLPeg 1.71x, Richards 1.59x, Json 1.52x, knucleotide 1.47x, List 1.37x, CD 1.36x, HashIds 1.35x, binarytrees 1.33x, Storage 1.23x, DeltaBlue 1.11x, Havlak 1.09x; geomean without the in-house BigLoop loop about 1.89x (derived from page data). Laurence Tratt's 2026 blog post reports 'a geometric mean speedup of a little under 2x' with about 400 lines added and under 50 changed in PUC Lua (snippet only); the Mandelbrot 3.2 s to 0.8 s figure in the original record was not found on any page opened.
compiler_and_flags: Baseline: Lua 5.5.0 stock Makefile (gcc -std=gnu99, -O2 in yklua's copy of the same Makefile) with MYCFLAGS=-flto; yklua: ykllvm (yk's LLVM/clang fork) via yk-config release --cflags --cppflags, -O2, -DUSE_YK -DLUA_USE_JUMPTABLE=0 (ykjit/yk-benchmarks common.sh, ykjit/yklua src/Makefile). gcc version not stated.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7F52 16-Core Processor (host bencher14), Debian kernel 6.12.57, recorded in the rebench results file
license: MIT (PUC-Rio Lua notice in src/lua.h and doc/readme.html); no repository-level LICENSE file covering the Yk additions
tradeoffs: Needs the Yk JIT built separately (README); marked experimental; the README says the test suite is currently failing for non-serialised compilation; tracks upstream PUC Lua instead of being stuck at Lua 5.1 like LuaJIT.
caveats: Experimental (README says so) and not drop-in: building needs the yk toolchain (Rust nightly, ykllvm, yk-config). Means include JIT warm-up iterations; gains are uneven (DeltaBlue 1.11x, Havlak 1.09x, Storage 1.23x) and the 5.84x Mandelbrot and 3.90x BigLoop results are loop-heavy microbenchmarks. Baseline and yklua are built by different compilers (gcc -O2 -flto vs ykllvm clang), and yklua disables Lua's jump-table dispatch. Results come from a rolling nightly snapshot on the gh-pages branch (force-pushed each run), so the cited data file may be replaced. Blog figures (under 2x geomean, about 400 lines added, does not reach LuaJIT's peak performance) are snippet only since tratt.net and infoq.com are blocked. No LICENSE file at the repo root: the Lua core carries PUC-Rio's MIT notice but the Yk-specific changes have no stated licence.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Yk meta-tracing JIT retrofitted Lua interpreter yklua speedup paper'

name: Zef
baseline: QuickJS-ng 0.14.0 (release binary qjs-linux-x86_64), Lua 5.4.7 (built with GCC 11.4.0), CPython 3.10 (Ubuntu 22.04 package)
workload: ScriptBench1 run by run-benchmarks: nbody (5000 advance steps), splay (32 runs on an 8000-node tree), richards (one run with COUNT 10000 in the Zef, Lua and Python ports, but 20 runs in richards.js) and deltablue (20 rounds of chainTest(100) plus projectionTest(100); the JS port adds one extra projectionTest). Wall-clock seconds of the whole process including interpreter startup, averaged over randomly interleaved runs (write-up says 30; the script defaults to --repeat 3), with a geomean row.
claimed_speedup: Write-up 'Raw Data' table, which matches run-benchmarks-results-1776652178.csv, gives geomean seconds: CPython 3.10 0.1296, Lua 5.4.7 0.0577, QuickJS-ng 0.14.0 0.2036, Zef Fil-C++ build #21 (no asserts) 0.2759, Zef in Yolo-C++ 0.0686. The author's table states Yolo-C++ Zef is 1.889x faster than CPython, 1.189x slower than Lua and 2.968x faster than QuickJS-ng; the memory-safe Fil-C++ build is 2.13x slower than CPython, 4.781x slower than Lua and 1.355x slower than QuickJS-ng. Per row, Yolo-C++ Zef beats QuickJS-ng on splay (0.3992 vs 0.7090), richards (0.0309 vs 0.7193) and deltablue (0.0784 vs 0.1585) but not nbody (0.0233 vs 0.0214); it beats CPython on all four rows and Lua only on splay and deltablue. The QuickJS-ng richards figure covers 20 runs of the benchmark (ScriptBench/richards.js loops runRichards() 20 times) while the Zef, Lua and Python ports run it once; dividing that row by 20 gives about 0.036 s per run, so Yolo-C++ Zef is about 1.16x faster on richards and about 1.40x faster than QuickJS-ng on the geomean, not 2.97x (derived from page data). The write-up's own headline is a 16x speed-up (67x with the Yolo-C++ port) that brings the interpreter 'into the ballpark' of QuickJS, CPython and Lua.
compiler_and_flags: Fast column: Yolo-C++ build with GCC 11.4.0 (write-up); meson.build sets buildtype=debugoptimized (-O2 -g), cpp_std=c++20, -fno-exceptions, -fno-rtti, -D_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_NONE. The exact configure command and source revision of the pizlscript/yoloBuild directory are not stated. Memory-safe columns: Fil-C++ 0.677 (write-up; README asks for 0.678 or later) with the same meson.build.
hardware: Intel Core Ultra 5 135U, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04.5
tradeoffs: AST-walking interpreter (NaN boxing, stack-frame slots, watchpoints, inline caches, no bytecode or JIT); the fast numbers need the memory-unsafe Yolo-C++ build, while the Fil-C++ build the README documents is memory-safe but 4.8x slower than Lua (derived from page data). Standalone interpreter with no documented embedding API; no GC-pause or memory data given.
caveats: First-party, four benchmarks only. The QuickJS-ng richards column runs 20x the work of the other ports, inflating the QuickJS-ng comparison (about 1.40x rather than 2.97x after correction, derived from page data). The fast Yolo-C++ build is, in the author's words, an incomplete and unsound port: GC allocations become calloc and memory is never freed, which only survives because the benchmarks are short; it was built from a separate checkout (pizlscript/yoloBuild) whose revision is not stated. The memory-safe Fil-C++ build documented in the README is slower than all three baselines. Wall-clock timing includes process startup, and several rows run only 14-40 ms. Splay's Python and Lua ports were written with Claude; the Lua richards check uses 'or' instead of 'and'. No LICENSE file (LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt and COPYING return 404) and the README names no licence, hence reference only. The write-up is checked into the repo at website/source/implementation.md, so its text was read directly.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (query '"How to make a fast dynamic language interpreter" Zef Show HN', plus the earlier restricted query 'Show HN tiny fast interpreter dynamic language register VM benchmark fib faster than Python Lua Wren') surfaced the thread 'How to make a fast dynamic language interpreter' (item 47843194); thread and blog could not be opened, numbers taken from the repo CSV.

verification.tier_reason: Benchmark code (run-benchmarks, ScriptBench/*.zef/.js/.py/.lua) and interpreter source are public, and the in-repo write-up (website/source/implementation.md) states the CPU (Intel Core Ultra 5 135U), GCC 11.4.0 for the Yolo-C++ build, with meson.build giving debugoptimized plus -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti, which is close to A. It stays at C because the fast column is a separate, undocumented checkout (pizlscript/yoloBuild) of what the author calls an incomplete, unsound port, and the QuickJS richards script runs 20x the work of the other ports, so the first-party comparison is not a clean run against the baseline.
verification.notes: Numbers match the CSV and the in-repo write-up, but the 2.97x win over QuickJS-ng is inflated because ScriptBench/richards.js runs runRichards() 20 times while the other ports run it once; corrected it is about 1.40x (derived). The fast build is an incomplete Yolo-C++ port that never frees memory (author calls it unsound), and the memory-safe Fil-C++ build is slower than CPython, Lua and QuickJS-ng. Kept at C with no licence (reference); not a reject because the CPython and Lua comparisons are like-for-like and the author documents the flaws.

name: Zipp (Rust JavaScript and Python VM)
baseline: QuickJS-NG v0.16.2 (maintained QuickJS fork) for the interpreter; Node.js, Bun and Deno for the JIT builds
workload: Frozen 'real13' set of 13 JavaScript programs and a 5-program micro set run as fresh processes (six counterbalanced repetitions, 10,000-sample bootstrap, exact-output checks) against pinned QuickJS-NG and Boa builds on one Windows x86-64 host; separate canonical captures against Node, Bun and Deno.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter (ZIPP_NOJIT=1) vs QuickJS-NG v0.16.2 on real13: v0.0.5 startup-adjusted geomean 0.6413x of QuickJS-NG's time (cold 0.6439x; 12 of 13 point wins; about 1.56x faster, derived from page data); v0.0.6 at e3acee352074 cold 0.6090x and startup-adjusted 0.6058x (13 of 13 wins; about 1.64x faster, derived from page data). micro5 vs QuickJS-NG: 0.8556x startup-adjusted (5 of 5). With JITs on, vs Node v24.12.0 / Bun 1.3.14 / Deno 2.6.10 (canonical PGO capture at 8229b3fc): 0.728x / 0.594x / 0.460x across all 30 rows; 0.614x / 0.531x / 0.521x on the 13 normal rows; 0.878x / 0.752x / 0.765x on the retained ten without the three architecture diagnostics; hostile 17 0.829x Node. Median launch 7.4 ms vs Node 30.4 ms, Bun 43.3 ms, Deno 82.6 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Zipp: Rust/Cargo 1.92.0, repository release profile (opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, aborting panics), default features, no extra RUSTFLAGS and no PGO for the QuickJS-NG and Boa runs; the Node/Bun/Deno capture used a Windows PGO build via tools/pgo.sh. QuickJS-NG: official v0.16.2 release binary qjs-windows-x86_64.exe (SHA-256 7b27412de844403545bd151fbe49191b4d5b91a9e15b5db7c863fea54639a82b), built by upstream CI under MSYS2 UCRT64 in CMake Release mode with static mimalloc; exact compiler package revision not stamped.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D, Windows 11 (bench/comparison/README.md); the raw canonical JSON reports platform 'Windows-10-10.0.26200-SP0', processor 'AMD64 Family 26 Model 68 Stepping 0, AuthenticAMD'
tradeoffs: Embeds as a Rust library or runs in the browser as WebAssembly; the browser WASM module was 2.1x slower than QuickJS-NG and 3.6x larger (5.56 MB vs 1.53 MB raw) in the README's own historical capture. Not a drop-in C API. Python frontend is experimental and a GPU lab is bundled, so the crate is large.
caveats: First-party, self-labelled diagnostic captures (diagnostic_only:true) with only six repetitions for the QuickJS-NG runs. The QuickJS-NG raw result JSONs sit in gitignored target/comparison/results by policy; only summaries and hashes are committed. The QuickJS-NG ratios are for v0.0.5 and v0.0.6 and were not rerun on current main (0.0.21). The Node/Bun/Deno canonical capture at 8229b3fc predates B280 (v0.0.15), which fixed method-call ordering that was 'observably wrong for a getter or proxy trap'. The later 14770703 capture is slower (headline ten 1.0025x Node, all 13 0.677x), and no headline is claimed for it. The 13-normal geomean (0.614x Node) leans on three architecture diagnostics (property-ic-shapes 0.04x, polymorphic-objects-v2 0.30x, sparse-array-v2 0.59x); the retained ten give 0.878x. 'Faster than Node on every row' is not met (21 of 30). The canonical raw JSON reports zipp 0.0.12 while the README says 0.0.13. The WASM build is slower than QuickJS-NG: v0.0.5 adjusted 2.107x, and v0.0.6 compared only 5 of 30 rows (0.96x). The five-kernel WASM speed-up (0.095x QuickJS-NG) was dominated by exact bytecode-shape lanes (1.815x with them off). Those lanes (vm/array_ops.rs) compile only when not (jit and x86_64), so the native x86-64 captures exclude them. The project is a rapid, largely machine-assisted rewrite with 6 stars; Rust, not C++. [retier] Native x86-64 comparison against QuickJS-NG v0.16.2 is public and pinned (Rust 1.92.0, fat LTO, Ryzen 9 9950X3D, Windows 11; MSYS2 GCC revision unstamped). The Node, Bun and Deno rows predate the later-fixed B280 call-order bug and a later capture is slower (retained-ten 0.878x of Node; the 13-row geomean drops to 0.614x once three self-written diagnostic rows are included, and the property-ic-shapes row measures loop elimination rather than inline caches). array_ops.rs pattern-matches three Wasm-workload callbacks in the Wasm and ARM64 builds, so only the native x86-64 numbers are free of benchmark-specific fast paths; the Wasm build is 2.107x slower than QuickJS-NG. Six repetitions, per-row QuickJS-NG raw data gitignored, no C API, 256 MiB stack.

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded C to A for the QuickJS-NG headline. bench/comparison/README.md gives the public harness (bench/comparison/run_native.py over the bench/real 13-case corpus) and Zipp's compiler and flags (Rust/Cargo 1.92.0, release profile: opt-level 3, fat LTO, one codegen unit, no RUSTFLAGS, no PGO). The baseline is the official QuickJS-NG v0.16.2 qjs-windows-x86_64.exe, pinned by SHA-256 and built by upstream CI under MSYS2 UCRT64 in CMake Release mode (exact GCC revision unstamped), and the host is named as AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D on Windows 11. The Node/Bun/Deno numbers alone would be C: they were measured at 8229b3fc, before B280 fixed call ordering that was 'observably wrong for a getter or proxy trap', and the later capture is slower.

name: MicroQuickJS (MQuickJS)
baseline: QuickJS (Bellard); the README is the only comparison and gives no QuickJS numbers
workload: Not measured against QuickJS in the README; the README describes running JavaScript in as little as 10 kB of RAM with about 100 kB of ROM (ARM Thumb-2 code including the C library) and references 'make microbench' and an Octane run.

MQuickJS supports only a subset of JavaScript close to ES5 (stricter mode), so it is not a drop-in QuickJS replacement. name: Ravi
baseline: Lua 5.3 (the dialect it extends; LuaJIT is named as a different-goal alternative)
workload: Numeric micro-benchmarks in tests/performance (fornum loop tests, mandel1 at 4000, fannkuchen at 11, matmul1 at 1000), each as plain Lua and as Ravi-typed variants, timed under Lua 5.3.2, the Ravi interpreter, Ravi with the LLVM JIT, and LuaJIT 2.1 interpreter and JIT.
claimed_speedup: readthedocs/ravi-benchmarks.rst (llvm branch, Lua 5.3.2 baseline, archived LLVM 3.9 backend): the 29x fornum row is a dead-store loop (0.3 ns per iteration, loop overhead only) and the 26x matmul1.ravi row is a different program (flat 1-D arrays with omitArrayGetRangeCheck); the closer typed port matmul1_ravi.lua runs at 1.137 s. Typed mandel and fannkuchen 10-26x with range checks skipped; untyped code only 1.6-2.5x. LuaJIT is equal or faster throughout.
compiler_and_flags: Ravi and Lua 5.3.2 compiled with Visual C++ 2015 (flags not stated); LLVM 3.9 JIT backend.
hardware: Windows 10 64-bit; CPU not stated.
tradeoffs: Dialect of Lua with optional type annotations (not a drop-in for LuaJIT-style Lua 5.1 code); JIT backend is MIR, with AOT compilation to shared libraries; Lua 5.4 generational GC backported. Compatible with Lua 5.3 programs.
caveats: All numbers are the author's own, from about 2016 (Lua 5.3.2, LLVM 3.9, Visual C++ 2015, Windows 10) with no CPU or flags given. They measure the LLVM JIT backend, which the README says is archived; the current MIR backend has no published numbers that were found, so today's performance is unverified. JIT compilation time is excluded, the large wins need Ravi type annotations (untyped Lua code gains only 1.6-2.5x), and matmul ran with array read bounds checks disabled. The README says Ravi favours maintainability, safety and Lua 5.3 compatibility over maximum performance, and LuaJIT 2.1 is as fast or faster on every benchmark. The benchmark page is no longer in master's readthedocs folder (only on the llvm branch; the readthedocs.io copy is blocked here, its numbers were confirmed from a search snippet and the branch file).

name: Chez Scheme
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1, PyPy 3 and Node.js (V8)
workload: kostya/benchmarks brainfuck interpreter (bench.b and mandel.b); plb2 nqueen and matmul.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks), Chez Scheme 10.0.0, brainfuck bench.b: 1.758 s vs Node.js 2.954 s, Lua/luajit 5.686 s, Python/pypy 9.398 s (about 1.68x, 3.23x and 5.35x, derived from page data); Java 1.191 s is faster. mandel.b: 30.884 s vs luajit 31.804 s, Node.js 34.692 s, pypy 41.153 s (about 1.03x, 1.12x and 1.33x, derived from page data); Java 13.041 s is faster. Second source plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Chez 9.5.8, Apple M1): nqueen 3.54 s vs luajit 5.31 s, PyPy 6.91 s, Node 3.73 s and Java 3.92 s (faster than all four), but matmul 18.98 s vs luajit 2.66 s, Node 2.88 s, PyPy 4.89 s and Java 1.14 s (7.1x slower than LuaJIT and 16.6x slower than Java, derived from page data); plb2 has no Chez sudoku or bedcov.
compiler_and_flags: kostya: `scheme --optimize-level 3 --program` (common/commands.mk SCHEME_RUN), Chez Scheme 10.0.0 from the Debian chezscheme package; baselines luajit 2.1.1748495995, pypy 7.3.23, Node.js v26.5.0, Java 24.0.2, all run with default flags. plb2: src/scheme/run.sh uses the same `scheme --optimize-level 3 --program`, Chez 9.5.8.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (kostya/benchmarks); Apple M1 (plb2)
tradeoffs: Incremental native-code compiler with a Scheme runtime, not a general-purpose embeddable JIT; C interface exists; optimize-level 3 removes safety checks.
caveats: Mixed results: Chez wins only the brainfuck interpreter tests in kostya (the only kostya tests that have a Chez row) and plb2 nqueen; plb2 matmul is 7-17x slower than every JIT baseline (its source stores doubles in a generic Scheme vector, so every element is a boxed flonum). The mandel.b margin over LuaJIT is about 3%. Java (HotSpot) beats Chez on both kostya brainfuck tests. optimize-level 3 is Chez's unsafe mode (type and bounds checks removed), which the baselines do not get. Chez is not a tracing or profiling JIT: the full compiler (Debian chezscheme package) compiles the program to native code when it is loaded, so the category fit is load-time compilation. The brainfuck programs differ in shape across languages (Chez walks a parsed op list recursively; LuaJIT's bf_jit.lua dispatches through one closure per op; Node, Java and C# use a parsed op tree with a switch), so the comparison is per idiomatic implementation, not identical code. plb2 numbers are from Chez 9.5.8 (early 2024 versions) and its author notes his non-C implementations may be suboptimal.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): kostya/benchmarks brainfuck tables read after the plb2 README surfaced the 'scm:ch' row

verification.tier_reason: kostya/benchmarks README rows match exactly; benchmark code brainfuck/bf.ss is public, run via common/commands.mk SCHEME_RUN (`scheme --optimize-level 3 --program`), Chez Scheme 10.0.0 from the Debian chezscheme package in docker/Dockerfile, Intel Xeon E-2324G, and the LuaJIT/PyPy/Node.js baselines' versions and run commands are in the same files.
verification.notes: All kostya and plb2 numbers verified on the pages; added that Chez also beats Java on plb2 nqueen and that the mandel.b win over LuaJIT is only 3%. Resolved the execution-mode question: the Docker image installs the full Debian chezscheme package and both suites run `scheme --optimize-level 3 --program` (compiled to native code at load, unsafe mode). Metadata verified: Apache-2.0, 7.4k stars, last commit 2026-10-01, not archived.

Second source plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Chez 9.5.8, Apple M1): nqueen 3.54 s vs luajit 5.31 s, PyPy 6.91 s and Node 3.73 s, but matmul 18.98 s vs 2.66 s (luajit) and 4.89 s (PyPy).

name: CRuby RTL + MJIT (vnmakarov/ruby rtl_mjit_branch)
baseline: Ruby MRI 2.0 (primary) and Ruby MRI 2.5-development trunk the branch is based on ('base')
workload: 23 microbenchmarks from MJIT-benchmarks (while, nest-while, ivread, aref, fib, fannk, sieve, mandelbrot, meteor, nbody, norm, trees, pent, red-black, bench, ...) plus the optcarrot NES emulator at 180 and 2000 frames; wall time, CPU time and peak memory, minimum of 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: README 'Update: 15th June, 2017' wall-time speedup over MRI 2.0, geomean of 23 microbenchmarks: mjit (GCC 6.3.1 -O2) 6.18x, mjit-cl (Clang 3.9.1 -O2) 4.02x, rtl without JIT 1.39x, base MRI 2.5-dev 1.12x; against base that is about 5.5x (mjit) and 3.6x (mjit-cl). The 'while' row (387.29x for mjit) is an empty loop whose result is unused; without it the mjit geomean is about 5.1x over MRI 2.0 and 4.5x over base, and on the ten algorithmic benchmarks (fannk through bench) mjit is about 1.93x over MRI 2.0 and 1.74x over base (all derived from page data). Optcarrot 2000 frames: 28.96 FPS MRI 2.0, 39.43 FPS base, 78.22 FPS mjit (2.7x), 90.58 FPS mjit-cl (3.13x); default 180 frames: 82.06 FPS mjit (2.83x), 85.43 FPS mjit-cl (2.94x). Optcarrot against base about 1.98x (mjit) and 2.30x (mjit-cl) at 2000 frames (derived from page data). CPU-time geomean 5.55x (mjit) and 3.67x (mjit-cl) on the microbenchmarks; optcarrot CPU-time speedup only 1.45x to 1.53x.
compiler_and_flags: MJIT-generated C compiled with GCC 6.3.1 -O2 (mjit) or LLVM Clang 3.9.1 -O2 (mjit-cl); build flags of the MRI 2.0 and base interpreters not stated
hardware: Intel 3.9GHz i3-7100, 32GB memory, x86-64 Fedora Core 25
tradeoffs: Method JIT that generates C code and runs GCC or Clang at runtime, loading the result as a shared object from /tmp; needs a C compiler installed at run time. Compiling a small ISEQ takes about 50-70 ms. Peak memory geomean 4.15x (GCC) and 6.44x (Clang) of MRI 2.0 including the compiler. README says it is at a very early stage and only ready for a few small, simple Ruby programs (June 2017 update).
caveats: Numbers are from June 2017 on a prototype branch, last commit 2017-09-29; the branch is not maintained. The headline 6.18x is against Ruby 2.0, an old baseline; against the 2.5-development trunk it is about 5.5x. The 'while' microbenchmark (387x for GCC mjit) times an empty while loop inside a method whose result is discarded, which GCC -O2 can remove entirely, so that row measures dead-loop elimination and skews the geomean (about 5.1x over MRI 2.0 without it; about 1.9x on the ten algorithmic benchmarks, derived from page data). Compiler and flags of the MRI 2.0, base and rtl_mjit interpreter builds are not stated (only the JIT's C compiler: GCC 6.3.1 -O2 or Clang 3.9.1 -O2). Optcarrot is the only real-program result: 2.7x to 3.13x over MRI 2.0, about 2x over base, and CPU-time gain only 1.45x to 1.53x. Benchmark scripts are in the branch under MJIT-benchmarks (compare.rb, optcarrot-compare.rb; minimum of 3 runs timed with /usr/bin/time, start-up included). Not the same as the MJIT later shipped in Ruby 2.6 to 3.2 or today's YJIT (ruby/ruby is listed separately for YJIT); vnmakarov/mir is already catalogued and is not duplicated here. License: Ruby's dual licence (BSD-2-Clause or the Ruby terms), per COPYING. [retier] 2017 prototype branch, abandoned 2017-09-29 (successor sir-mirjit dormant since 2023). The 6.18x geomean over Ruby 2.0 (GCC MJIT, 2-core i3-7100) includes a 387x 'while' row that is an empty counting loop GCC -O2 collapsed; about 5.1x without it and about 1.9x on the 10 algorithmic benchmarks against the 2.5-dev base. optcarrot: 2.7x-3.13x wall over MRI 2.0 but about 1.13x CPU time against base (derived from page data), since compilation ran on the second core; compare.rb drops system time. Interpreter build flags unstated; predictable /tmp JIT file names; Rails Ruby Bench crashes with --jit under threads (#10).
found_via: seed-record pass: lead 'rtl_mjit_branch README claims 6.18x geomean over Ruby 2.0'; read https://github.com/vnmakarov/ruby/blob/rtl_mjit_branch/README.md and the MJIT-benchmarks directory listing

verification.tier_reason: First-party README tables with public scripts (MJIT-benchmarks/compare.rb, optcarrot-compare.rb and the .rb workloads) and a named CPU (i3-7100), but only the JIT's C backend is specified (GCC 6.3.1 -O2, Clang 3.9.1 -O2); the compiler and flags used to build the MRI 2.0, base and rtl_mjit interpreter binaries themselves are never stated, so not A; no paper or independent run, so C.
verification.notes: Every number in the record matches the README; downgraded A to C because the interpreter builds' compiler and flags are unstated. Shortcomings: 2017 prototype branch (abandoned), headline geomean against Ruby 2.0 and inflated by the 387x empty 'while' loop that GCC -O2 eliminates (about 1.9x on the algorithmic benchmarks, about 2x on optcarrot vs base); optcarrot CPU-time gain is 1.45x to 1.53x, not 1.49x to 1.53x. Fork of ruby/ruby, 206 stars, last commit 2017-09-29 confirmed; distinct from the listed ruby/ruby (YJIT) entry.

name: FakeLua
baseline: PUC Lua 5.4.7 (LuaJIT not compared)
workload: 51 Lua micro-scenarios in 6 categories (algorithms, strings, tables, function calls, ...), Google Benchmark harness bench_mark, FakeLua JIT_GCC and JIT_TCC backends versus Lua 5.4 and hand-written C++.
claimed_speedup: JIT_GCC vs PUC Lua 5.4 (CPU-time ratios, 2026-08-14 run): Fibonacci n=32 36.6x (277.9 ms vs 7.59 ms CPU), Sum n=5M 30.4x, Popcount n=100K 37.3x, FloatPoly n=1M 34.9x, Recursion n=25 42.9x, TailRecursion n=5K 107.5x (that bench has since been removed from the harness); TCC backend Fibonacci n=32 11.2x (derived from page data: 277.9 ms vs 24.86 ms CPU). Most table and string rows are only 1.0-6.1x (TableChurn 9.3x); GCD 0.45x, ToNumber 0.53x, Variadic 0.91x and StringFind 0.85x are slower, and the Boost.Regex rows are much slower (0.06-0.21x).
compiler_and_flags: Release build, -O3 -DNDEBUG (plus -g3 -fPIC from the top-level CMakeLists); GCC 15.1.0 for the JIT_GCC run, whose generated C is compiled at -O3 at script load; GCC 16.2.0 for the interpreter run. Lua baseline is the system liblua5.4 found via pkg-config (distro build flags not stated); Lua 5.4.7 is named only for the 2026-09-16 interpreter run. Google Benchmark v1.9.4.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7K62 48-Core Processor, 2-vCPU VM at 2595 MHz, load average 5.87 during the run (GCC/TCC JIT run, 2026-08-14); AMD EPYC 7551, 16-vCPU KVM (interpreter run, 2026-09-16)
tradeoffs: Runs a Lua 5.4 subset: no coroutines, metatables or require, and no implicit string-number coercion; arena allocation with per-frame reset instead of GC. JIT_GCC shells out to the system GCC at run time (compile latency and a compiler dependency); JIT_TCC uses embedded TinyCC; JIT_INTERP bytecode VM needs no compiler.
caveats: Baseline is PUC Lua 5.4 (distro liblua5.4), not LuaJIT, so the result does not show a win over LuaJIT. Lua source is compiled to C and built by GCC/TCC at script load; that compile time is outside the timed region. The GCC JIT numbers come from a 2026-08-14 run on a loaded 2-vCPU cloud VM (wall times about 1.6x CPU times; the ratios use CPU time) and predate many later correctness fixes, including math-specialization eligibility fixes (commits 236a757 and 598632f, 2026-10-02); those fixes target shadowed, nested, multi-return and vararg functions that the bench scripts do not use, and the harness verifies every result, but the GCC run has not been repeated on current code. The TailRecursion bench (107.5x) was removed from the harness on 2026-09-18 (commit 12fbcd7), so that row is not reproducible from HEAD. The regex rows used Boost.Regex; commit a55a4bf (2026-10-03) implements Lua 5.4 patterns, so those rows may be obsolete. Some StringFindPattern/StringGmatch raw lines predate a workload correction (the page says so). The hand-written C++ reference column is not credible: the page says some references are folded, and C++ Sum n=5M took 27.4 ms CPU against 1.55 ms for FakeLua's GCC-compiled version of the same loop, so 'faster than C++' claims should be ignored. The bytecode interpreter tier is 1.3x to 7.6x slower than Lua 5.4 in its algorithm rows (34x on TailRecursion). Very young, fast-moving repository. [retier] Baseline is PUC Lua 5.4 (distro liblua5.4), not LuaJIT. The 2026-08-14 GCC run (EPYC 7K62, loaded 2-vCPU VM) predates the math-spec fixes 236a757 and 598632f. CPU times 277.9 ms vs 7.59 ms on Fib (36.6x); TCC 11.2x derived. The C++ reference column is invalid: 8-18x slower than the GCC JIT on identical loops (Fib n=32 60.6 vs 7.59 ms, Sum 27.4 vs 1.55 ms, Popcount 5.0 vs 0.59 ms), a 5.5-8.6 ns per-step cost that fits a coverage-instrumented (USE_COV) or unoptimized host build, so ignore any 'faster than C++' reading. TailRecursion bench removed in 12fbcd7; regex rows obsolete after a55a4bf; MultiReturn bench returns a single value; README headline table disagrees with the raw rows; TinyCC pulled unpinned from 'mob'; OpenSSL REQUIRED.
found_via: GitHub topics page github.com/topics/jit?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars (item 19), then README and benchmark/README.md.

verification.tier_reason: Public Google Benchmark harness (benchmark/benchmark_algo.cpp, benchmark_function.cpp, benchmark_string.cpp, benchmark_table.cpp, benchmark_gc.cpp, benchmark_math.cpp; benchmark_common.cpp checks every iteration's result with VerifyEqual, which throws on a wrong answer) runs FakeLua JIT_GCC/JIT_TCC/JIT_INTERP against PUC Lua 5.4 in the same binary, and benchmark/README.md states GCC 15.1.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG (Release) and the CPU model (AMD EPYC 7K62) for the GCC JIT run, with full raw output. All A criteria are met; the headline ratios match the page's CPU-time rows.
verification.notes: Ratios check out against the raw CPU-time rows (Fib 277,915,868 ns vs 7,590,283 ns; Sum 46.98 ms vs 1.55 ms; Popcount 22.1 ms vs 0.593 ms; TailRecursion 209.8 us vs 1.95 us), but the record's '297.9 ms vs 6.8 ms' Fibonacci figures are not on the page and were corrected; the TCC 11.2x is a derived ratio. Shortcomings to record: baseline is PUC Lua not LuaJIT; GCC numbers come from an older (2026-08-14) run on a loaded 2-vCPU VM that predates later math-specialization correctness fixes (edge cases outside the bench scripts; results were verified); the TailRecursion bench was later removed; the C++ reference column is anomalous. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 214 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-03.

name: goja-perf
baseline: Upstream dop251/goja at merge base 8f1c069 (pure-Go JavaScript interpreter); V8 comparison suite exists but publishes no numbers
workload: 55 shared Go benchmarks from goja's suite, ten samples per version interleaved on Go 1.26.2, comparing fork commit 35cc441 with its upstream merge base; seven benchmarks improved significantly and none regressed significantly.
claimed_speedup: Over upstream goja (benchjs harness): MainLoop 24.541 ms to 98.277 us (249.71x) via a special-case lowering for the benchmark's empty global-counter loop; CallJS 2.86x, CallNative 2.07x, FuncCall 1.81x, CallReflect 1.39x. The VmNOP2 (1.96x) and MapDelete (1.48x) rows have no code change behind them (layout or noise artifacts; benchjs reports Goja CV 29-209% on that laptop). benchjs/README.md also shows V8 about 15x faster at steady-state geomean, with Goja runtime setup 25-60x cheaper.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26.2; go test -run '^$' -bench . -benchmem -count=10 (default Go build flags), ten samples per version interleaved and compared for significance; eligible integer loop traces compile to native code on Windows/amd64 and Linux/amd64, other platforms use a portable typed Go executor
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 PRO 7940HS, Windows/amd64
tradeoffs: API-compatible fork that keeps the upstream package name and swaps the import path; adds adaptive quickening, typed traces with native code for supported numeric loop shapes, cheaper Go/JS boundary calls and an opt-in capability sandbox. Native traces cover only supported integer and float accumulation and counter loops.
caveats: The 249.71x headline is BenchmarkMainLoop (runtime_test.go), an empty 'for (var i=0; i<100000; i++) {}' loop over a global variable, and global_counter_trace.go is a dedicated lowering for exactly that empty global integer counter loop shape: it keeps the counter in a Go integer (with a per-iteration interrupt check) and writes the property back on exit. The result is semantically correct and the loop still runs (about 1 ns per iteration), but the headline is a special case built for the benchmark's own shape and says little about general code. The other significant rows are 1.39x-2.86x (call boundary and VM dispatch micro benchmarks) and 48 of 55 shared benchmarks did not change significantly. Raw benchstat output is not published, only the summary table. The benchjs suite compares the same JS workloads with V8 but publishes no results; V8 would be far faster on compute. Independent fork with two stars and a separate module path (github.com/maclof/goja-perf), so its Goja values are distinct Go types from upstream's and goja_nodejs needs an adapter. Measured on one Windows laptop CPU. [retier] The 249.71x MainLoop row comes from global_counter_trace.go, written for exactly the benchmark's empty global-counter loop (output still correct), and the native JIT handles only 'sum += i' loops; VmNOP2 and MapDelete gains are artifacts (identical code to upstream apart from import paths). The fork stopped 2026-09-02 and lacks upstream September-October fixes. Go fork of goja; off the category baselines.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/jit?l=go topic page (maclof/goja-perf listed as 'ECMAScript/JavaScript engine optimized for performance')

verification.tier_reason: The README 'Measured performance' table carries every quoted number for fork commit 35cc441 against its upstream merge base 8f1c069, with Go 1.26.2, Windows/amd64 and the AMD Ryzen 9 PRO 7940HS named and the exact command given (go test -run '^$' -bench . -benchmem -count=10). The benchmark code is public and shared with upstream (runtime_test.go BenchmarkMainLoop is byte-for-byte the same script in dop251/goja), so the comparison is reproducible.
verification.notes: Numbers match the README exactly and the MainLoop benchmark source is identical upstream, so the comparison is fair as measured; the shortcoming is that the 249.71x row comes from global_counter_trace.go, an optimization that matches only the empty global counter loop the benchmark uses. License MIT (Dmitry Panov / Robert Krimen text), 2 stars, last commit 2026-09-02 (v0.2.2), fork of dop251/goja (verified in wave 12 batch-59).

name: JRuby
baseline: CRuby (MRI) 2.7.7p221
workload: Same 13 single-threaded Benchmarks-Game-style programs as the Topaz entry (JRuby 9.4.1.0 on OpenJDK 19.0.1, default flags and `-Xcompile.invokedynamic=true`), best of up to 5 runs, time measured inside the language by the shootout harness.
claimed_speedup: Mixed result. JRuby with invokedynamic is faster than CRuby 2.7.7 on 9 of 13 programs (derived from page data): binarytrees 1.24 s vs 6.75 s, fannkuchredux 1.19 s vs 4.34 s, nbody 14.85 s vs 43.56 s, spectralnorm 4.09 s vs 17.18 s, mandelbrot 7.12 s vs 16.74 s; slower on fasta (26.86 s vs 18.19 s), regexdna (9.49 s vs 6.25 s), revcomp (8.78 s vs 4.2 s) and about equal on matmul (18.9 s vs 18.39 s). Default JRuby (no invokedynamic) is faster on 8 of 13 and slower on matmul, nbody, fasta, regexdna, revcomp.
compiler_and_flags: jruby-dist 9.4.1.0 binary tarball from Maven Central on OpenJDK 19 (openjdk-19-jre-headless from apt; README lists openjdk 19.0.1), run as `jruby <file>` (JRuby row) and `jruby -Xcompile.invokedynamic=true -S <file>` (JRuby_InDy row) per tools/languages.rb; CRuby 2.7.7 built from source with gcc 12.2.0 (ubuntu:22.10 build-essential) using `./configure --prefix=/opt/ruby --disable-install-doc --disable-install-rdoc --disable-install-capi --with-openssl-dir=/opt/openssl1.1.1q` and `make -j4` (default CRuby optimization flags), per docker/ruby2.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80 GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10
tradeoffs: Runs on the JVM (repo page: current branches need JRE 21 or newer), so JVM startup and memory apply: in the same shootout JRuby used about 1.2-2.1 GB on binarytrees versus 44.6 MB for CRuby. Repo page lists no global interpreter lock and tight Java integration.
caveats: Mixed evidence: JRuby loses to CRuby on several programs (fasta, regexdna, revcomp with invokedynamic; also matmul and nbody without it), so this is not a uniform speedup. Baseline is CRuby 2.7.7; against the same run's Ruby 3.2.1 interpreter row JRuby_InDy is faster on 10 of 13 and still slower on fasta, regexdna and revcomp (derived from page data). The shootout has no YJIT row: its base image installs no Rust toolchain, which Ruby 3.2's YJIT needs at build time. Times are measured inside the program after a 'started' marker and the table reports the best of up to 5 iterations, so JVM startup (shown in the separate 'Compile T,s' column, 1.6-2.2 s) and part of the warm-up are excluded, which favours JRuby; several CRuby baseline rows (brainfuck, knucleotide, nbody, regexdna, revcomp) completed only 1 iteration inside the time limit. JRuby uses 0.8-2.1 GB of RAM on these programs versus tens of MB for CRuby. name: Julia
language: Julia (C/C++ runtime on LLVM; embeddable from C/C++ through libjulia)
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1, PyPy 3 (7.3.x), Node.js (V8) and OpenJDK HotSpot, on the same CPU-bound algorithms
workload: Single-threaded CPU-bound programs written with the same algorithm in every language: kostya/benchmarks brainfuck interpreter (bench.b, mandel.b) and naive matrix multiply; plb2 nqueen, matmul (1500x1500), sudoku, bedcov.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks brainfuck bench.b: Julia 1.564 s vs luajit 5.686 s, pypy 9.398 s, Node.js 2.954 s (about 3.6x, 6.0x and 1.9x, derived from page data); Java 1.191 s is faster. mandel.b: Julia 30.315 s vs luajit 31.804 s, Node.js 34.692 s, pypy 41.153 s; Java 13.041 s is faster. The kostya matmul 'no BLAS' row (1.113 s vs Java 3.057 s) is not like for like (see caveats); like-for-like plb2 matmul (Apple M1) gives about 1.5x over Java. plb2 Julia 1.10.0: nqueen 3.02 s, matmul 0.76 s, sudoku 2.18 s.
compiler_and_flags: kostya/benchmarks: julia v1.11.6 run as `julia --optimize=3 --check-bounds=no`; Java 24.0.2, Node.js v26.5.0, luajit 2.1.1748495995, pypy 7.3.23 (Python 3.11.15), Docker on Debian; run commands in common/commands.mk. plb2 versions in its README table (Julia 1.10.0, Java 20.0.1, PyPy 7.3.14, LuaJIT 2.1, Node 21.5.0).
hardware: kostya/benchmarks: Intel Xeon E-2324G; plb2: Apple M1 MacBook Pro
tradeoffs: Per-process JIT warmup and large footprint (kostya bench.b base RSS about 244 MB vs 2.5 MB for LuaJIT); package precompilation latency; garbage collected; embedding in C++ goes through the libjulia C API and is heavier than embedding LuaJIT.
caveats: Workload specific: Java beats Julia on kostya's bench.b and mandel.b, and in kostya's other tests Julia loses to most baselines: base64 3.085 s vs Node.js 0.635 s and Java 1.435 s (Julia does beat PyPy 3.534 s there); primes 0.680 s vs Java 0.161 s, Node.js 0.207 s, luajit 0.309 s and PyPy 0.617 s; JSON (JSON3) 0.700 s vs Node.js 0.374 s, Java DSL-JSON 0.571 s and PyPy 0.606 s. In plb2 Julia beats all four baselines. The kostya run uses --check-bounds=no (bounds checks removed) and plb2's Julia sources use @inbounds in hot loops, which other languages' sources do not. The kostya 'no BLAS' matmul source is not a plain triple loop: it uses @simd ivdep and @fastmath (allowing reassociation and vectorized FMA, which Java and V8 cannot do) and wraps the outer loop in Threads.@threads (single-threaded here, since JULIA_RUN passes no -t and sets no JULIA_NUM_THREADS). Julia matmul rows at 0.12-0.17 s use BLAS and are not comparable. The kostya brainfuck bf.jl scans raw characters and brackets at run time, while the Node, Java and C# versions parse an op tree first, so the code shapes differ. Each program runs a small verify() before the timer starts, which warms the JIT on the same functions, so most compile time is outside the timed region; plb2 includes startup and compile time. kostya's docker/Dockerfile now pins julia-1.12.6 while the README environment lists v1.11.6, so the published numbers predate the current image.

name: musql
baseline: SQLite (C, via mattn/go-sqlite3); Turso's Go driver is also compared
workload: Read queries over 100,000 rows on disk-backed files with a warm cache, each checked against C SQLite on 40 bind values before timing, then timed for about 200 ms; musql run with and without its JIT (MUSQL_JIT=0).
claimed_speedup: docs/benchmarks.md (engine-direct API, selected read shapes): up to about 77x over C SQLite on the published rows; through database/sql (an arm the harness times but the docs omit, about 0.2 ms driver cost per statement per format-design.md) the gain is roughly 9-10x (derived from page data). The 17 non-JIT read shapes dropped by BENCH_SKIP trail C SQLite by about 3.5x per the harness notes; writes, BETWEEN and min/max are not published.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.0 per go.mod and compat-harness/go.mod (the benchmark page states no toolchain version); default go test build; C SQLite is mattn/go-sqlite3 v1.14.48 built through cgo with default flags (C compiler not stated); Turso via turso.tech/database/tursogo v0.7.2; harness compat-harness/bench_columnar_vs_c_test.go (TestBenchColumnarVsC), JIT on vs MUSQL_JIT=0
hardware: Apple M4 (arm64, macOS) and Intel Xeon D-2123IT (amd64, Linux)
tradeoffs: SQLite-compatible SQL on a new columnar .musq segment format with an append-only delta; import/export tools to and from SQLite files. The JIT covers only supported scan/filter/aggregate query paths; point lookups and joins do not use it. Pure Go driver, but the benchmark harness needs cgo.
caveats: The published run sets BENCH_SKIP to drop 17 read shapes that no musql fast path answers (min/max, GROUP BY with HAVING, OR, BETWEEN, IN list, IS NULL, LIKE, ORDER BY text, group_concat, DISTINCT, subqueries, EXISTS, UNION, OFFSET, join projecting) plus every write (UPDATE, INSERT, DELETE); the harness's own comments say those shapes run the ordinary VDBE, which trails C SQLite by about 3.5x on a scan, and that writes are where the engine is at its worst, so the published table shows the JIT-served shapes plus three point lookups only. The win comes from columnar storage plus JIT against SQLite's row store (musql reads its own .musq format after VACUUM; SQLite files need conversion); without the JIT musql is much slower than C SQLite on the same scans (9.83 ms vs 2.17 ms for the one-predicate filtered count on M4). Arms are not identical: musql is timed through its direct engine API while C SQLite is timed through database/sql and cgo with each result rendered to a string, which matters only for the microsecond rows. Whole-table count is answered from segments' recorded row counts, not a scan. Microsecond-scale rows vary run to run, more on amd64. The README headline 75x is the two-machine average of the one-predicate (73x) and two-predicate (77x) rows. The repository history is a single squashed commit (2026-10-05). [retier] Published table is engine-direct and cherry-picked (BENCH_SKIP drops 17 non-JIT read shapes, writes, BETWEEN and min/max); the database/sql arm is omitted; C SQLite is untuned (no cache_size or mmap PRAGMA); the speedup comes mostly from the columnar storage format rather than the JIT. No Go or cgo C compiler version (go.mod 1.27.0 only); the repo is one squashed commit. Off-baseline (C SQLite); Go.

name: Objeck
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1 (tracing JIT); the same table also lists Java 21 (OpenJDK 21.0.12 HotSpot, tiered JIT), CPython 3.12.3 and Ruby 3.2.3
workload: Computer Language Benchmarks Game programs (nbody 50M, binarytrees 17, spectralnorm 5500, fannkuchredux 12) in one Docker run, median of 3 runs; Objeck programs compiled with -opt s3 and JIT-compiled at runtime.
claimed_speedup: docs/performance.md (2026-09-12 Docker run, median of 3): binarytrees 17 Objeck 2.14 s vs LuaJIT 3.57 s (1.7x faster, the one like-for-like win) and Java 21 0.26 s; nbody 50M Objeck 8.14 s vs LuaJIT 4.37 s and Java 2.35 s (slower); spectralnorm 5500 Objeck 2.72 s vs LuaJIT 1.12 s and Java 1.18 s (slower); fannkuchredux 12 Objeck 32.76 s vs LuaJIT 117.99 s (page says 3.6x faster) and Java 20.70 s, but that row is not like-for-like because Objeck runs the optimized CLBG algorithm and LuaJIT a naive port that allocates a table per permutation. Objeck beats CPython 3.12 and Ruby 3.2 on all four rows (for example nbody 16.6x and 27.0x).
compiler_and_flags: Objeck v2026.9.1 (f6b3b09046), VM (obr) and compiler (obc) built from source in Ubuntu 24.04 with g++ from build-essential using core/vm/make/Makefile.amd64 (-O3 -flto=auto -mavx2 -std=c++20); programs compiled with -opt s3; LuaJIT, Python 3.12.3, Ruby 3.2.3 and OpenJDK 21.0.12 from Ubuntu apt packages (perf-results/docker/Dockerfile); Objeck timed with /usr/bin/time %e, the other languages with date +%s%N around each process
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D (16C/32T), 128 GB RAM (62 GB visible in Docker), Docker on a Windows 11 host
tradeoffs: A separate language (Objeck), not a drop-in for Lua or Java code. Method JIT applies to methods annotated native and to auto-JIT for methods containing MTHD_CALL. binarytrees peaks at 209 MB RSS against single-digit MB for the others. Interpreter-bound rows run 30-50% slower in Docker than natively, per the page.
caveats: The Lua source behind the 117.99 s LuaJIT fannkuchredux time (perf-results/cross-lang/benchmarks/fannkuchredux.lua) creates a new table with 'local perm = {}' and copies 12 elements into it for every permutation (hundreds of millions of table allocations and resizes for n=12) and reverses from index 0, whereas the Java port reuses one preallocated array and Objeck's programs/tests/clbg/fannkuchredux.obs is the optimized CLBG algorithm (first-element swap trick, reversal of the inner span only) inside a native-annotated function; the Python and Ruby ports are the same naive algorithm. The 3.6x fannkuchredux win over LuaJIT therefore measures a weaker Lua program, not LuaJIT, and Java, running the naive algorithm, still beats Objeck on it. The Java and Python ports also compute the checksum sign from the checksum's parity rather than the permutation index, and every program's output goes to /dev/null unchecked. Like-for-like rows: Objeck beats LuaJIT only on binarytrees (1.7x) and loses on nbody (1.9x) and spectralnorm (2.4x); Java wins 3 of 4 rows. Only four benchmarks are in the cross-language table, all in Docker on a Windows 11 host; LuaJIT is the distro package with the exact build not recorded. Objeck is a language VM with a JIT, not a drop-in library. The most recent commit seen was a bot download-stats snapshot (2026-10-05); the last code commits are 2026-10-03 and release notes for v2026.10.0 were added on 2026-10-02, while the repo page shows v2026.9.7 as the latest release. [retier] The 3.6x fannkuchredux win over LuaJIT is not like for like (the Lua port allocates a fresh table per permutation with naive full reversal while Objeck runs the optimized CLBG algorithm in a native-annotated function); the only fair win over LuaJIT is binarytrees at 1.7x, it loses nbody 1.9x and spectralnorm 2.4x, and Java wins 3 of 4. All benchmark outputs go to /dev/null unchecked and the cross-language runner drops stderr (the page admits this hid a fasta failure); v2026.10.0 later fixed an -opt s3 miscompile (#1037) at the optimizer level used. Open #925: Try() cannot catch errors raised in JIT code; the JIT does no inlining.

name: Cuik (C compiler with the TB backend)
baseline: clang 22.1.8 (LLVM) and gcc 16.2.1 / gcc-15 15.3.0, compile and build time at their default optimisation level
workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark generates a synthetic C program (a grid of nested function call chains, 'return expr' bodies, long type) and measures minimum time per generated function over 5 runs for the check (syntax-only), compile (-c) and build (link to an executable) operations; Cuik is capped at 100 x 100 functions, the other C compilers run 200 x 200.
claimed_speedup: README sample run (us per generated function, lower is better), Cuik versus clang 22.1.8 versus gcc 16.2.1: check 6.0 / 15.4 / 18.2, compile 60.6 / 123.3 / 732.5, build 57.6 / 60.3 / 500.7. That is Cuik about 2.0x faster than clang and about 12x faster than gcc at compile, about 2.6x and 3.0x at check, and about 1.05x and 8.7x at build (all derived from page data). tcc 0.9.28rc is faster again (check 2.9, compile 3.5, build 2.6) and cproc is slower (check 10.6, compile 114.8). README conclusion: 'TCC is by a large margin the fastest compiler in build speed, followed by the C compiler Cuik and D's dmd.'
compiler_and_flags: Cuik ~master (no commit given) invoked with -c -xe (check), -c (compile) and plain -o exe (build); clang 22.1.8 and gcc 16.2.1 invoked with -fsyntax-only, -c and plain build with no -O flag (so their default O0 code generation) plus warning-silencing flags, from the benchmark script.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8) @ 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, sample run as of 2026-09
tradeoffs: Cuik's own README: 'warning: unfinished and buggy'. Fast, thread-safe C11 front end (libCuik) plus the Tilde Backend (tb) with a sea-of-nodes IR, x64 and AArch64 codegen, ELF, COFF, PE and Mach-O output, and JIT or AOT use; MIT licensed. In the benchmark Cuik's build peak memory is far higher per function (69.9 kB/f versus clang 8.8 and gcc 17.5) and the benchmark had to cap Cuik at 100 x 100 for 'compiler stability limits'. No optimising pipeline comparable to LLVM, so it competes on compile speed rather than code quality.
caveats: Independent third-party suite, but the gap to tier A is the Cuik build: the script hard-codes its version as '~master' (no commit, no build compiler or flags), and results are from one sample run on one machine (best of 5 per cell). The comparison is at default settings for all three (gcc and clang with no -O flag plus -Wall -Wextra, which they pay for and Cuik does not; Cuik's optimizer is off unless -O is passed, and its check mode -xe is 'type check only', comparable to -fsyntax-only), on one synthetic program shape (long chains of one-line 'return x + ...' functions), so it measures front end plus unoptimised codegen speed only; the 'Run' column (105 us/f for Cuik versus 155 clang and 98 gcc) is of unoptimised output on a synthetic program and says nothing about optimised code quality, which the lead named as a baseline and for which no numbers were found. Timing noise is visible: the suite runs tasks in parallel, one worker pinned per logical CPU (SMT siblings share cores), and the Compile column is larger than the Build column (compile plus link) for every C compiler (Cuik 60.6 vs 57.6, clang 123.3 vs 60.3, gcc 732.5 vs 500.7), so the 1.05x Build win over clang is a tie within noise and the 2x Compile win over clang may be inflated by contention. Numbers are normalised per function while Cuik is capped at 100 x 100 (10,000 functions, 'due to compiler stability limits') against 200 x 200 for the other C compilers, so fixed start-up cost weighs more on Cuik, which if anything understates its speed. The README conclusion ranks Cuik second in build speed after tcc, but its own table shows D's dmd (11.2 us/f) and LuaJIT (4.8) building faster than Cuik (57.6). Cuik's own README says 'unfinished and buggy' and carries no benchmark; a search-result snippet saying its preprocessor is about 2x faster than Clang's was not verified. LLVM as a library (TB versus LLVM backend) is not measured here. Category fit is loose: Cuik is an ahead-of-time C compiler toolchain measured on compile time, filed under jits. [retier] nordlow/compiler-benchmark (Cuik at an unpinned master, one parallel sample run, clang and gcc at default flags): Cuik ran 10,000 generated functions against 40,000 for the others, so the per-function Run column is not comparable; Build time is below Compile time, so at least 5% contention noise; no output or exit-code check; the build win over clang is 1.05x, a tie, and dmd (11.2x) and LuaJIT (4.8x) build faster. -xe is type checking only and the optimiser is off by default. An AOT C compiler with the TB backend, loose fit under jits; open #37 miscompiles calls with more than 5 arguments on Linux.
found_via: seed-record pass: WebSearch 'Cuik C compiler RealNeGate Tilde Backend TB compile time faster than clang LLVM benchmark numbers' surfaced https://github.com/nordlow/compiler-benchmark; Cuik repo README, docs/*.txt and commits page opened

The -O0 cap was considered and does not apply: the metric is compile time, the baseline compilers are release builds, and Cuik's optimizer is also off by default (-O enables it), so both sides run unoptimised codegen.

The comparison is at default (effectively -O0) settings for clang and gcc, on one synthetic program shape (long nested one-line functions), so it measures front end plus unoptimised codegen speed only; the 'Run' column (105 us/f for Cuik versus 155 clang and 98 gcc) is of unoptimised output on a synthetic program and says nothing about code quality, which the lead named as a baseline and for which no numbers were found. Numbers are normalised per function while Cuik runs a smaller 10,000-function program than the others (40,000 functions), so fixed start-up cost weighs more on Cuik, which if anything understates its speed. baseline: HotSpot C2 JIT (OpenJDK HotSpot VM, JDK 25)
workload: JMH suite from the ionutbalosin/jvm-performance-benchmarks repository on JDK 25 x86_64: 298 compiler-optimization microbenchmarks (inlining, loop unrolling, escape analysis, devirtualization and similar) and 1136 benchmarks overall including Java API and classic programs.

The compiler category is made of handwritten patterns chosen to exercise optimizations, so the 16% geomean gap is not an application speedup; the other categories are smaller (api 0.92 over 756 benchmarks, miscellaneous 0.91 over 82, whole suite 0.9 over 1136, in sibling geomean CSVs).
