name: riscv-sbt (OpenISA RISC-V static binary translator)
baseline: QEMU (user-mode RISC-V dynamic binary translation) and rv8
workload: MiBench programs (dijkstra, crc32, rijndael encode/decode, sha, adpcm encode/decode, stringsearch, blowfish encode/decode, basicmath, bitcount, fft std/inv, patricia, susan smoothing/edges/corners, lame; 19 rows) built for RV32 and translated ahead of time to 32-bit x86 (AVX) with LLVM, run time measured with perf as slowdown versus the same program built natively for 32-bit x86; QEMU and rv8 run the RV32 binaries.
claimed_speedup: Committed result CSVs (mibench/results): geomean slowdown versus native 32-bit x86 of 1.08x (abi mapping) and 1.23x (locals mapping) over 19 MiBench programs, counting only cycles spent in the benchmark's own code (x86-avx-gcchf.csv 'x' columns, derived from page data); with libc time included the SBT geomeans are 1.02x abi and 1.11x locals (x86-avx-gcchf-wlibc.csv, derived from page data). QEMU 6.13x total-time geomean over 19 programs (qemu_slowdown.csv geomean row) and rv8 2.85x over the 10 programs it could run (rv8_slowdown.csv geomean row; the other 9 rows are zero-filled placeholders). On the same 10 programs: SBT abi 1.10x, SBT locals 1.24x, QEMU 5.39x, rv8 2.85x (derived from page data). Per-benchmark example: rijndael-encode 14.54x under QEMU, 4.51x under rv8, 1.11x for the SBT (abi). The 2018 paper gives an SBT average of 1.12x versus 3.16x for RV8 (commit 1d4d1ee) and 7.07x for QEMU (v2.12.0-835-g360a7809d2-dirty) (search snippet of the ResearchGate figure caption only; paper not opened).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -fno-exceptions for both RISC-V and native binaries (scripts/auto/config.py: GOPTS.cc and rvcc = gcc, _O = -O3); RISC-V binaries use -march=rv32g with the ilp32d hard-float ABI; native x86 binaries are 32-bit (i686-linux-gnu-gcc-7 when present, otherwise gcc -m32) with -mfpmath=sse -mavx; the SBT lowers translated code with LLVM llc -relocation-model=static -march=x86 -mattr=avx; static linking is forced only for rv8 and OVP runs (GOPTS.static), QEMU runs as qemu-riscv32 -L <sysroot>. gcc, LLVM, QEMU and rv8 versions are not stated in the repo (the paper snippet names RV8 commit 1d4d1ee and QEMU v2.12.0-835-g360a7809d2-dirty).
tradeoffs: Static (ahead-of-time) translator: no self-modifying code, JIT-generated code or dynamic loading of untranslated binaries; translates RV32 ELF to x86 and ARM through LLVM IR; needs a custom RISC-V toolchain and the MiBench programs rebuilt, so it is a research prototype rather than a drop-in emulator. ecall translation is limited.
caveats: CPU model is not stated in anything reachable (the paper is blocked in this environment), so tier A is unmet; the paper numbers (1.12x, 3.16x, 7.07x) come only from a search snippet and differ from the committed CSVs. Metric mismatch in the committed CSVs: scripts/auto/measure.py multiplies run time by the fraction of perf cycles in the benchmark's own DSO for the SBT runs (x86-avx-gcchf.csv, so libc time is excluded), while --rv32 emulator runs disable perf_libc and use total time (qemu.csv and rv8.csv show 100% for every row); the like-for-like total-time file x86-avx-gcchf-wlibc.csv gives 1.02x abi and 1.11x locals, so the win holds either way. The rv8 column covers only 10 of 19 programs (notes/rv8: basicmath crash, bitcount wrong result, fft never ends, patricia does not build, susan and lame fail) and its geomean row is over those 10; QEMU's 6.13x is over all 19 (5.39x on the same 10, derived). rv8 and QEMU are dynamic translators that pay translation cost at run time, while the SBT output is native x86 produced ahead of time, so the comparison is not like for like. github.com/OpenISA/riscv-sbt now redirects to github.com/lmcad-unicamp/riscv-sbt (current owner; same 18 stars and 5 forks). The OpenISA-input SBT results (x86-oi_slowdown.csv) are a separate translator and not this claim. Last commit 2019-03-06.

name: TPDE (TPDE-LLVM back-end)
baseline: LLVM -O0 code generation (clang/llc back-end)
workload: Compiling LLVM-IR to machine code at -O0 quality with TPDE-LLVM versus LLVM's -O0 back-end.
claimed_speedup: README: TPDE-LLVM compiles 10--20x faster than LLVM -O0 with similar code quality. docs/tpde-llvm/main.md: compile times typically 10--20x faster than the LLVM -O0 back-end with similar execution time; code size ~10-30% larger for -O0 IR and similar for -O1 IR.
stars_or_usage: 671 stars; used for a Wasmtime back-end and in Umbra per search snippets
tradeoffs: Single-pass back-end aimed at -O0 quality baseline code, not optimized code. Targets ELF-based x86-64 and AArch64 (Armv8.1) only. Usable as library for JIT, as tpde-llc tool, or in Clang/Flang 22+ with a patch. Needs LLVM-IR (or another SSA IR through its adapters).
caveats: Compile-time win only; generated code is -O0 quality, not comparable to V8 TurboFan, HotSpot C2 or LLVM -O2. TPDE-LLVM supports a subset of LLVM-IR (x86-64-v1 and AArch64 Armv8.1 ELF only; Clang -O2 and higher IR typically fails on unsupported vector operations and falls back to the full LLVM back-end); code size 10-30% larger for -O0 IR. The README cites only the arXiv preprint 2505.22610; the peer-reviewed version is CGO 2026 (Schwarz, Kamm, Engelke) with an artifact on Zenodo (record 17619677) running SPEC CPU 2017, which is proprietary, so the evaluation is not fully reproducible. Paper numbers are snippet only and differ by version: arXiv snippet says 8-24x faster than LLVM -O0 on SPEC CPU 2017 with geomean 12.15x (x86-64) and 18.96x (AArch64) and run time within +-9%; the CGO snippet says 8-26x, geomean 16.2x/18.7x over -O0 and 85.8x/80.0x over -O1. The search agent's Wasmtime/Cranelift figures (4.27x faster compile than Cranelift, Cranelift code 1.64x faster) were not re-checked.

name: WasmNow (copy-and-patch WebAssembly baseline compiler)
baseline: Google Chrome (V8) Liftoff baseline WebAssembly compiler; also Wasmer Singlepass named in README
workload: Coremark and PolyBenchC compiled to WebAssembly: compile time and generated-code speed versus Liftoff.
claimed_speedup: Versus Chrome's Liftoff: on Coremark compiles 5x faster while generating 39% faster code; on PolyBenchC compiles 6.5x faster while generating 63% faster code (README).
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 10.0.0 (LLVM 10.0.0 release binaries installed in dockerfile/Dockerfile on Ubuntu 18.04); production flavor adds -O3 -DNDEBUG, plus -pthread -mavx2 (CMakeLists.txt); built via pochivm-build cmake/make production. Liftoff/Chrome version and flags not stated in the repo.
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700HQ 2.80 GHz (single CPU), from the OOPSLA 2021 paper
tradeoffs: Research-grade proof of concept: README warns not to run untrusted WebAssembly with it. Only WebAssembly 1.0 core, partial WASI, Linux plus docker only, dead code left over from PochiVM. Only a baseline tier; no optimizing tier.
caveats: Peer-reviewed support is the OOPSLA 2021 paper 'Copy-and-Patch Compilation' (Xu and Kjolstad, Distinguished Paper Award); its abstract per search snippet gives 4.9x-6.5x faster compilation and 39%-63% faster generated code than Liftoff on Coremark and PolyBenchC, matching the README; the PDF was not opened (fredrikbk.com, sillycross.github.io, arXiv blocked; no copy in the sillycross.github.io repo). The repo benchmark harness (test_parser.cpp) measures WasmNow only; Liftoff measurements and the CPU model are not in the repo. Beats Liftoff, a baseline tier, not V8's optimizing TurboFan. Research prototype: 4 commits, last in Oct 2021; WebAssembly 1.0 core only with partial WASI (runs Coremark and PolyBenchC, other modules may hit unimplemented imports); requires AVX2 (-mavx2); the author warns not to run untrusted WebAssembly with it (unaudited JIT, sandbox-escape risk). [retier] Research prototype abandoned in 2021: partial WASI, README security warning, RWX code region, no CLI or API (PR #1 unmerged since 2023). Paper setup (OOPSLA 2021, PDF in the sillycross.github.io repo): Chrome 81 Liftoff and Wasmer 1.0 as baselines, 30+ runs, single CPU; the Liftoff JS harness and Chrome flags are not published. The timed ParseModule skips validation (the parser assumes a validated module, its checks are assert() only and compiled out by -DNDEBUG) while Liftoff is timed through new WebAssembly.Module, which must validate per the JS API, so part of the 4.9-6.5x compile-time gap may be skipped validation.

name: AsmJit
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit) in the pg_jitter shootout
workload: Machine-code generation for PostgreSQL expression evaluation through the pg_jitter AsmJit backend (PostgreSQL 18.1, 1M-row tables, thresholds forced to 0).
claimed_speedup: pg_jitter benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md), JIT compilation overhead from EXPLAIN JSON: SUM_int llvmjit 22.263 ms vs asmjit 0.109 ms; GroupBy_5agg llvmjit 45.5 ms vs asmjit 0.245 ms (about 200x less compile time, derived from page data). Query time with JIT forced on: SUM_int llvmjit 68.090 ms vs asmjit 42.201 ms (interpreter 44.859 ms); GroupBy_5agg llvmjit 149.033 ms vs asmjit 98.079 ms (interpreter 117.367 ms). pg_jitter README: AsmJit compile 'hundreds of microseconds' vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'; its 'up to 32% faster' for AsmJit on wide-row/deform-heavy queries is relative to the PostgreSQL interpreter, not to LLVM.
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 18.1; build flags not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Assembler-level C++ API for x86, x86-64, AArch32 and AArch64 with a register allocator in the Compiler layer; no mid-level optimizer; the pg_jitter AsmJit backend supports only arm64 and x86_64.
caveats: Indirect evidence: the numbers measure pg_jitter's AsmJit backend (pg_jitter's own code generator design, no optimization passes) inside PostgreSQL, not AsmJit as a library, and the AsmJit repo carries no benchmark against LLVM. The harness forces jit_above_cost, jit_inline_above_cost and jit_optimize_above_cost to 0, so LLVM pays full optimization and inlining on every query and its compile time is inside the measured execution time; execution-only, SUM_int is about 45.8 ms llvmjit vs 42.1 ms asmjit (derived from page data). On the same page the sljit backend compiles about 2x faster than AsmJit (SUM_int 0.052 ms vs 0.109 ms), so AsmJit is not the fastest emitter there. name: Box86 (x86 userspace emulator for ARM with dynarec)
baseline: QEMU user-mode (x86 guest) and FEX; also Box86's own interpreter

name: Copapy
language: Python (tracing compiler) with C runner and stencils
baseline: NumPy 2.3.5 (also a pure-Python case in tests/benchmark.py)
workload: 30,000 iterations of sum((v1 + i) @ v2 for i in range(10)) with vector length v_size varied from 10 to 500; Copapy traces the expression, compiles it once with its copy-and-patch compiler and calls one compiled function per iteration, while the NumPy version vectorises the loop with np.sum((v1 + i) @ v2).
claimed_speedup: README chart only, no numbers in text. Read from the SVG marker coordinates (derived from page data): 30,000 iterations take about 0.079 s for Copapy versus 0.308 s for NumPy 2.3.5 at v_size 10 (about 3.9x, roughly 2.6 versus 10.3 microseconds per iteration), 0.125 s versus 0.351 s at v_size 100 (about 2.8x), and 0.321 s versus 0.555 s at v_size 500 (about 1.7x). The absolute gap stays near 7.7 microseconds per iteration at every size, so the lead is NumPy's per-call overhead; the slopes are nearly equal.
compiler_and_flags: x86_64 stencils are built by tools/build.sh with gcc -fno-pic -ffunction-sections -O3 (Target default optimization 'O3'); the GCC version, the Python version and whether the benchmark used the PyPI wheel or a local build are not stated.
hardware: Ryzen 5 3400G
tradeoffs: Not a general-purpose JIT: a tracing copy-and-patch compiler for statically typed numeric computation graphs aimed at deterministic realtime use (x86_64, ARM32, AArch64 and RISC-V); generated code makes no syscalls and needs no libc; the C runner builds with GCC (tail-call optimisation required). Hardware I/O is not yet available per the README.
caveats: Baseline is NumPy 2.3.5 (float32 arrays), not PyPy, V8, LuaJIT or HotSpot; the win is small-vector call overhead: the gap is a constant ~7.7 microseconds per iteration from v_size 10 to 500 (derived from the chart), so the ratio shrinks from about 3.9x to 1.7x as vectors grow. Numbers exist only as a chart image; the results JSON the script writes is not in the repo. The Copapy case calls tg.run() (which still builds a small command buffer in Python and calls the in-process coparun runner) and never reads the result back, while the NumPy case returns a scalar each iteration; the README discloses that no data moves between Python and compiled code. The work is real, not a no-op: cp.value inputs are non-anonymous constants that the compiler keeps as runtime data. Harness nits: the pure-Python row runs iter_size//100 iterations but records iter_size//10 (that row is not plotted), and the unused cp_vs_python_sparse function contains an 'assert False'. A @cp.jit decorator exists for ordinary Python functions, but the README benchmark does not cover it and says cp.jit is not optimized for data transfer.

name: Cranelift code generator (Bytecode Alliance Wasmtime)
baseline: V8 (TurboFan) for generated-code speed; WAVM (LLVM-based Wasm engine) for compile speed
workload: CoreMark 1.0 and the 30 PolyBenchC 4.2.1 kernels compiled to WebAssembly (execution time and startup delay), plus the AutoCAD (47.5 MB) and clang.wasm (30.5 MB) modules for code-generation time only; compilation limited to one CPU for every engine; Wasmtime 0.26 Cranelift against Chrome 81 V8 TurboFan, Wasmer 1.0 and WAVM (Figs. 17-22 of the paper).
claimed_speedup: README (citing the paper's Fig. 22): generated code about 2% slower than V8 TurboFan and about 14% slower than WAVM (LLVM); compilation about an order of magnitude faster than WAVM. Paper figures, read from the bar charts (approximate): PolyBenchC average execution time normalized to copy-and-patch 0.70 for Wasmtime Cranelift, 0.69 for V8 TurboFan and 0.61 for WAVM (Fig. 22); startup delay normalized to copy-and-patch about 105-110 for Wasmtime Cranelift against about 800-1150 for WAVM on CoreMark, PolyBenchC and clang.wasm, so roughly 7-10x faster compilation than LLVM (derived from page data), while V8 TurboFan compiled faster than Cranelift on CoreMark, PolyBenchC and clang.wasm (about 45-88) and tied on AutoCAD (Fig. 18); CoreMark 10000 iterations about 0.59 s for Wasmtime Cranelift, 0.94 s for TurboFan and 0.43 s for WAVM (Fig. 20).
compiler_and_flags: Wasmtime 0.26 (Cranelift), Chrome 81 V8 (TurboFan selected with browser developer flags), Wasmer 1.0, WAVM (version not given); compilation single-threaded; the flags used to build the Wasm benchmark modules are not stated in the methodology section
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700HQ at 2.80 GHz, turbo on, 8 logical cores, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04
stars_or_usage: 18.7k stars (wasmtime repository); crate cranelift-codegen has about 51.6M downloads on crates.io; used in production inside Wasmtime
tradeoffs: Code generator tuned for fast compilation with a small trusted code base and fuzzing against V8; backends for x86-64, aarch64, s390x and riscv64. Cranelift itself is a Rust library; C and C++ programs reach it through the Wasmtime C API (wasmtime.h, wasm.h) or by compiling Wasm to native code, not through a stable Cranelift C API.
caveats: Numbers come from a 2021 third-party paper (Xu and Kjolstad, Copy-and-Patch Compilation, OOPSLA 2021, arXiv 2011.13127) measuring Wasmtime 0.26; current Cranelift (0.137) differs, so the figures are dated. The runtime result is a loss: about 2% slower than V8 TurboFan and about 14% slower than WAVM (LLVM) on the PolyBenchC average, though on CoreMark Cranelift's code ran faster than TurboFan's. The only win is compile speed against LLVM (WAVM), and V8 TurboFan compiled faster than Cranelift on three of four modules, so against V8 Cranelift loses on both axes. Figs. 21-22 are averages of three runs without confidence intervals; WAVM never finished AutoCAD (LLVM dead loop). Ratios above are read from bar charts and approximate. Rust, not C++. rustc_codegen_cranelift (wave 2, compilers-frontends) is a separate catalogue entry that uses Cranelift as a rustc backend.

name: DIO-JIT
baseline: CPython 3.8 and 3.9 (PyPy is not compared)
workload: Seven small Python programs (brainfuck interpreter, append3, DNA read, fib(15), hypot on strings, selection sort, trans), pure CPython versus the same code under the DIO-JIT decorator; each script in benchmarks/ times a fixed number of calls with timeit (fib.py 100,000 calls of f(15), trans.py 111,111,111 calls), so the README figures are presumably total seconds, though the table states no units.
claimed_speedup: fib(15): 11.63 vs 1.54 on Python 3.8 and 10.41 vs 1.51 on 3.9 (about 7x); trans 24.22 vs 7.79; append3 23.94 vs 10.70; BF 265.74 vs 134.23; selection sort 46.95 vs 33.88; DNA READ shows little gain (16.96 vs 14.82). The README also claims 500x on a partial-evaluation fib example.
tradeoffs: A JIT that runs inside CPython (3.8 and later, relies on LOAD_METHOD) and optimizes by type specialisation rules; users add @jit.jit decorators. The README says it is not production ready and many specialisation rules are still missing. Programs using bytearray and bytes see no gain.
caveats: No hardware, no units, no CPython build details, and no comparison with PyPy, which is the strong baseline for Python JIT speed. Only microbenchmarks. The docstring timings inside the scripts (fib 1.33 s vs 0.18 s, trans 2.68 s vs 0.85 s) differ from the README table, so the table came from a separate unrecorded run. In fib.py the pure-Python baseline uses a - 1 while the JIT version uses a + -1 because no rule for subtraction exists. The README's 500x partial-evaluation example (benchmarks/const_fib.py) specialises the function on the literal value 20 (jit.ofval(20)), so the JIT side returns a constant-folded result; it is not a general speedup. Requires Julia plus the DIO.jl package at runtime; no for loops, exception handling or closures inside JIT functions; README says not production-ready. LICENSE is BSD-2-Clause but setup.py declares 'mit'. Last commit 2021-02-18.

name: Easy::jit
baseline: the same kernel compiled ahead of time (non-specialised) with clang
workload: Runtime specialisation of C++ functions by embedding their LLVM IR in the binary and recompiling with LLVM ORC when argument values are known: an image convolution kernel and a quicksort kernel.
claimed_speedup: Quarkslab blog (snippet only, page blocked): the Easy::jit-specialised kernel runs 'roughly 4.5x faster than the original version' for the convolution kernel and 'around 2x faster' for the quicksort kernel, input sizes 16 to 1024; code generation stays costly, needing at least 2 convolution iterations and 29 quicksort iterations at size 1024 to pay back. The repo README and doc/slides/cppcon'18.pdf contain no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Toolchain clang/LLVM 6.0 per the README build instructions; flags used for the blog numbers not stated
tradeoffs: Compiler-assisted: needs a Clang/LLVM pass plugin and an LLVM runtime library; functions must be annotated; compile cost paid at run time, with a cache to avoid recompiling.
caveats: Snippet only: numbers come from the first-party Quarkslab blog (EuroLLVM'18 / FOSDEM'18 era), which could not be opened; no CPU or flags. Harness flaws in benchmark/benchmark.cpp: Qsort tests 'if (cmp(v[i], v[left]))' where the K&R original tests '< 0', so with int_cmp returning -1/0/1 it is not a correct sort, and it re-sorts the same vector in place every iteration; BM_convolve allocates out with (n-3)^2 ints but the kernel writes index i*(n-m+1)+j up to (n-4)(n-1), out of bounds for every tested n (both the JIT and AOT paths run the same code, so the ratio is not fabricated, but the harness has undefined behaviour); the image is all zeros; JIT compile time is excluded from the timed loop. Baseline is AOT code of the same generic function, not PyPy, LuaJIT, V8 or HotSpot. Last commit 2021-05-15; needs an LLVM 6-era toolchain. [retier] The 4.5x and 2x figures exist only in a snippet of the first-party Quarkslab blog (blocked), with the build type unknown; following the README builds the AOT baseline (kernel, Qsort) at -O0 for a generic ISA (benchmark/CMakeLists.txt sets no -O level, the cmake line passes no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE) while the JIT side always runs LLVM -O2 with CodeGenOpt::Aggressive and -mcpu=host, so the comparison is not like for like. benchmark/benchmark.cpp writes the convolution output buffer out of bounds and the qsort comparator lacks '< 0' (an O(n^2) comparator chain, not a sort). Runtime is the legacy MCJIT ExecutionEngine pinned to LLVM 6.0; abandoned since 2021-05-15; crash issues #43 and #45 unanswered.

name: Eclipse OpenJ9
baseline: HotSpot (AdoptOpenJDK 11.0.7)
workload: DayTrader7 on WebSphere Liberty with DB2 on a second machine: startup time to 'ready to run a smarter planet', RSS footprint after startup and during load, ramp-up and peak throughput.
claimed_speedup: DayTrader 3 on OpenJDK 9: with AOT enabled (shared class cache populated by an earlier cold run) OpenJ9 startup is almost 40% lower than HotSpot, with AOT plus -Xquickstart almost 50% lower (page headline '2x faster startup'); with no options OpenJ9 starts slightly slower than HotSpot. Footprint about 60% less right after startup; during ramp-up HotSpot used about 80% more RSS (headline '40% less footprint'). Similar peak throughput, reached about 7 minutes sooner by OpenJ9. Single-core cloud test (AOT plus -Xtune:virtualized): headline '4x faster ramp up', HotSpot needs about 30 minutes to peak vs 7.5 minutes for default OpenJ9. Newer pages in the same repo: OpenJDK 11 DayTrader7 51-55% faster startup and 45-57% smaller startup footprint with SCC/AOT (benchmark/openjdk11-daytrader7.md); Quarkus REST+CRUD 64-66% faster startup, 18-37% smaller startup footprint (benchmark/quarkus.md).
compiler_and_flags: AdoptOpenJDK OpenJDK9-OPENJ9 build 20170925 (OpenJ9 VM 2.9, based on jdk-9+181) vs AdoptOpenJDK OpenJDK9 HotSpot build of the same date; OpenJ9 options -Xshareclasses -Xscmx60M -Xscmaxaot8M (AOT), plus -Xquickstart, and -Xscmx150M -Xscmaxaot120m -Xtune:virtualized (cloud tuning); -Xmx1g; long --add-modules/--add-exports list for both JVMs. Native build compiler not applicable.
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770K @ 3.50GHz, 16GB RAM, HyperThreading (8 hardware threads), CentOS 7.3; JVM pinned to 4 hardware threads; Db2 and JMeter on separate machines over 10Gb Ethernet (benchmark page). The OpenJDK 11 and Quarkus pages use the same i7-3770K.
license: EPL-2.0 OR Apache-2.0 OR GPL-2.0-only WITH Classpath-exception-2.0 OR GPL-2.0-only WITH OpenJDK-assembly-exception-1.0
tradeoffs: The win is startup time and memory footprint, not peak throughput. Needs a shared class cache populated by a prior cold run for the startup gain; the AOT code is slightly larger than JIT code. Builds are AdoptOpenJDK-style OpenJDK binaries with the OpenJ9 VM and JIT in place of HotSpot.

name: Hana Jit (LLVM-backed Python JIT, hanajit)
baseline: Numba 0.66 (and NumPy 2.x)
workload: Numeric kernels compiled through llvmlite: a 5-operation fused NumPy expression, float reductions, polynomial evaluation, dot product, fib(30) recursion and call/dispatch overhead, compared with NumPy and Numba.
claimed_speedup: README summary: 5-operation fused NumPy expression 3.0x vs NumPy and 3.7x vs Numba; fib(30) 1.7x vs Numba; call/dispatch about 46 ns, 3.6x less than Numba. Four-way table: plain Hana Jit about equal to Numba (fp reduction 0.78 vs 0.74 ms, poly5 1.04 vs 0.96 ms, dot 0.80 vs 0.74 ms); evolve() 0.23, 0.22 and 0.31 ms against Numba 0.74, 0.96 and 0.74 ms, but fourway.py runs evolve(allow_fastmath=True) against plain njit without fastmath. The repo's fairer files show smaller wins: benchmarks/RESULTS-FOURWAY.md has the GA tying Numba fastmath on fp reduction (0.7 vs 0.7 ms) and the fused expression at 14.4 ms vs Numba fastmath 30.7 ms (about 2.1x, derived from page data); RESULTS-EVOLVE.md (fastmath on for both where allowed) gives a 1.19x geomean over Numba across 15 kernels; RESULTS-MICRO.md (hanajit 0.5.1) gives a 1.12x geomean over Numba across 52 workloads, driven by the dispatch rows (4.31x), with control 0.96x, recursion 0.92x and pointer 0.97x.

hardware: README: single core in a shared CI container; RESULTS.md and RESULTS-MICRO.md: x86_64, 1 core, Python 3.12.3; CPU model never stated
tradeoffs: Alpha Python package (about 3,000 lines) for numeric and array code; unsupported code falls back to the interpreter; also exports standalone x86-64 executables, WebAssembly and GPU kernels; Python-only, not callable from C++.
caveats: The README's evolve() wins over Numba compare fast-math code with strict Numba: benchmarks/fourway.py calls evolve(allow_fastmath=True) but times plain njit, and evolve.py then accepts candidates within a 1e-9 relative tolerance, so the README's 'guaranteeing an identical result' does not hold for that table; against njit(fastmath=True) the fp-reduction gain disappears (RESULTS-FOURWAY.md 0.7 vs 0.7 ms). name: Higgs (higgsjs/Higgs JavaScript JIT)
baseline: V8 (its baseline compiler; its optimizing Crankshaft compiler is faster than Higgs)
workload: 26 JavaScript benchmarks run on Higgs, a basic-block-versioning JIT for x86-64, versus V8 compilers, as reported in the DLS 2015 paper 'Extending Basic Block Versioning with Typed Object Shapes' (arXiv 1507.02437).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (paper not opened): with typed shapes and shape propagation, Higgs outperforms the V8 baseline (non-optimizing) compiler on all but one of 26 benchmarks, with speedups of up to 682%; it lags behind V8's Crankshaft (run without inlining, per one snippet), which performs 49% better on average. Abstract (snippet): the techniques eliminate on average 48% of type tests, reduce code size by 17% and reduce execution time by 25% versus Higgs with plain polymorphic inline caches.
tradeoffs: Research JIT written in D (needs the DMD compiler), x86-64 and POSIX only, needs GNU make and GNU time. Not callable from C++ without embedding a D runtime.
caveats: Weak claim: it beats only V8's old full-codegen baseline compiler (removed from V8 in 2017) and loses to Crankshaft by 49% on average; no comparison exists against any current engine. Numbers are from WebSearch snippets of arXiv 1507.02437, which could not be opened here, so hardware, V8 version and flags are unverified. Venue unverified: search results describe the paper as a CoRR/arXiv technical report from Universite de Montreal; the record's 'DLS 2015' label could not be confirmed, so it is not treated as peer-reviewed. name: Instrew
baseline: QEMU and HQEMU (LLVM-based dynamic binary translation)
workload: LLVM-based dynamic binary translator running SPEC-style integer and floating-point benchmarks for x86-64 and RISC-V64 guests on x86-64 hosts, emulation overhead relative to native.
claimed_speedup: VEE'21 paper 'Efficient LLVM-Based Dynamic Binary Translation' (snippet only, PDF blocked): on SPEC CPU2017, x86-64 guest on x86-64 host, Instrew 'achieves an emulation overhead of just 53% compared to QEMU with 648% and HQEMU with 124%'; another snippet gives mean overhead 53% (67% INT, 40% FP) for Instrew vs 124% (136% INT, 114% FP) for HQEMU and 716% (275% INT, 1541% FP) for QEMU, noting QEMU did not finish all FP benchmarks in reasonable time because of software floating point. Run time about 4.9x lower than QEMU and 1.46x lower than HQEMU (derived from snippet data, 7.48/1.53 and 2.24/1.53). The RISC-V guest figures in the search record (76% vs 202% INT, 40% vs 1267% FP) were not re-confirmed by any snippet seen here.

name: libriscv
baseline: LuaJIT (JIT mode); README also compares against wasmtime, wasm3 and Luau
workload: Embedded scripting micro-benchmarks run in the sandbox as RISC-V guest code with binary translation, versus the same tasks as LuaJIT scripts: host-to-guest call overhead, syscall cost, integer math loops, sieve of 10M.
claimed_speedup: Gist, libriscv with libtcc binary translation vs LuaJIT, medians over 200x1200 samples with call overhead subtracted for both: call overhead 2 vs 156 ns; call args=8 7 vs 197 ns; syscall args=0 10 vs 174 ns; syscall string 13 vs 186 ns; complex syscall 50 vs 873 ns; integer math 6 vs 52 ns; array append 5 vs table append 18 ns; memcpy 18 vs 87 ns; memset 15 vs 67 ns; micro threads 102 vs coroutines 166 ns; sieve(10M) 80 vs 123 ms; fib(40) 66 vs 66 ns (equal); taylor(1K) 2234 vs 858 ns (LuaJIT about 2.6x faster, derived from page data). README: VM function call 3 ns vs ~50-150 ns for other solutions; libriscv can call a 3x-sinf function 5.25-7.25 times before wasmtime has called it once.
hardware: Gist does not state the CPU; the README names a Ryzen 7950X for its other charts (CoreMark 38223 vs 41382 native, about 92%).
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; same organisation maintains godot-sandbox (487 stars)
tradeoffs: Emulator and sandbox for precompiled RISC-V programs rather than a general JIT for a dynamic language; full binary translation needs a C compiler (GCC or TCC) at run time, or the generated C99 can be embedded ahead of time for platforms that forbid executable memory. Needs a RISC-V toolchain to build guest code.
caveats: Gist does not state CPU, compiler flags, LuaJIT version or date (gist last active Oct 2025) and links no harness, so first-party tier C. The wins are mostly host-to-script call and syscall latency, which the author's rvscript README describes as the overhead of calling into Lua/LuaJIT from a game engine; it compares native-compiled RISC-V guest code against Lua scripts, not the same program. LuaJIT is about 2.6x faster on taylor(1K) (858 vs 2234 ns) and equal on fib(40); only sieve(10M) is a classic compute benchmark won (80 vs 123 ms). Benchmarks are hand-picked for game scripting; call overhead is subtracted from every result for both sides. Binary translation needs libtcc or an ahead-of-time translated build; the interpreted libriscv vs LuaJIT comparison is a separate gist. A sandbox/emulator with a JIT-like translator, not a drop-in replacement for LuaJIT as a language implementation. [retier] First-party gist without CPU model, flags or LuaJIT version; the record left out the taylor(1K) row where LuaJIT is about 2.6x faster (1038 vs 7875 ns). The LuaJIT comparison runs libtcc binary translation and the CoreMark 92%-of-native figure embedded AOT translation (libtcc 44%, interpreter 3,559 vs 41,382 native), while SECURITY.md says 'Do not use binary translation in production'. memcpy and memset wins are host-accelerated syscalls (guest naive memcpy 586 ns vs LuaJIT 87 ns). The interpreted and binary-translated gists disagree (3 vs 6-10 ns call latency), so they are not the same setup; harness source not found in rvscript. Open issue #311: default exit address raises call latency. Wins are mostly host-to-script call latency.

Cold start is a loss: the first eval of a small script takes ~47 ms against LuaJ's 13 ms. The coroutine win (19.4x) reflects virtual threads against LuaJ's platform-thread coroutines. name: oxtra
baseline: QEMU 4.1.0 (x86-64 binary translation)
workload: Static x86-64 guest programs (a primes calculator and gzip 1.10.7 compressing floating-point CSV files of 132 kB, 526 kB and 13 MB) translated to RISC-V by oxtra and by QEMU; also instruction counts and memory use.
claimed_speedup: Paper text: oxtra is 'up to twice as fast as QEMU' for small inputs. Medians, oxtra (c) vs QEMU 4.1.0: primes below 10,000 20.68 ms vs 54.71 ms (2.65x, derived from page data); gzip 132 kB 60.42 ms vs 154.83 ms (2.56x, derived from page data); gzip 526 kB 270.5 ms vs 348.9 ms (paper: 'merely 25% faster'); gzip 13 MB 2623 ms vs 3137 ms (paper: 20% faster); primes below 1,000,000 3685 ms vs 2720 ms (oxtra 35% slower). QEMU executes 1.70x (primes 10k) down to 1.13x (gzip 13 MB) as many RISC-V instructions as oxtra (c); oxtra (c) uses 3.87x (primes) and 2.55x (gzip) less peak memory than QEMU.
compiler_and_flags: Guests built with a modified musl-gcc fork (no SSE) and statically linked; host flags not stated
hardware: No real RISC-V hardware: everything ran inside system-mode QEMU running Fedora RISC-V (host CPU not stated); instruction counts given as a hardware-independent proxy
tradeoffs: Executes statically linked x86-64 programs only, no SSE support, needs a custom musl fork instead of glibc; RISC-V host only.
caveats: Student project report (documentation/paper/Paper.pdf, Results.tex), not peer reviewed. All timings were taken inside system-mode QEMU running Fedora RISC-V on an unstated host, which the authors say obscures the timing results; the large cases use only 5 runs. The README claims the current version 'consistently beats qemu in our toy examples', but the paper shows oxtra 35% slower on primes below 1 million and its advantage shrinking as inputs grow (the authors: 'oxtra quickly becomes slower than QEMU as input become larger'). The repo ships only the gzip input files, no benchmark scripts. Baseline is QEMU 4.1.0 (2019). oxtra supports only a small x86-64 subset, no SSE, statically linked musl binaries only (guests built with the project's musl-gcc fork). Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.

name: pg_jitter
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit); also PostgreSQL's expression interpreter
workload: PostgreSQL 18.1 queries on 1M-row tables (aggregation, joins, wide rows, text, numeric, jsonb), JIT thresholds set to 0, median of 3 timed runs after 2 warmups, parallel workers off.
claimed_speedup: Benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md): query time with JIT forced on, SUM_int no JIT 44.859 ms, llvmjit 68.090 ms, sljit 42.401 ms, asmjit 42.201 ms, mir 45.620 ms; GroupBy_5agg no JIT 117.367 ms, llvmjit 149.033 ms, sljit 99.530 ms, asmjit 98.079 ms, mir 125.102 ms. JIT compilation overhead (EXPLAIN JSON): SUM_int llvmjit 22.263 ms vs sljit 0.052 ms, asmjit 0.109 ms, mir 0.345 ms; GroupBy_5agg llvmjit 45.5 ms vs sljit 0.069 ms, asmjit 0.245 ms, mir 1.087 ms. README (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter): compile time 'tens to low hundreds of microseconds' (sljit) and 'hundreds of microseconds' (AsmJit) vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'; sljit '5-25% faster than the interpreter'; average speedup over the interpreter TPC-C 8%, TPC-H 6%, ecommerce 14%, OLAP 42%, CRM ~400%.
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 18.1; pg_jitter CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release; compiler, compiler version and PostgreSQL build flags not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB RAM, Darwin 25.2.0 arm64
tradeoffs: PostgreSQL extension only; beta quality by its own README; jit_above_cost must be lowered from 100000 to about 200-2000; avoid for point lookups; AsmJit backend only on arm64 and x86_64; adds embedded JIT libraries (sljit, AsmJit, MIR) in place of LLVM.
caveats: First-party benchmarks, one machine, ARM64 only (x86_64 results marked TBD), dated 2026-03-24 for release 0.3.0. The harness (tests/bench_all_backends.sh) sets jit_above_cost, jit_inline_above_cost and jit_optimize_above_cost to 0, so LLVM runs full optimization and inlining on every query and that compile time is inside the EXPLAIN ANALYZE execution time; most of the win over llvmjit is compile time (execution-only SUM_int about 45.8 ms llvmjit vs 42.3 ms sljit, derived from page data). Default thresholds would keep LLVM off these queries entirely. Per-query gains over the interpreter are small and some queries are slower (COUNT_star 0.94x for all three backends); pg_jitter.deform_cache (on by default) can reuse compiled deform code across the warmup and timed runs in one connection while LLVM recompiles, which may favour pg_jitter (not checked). The CRM benchmark is synthetic and built to show the strongest cases. Requires the author's patched forks of sljit and MIR. README calls the code beta quality. Baseline is PostgreSQL's LLVM JIT, not one of the category baselines. [retier] First-party, ARM64 only (single M1 Pro), compiler and flags unstated. The PostgreSQL 18 page comes from tests/bench_comprehensive.sh, which sets llvmjit's jit_inline_above_cost and jit_optimize_above_cost to 0 but pg_jitter's to 500000, so most of the llvmjit gap is forced LLVM compile time; execution gains over the interpreter are small (COUNT_star 0.94x). Each run is a fresh psql -c backend (about 2-2.4 ms per-connection cost where nothing compiles). Open wrong-result issue #84: the sljit backend evaluates '(SELECT 0) > 0.1' incorrectly, unanswered. The run (2026-03-24) predates the v0.3.0 tag and v0.3.1's deform-dispatch fix; no commits since 2026-05-03. Off-baseline (PostgreSQL llvmjit).

name: PochiVM (copy-and-patch baseline compiler)
baseline: LLVM 10.0.0 JIT backend of the same metaprogramming system at -O0 (also -O1/-O2/-O3) for code-generation time and generated-code speed, plus an in-house AST interpreter (about 1.5x faster than the Peloton interpreter)
workload: Eight TPC-H queries (Q1, Q3, Q5, Q6, Q10, Q12, Q14, Q19) with hand-coded query plans over a dbgen scale-factor-0.3 database (about 380 MB), lowered through PochiVM's C-like DSL to copy-and-patch, LLVM -O0..-O3 or an AST interpreter; plus Fibonacci, Euler sieve and quicksort microbenchmarks. Harness: test_mini_db_backend_unit_test.cpp (PaperBenchmark.TpchQuery*) and test_paper_microbenchmarks.cpp; each configuration repeated at least 100 times, average reported.
claimed_speedup: OOPSLA 2021 paper, Section 7.3 and Fig. 24: on 8 TPC-H queries copy-and-patch generates code two orders of magnitude faster than LLVM -O0 (up to 276x) and three orders of magnitude faster than -O1/-O2/-O3 (1083x-1435x, average 1286x); the generated code runs on average 14% faster than LLVM -O0 but 22% slower than -O1, 25% slower than -O2 and 24% slower than -O3; the AST interpreter executes 6x-27x slower than copy-and-patch (Fig. 25). Example: TPC-H Q5 code generation takes 178 us versus 0.25 s with LLVM -O3, whose code is 1.2% faster.
compiler_and_flags: Stencils and copy-and-patch runtime compiled by Clang++ 10 with -O3 -DNDEBUG; LLVM backend uses the LLVM 10.0.0 library (paper Section 7.1); repo CMakeLists.txt production flavor: clang++ -O3 -DNDEBUG -pthread
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700HQ at 2.80 GHz, single socket, 8 logical cores, turbo boost on, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04 (paper Section 6.1, reused in 7.1)
tradeoffs: Generated code is written through a C-like C++ API; research prototype, last touched 2021.
caveats: Numbers are from the authors' peer-reviewed OOPSLA 2021 paper (Xu and Kjolstad, 'Copy-and-Patch Compilation'), not an independent run; the README itself has no numbers. Generated code beats only LLVM -O0 and is 22%-25% slower than -O1..-O3; the win is compile latency. The query compiler is a 600-line prototype with hand-coded plans for only 8 TPC-H queries (no SQL parser or planner). The stencil library takes 14 minutes on 6 threads to build at install time and uses 17.5 MB at runtime. The repo has no LICENSE file; the Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception grant is stated only in the README, alongside a non-binding request not to use it for harmful projects. Abandoned research prototype (last commit 2021-09-09, a July 2021 commit adds a FIXME for a known, unfixed bug). The WebAssembly numbers in the same paper belong to WasmNow (already catalogued). Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.

name: RapidUDF
baseline: native scalar C++ (GCC -O2 for the fib comparison; native loops for the vector cases)
workload: LLVM-JIT compiled expressions/UDFs: Fibonacci function, a trigonometric expression over a 4099-element double array, and a Wilson CTR formula over float vectors, JIT with SIMD vectorisation versus the equivalent native C++ function.
claimed_speedup: README: trigonometric expression over a 4099-element double array, vectorised JIT 33,962 ns vs native 207,145 ns and scalar JIT 207,713 ns (6.10x, derived from page data); Wilson CTR over floats, vectorised JIT 6,661 ns vs native 69,961 ns ('10.5x'), but the native baseline used double literals (1.96) and ran in f64, so this is f32 SIMD against f64 scalar; the PR #9 rerun with T(1.96) gives 9.3x f32 against f32 (32-core Skylake, debug bazel build). Scalar JIT fib is 5-17% slower than native -O2.
compiler_and_flags: README: optimisation flag -O2 for the vectorised tests; native fib built at GCC -O0 and -O2; JIT at RapidUDF's default LLVM optimize_level 2 (LLVM 18+); compiler version and -march not stated. Current harness rapidudf/tests/BUILD builds benchmark.cc with copts -O2.
hardware: a CPU supporting AVX2 (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Requires LLVM 18+, highway, x86-simd-sort, sleef, abseil and others; C++17; supports a C-like DSL and table API.
caveats: The 6x and 10.5x wins come from SIMD vectorisation (Highway, AVX2) against a scalar native loop that GCC cannot auto-vectorise at -O2 because of libm calls; scalar JIT is 17% slower than native -O2 on fib, and the only 'faster than native' scalar result is against a -O0 build. In the current code sin, cos and log10 on vectors use Highway contrib math (hn::Sin, hn::Cos, hn::Log10, a few ULP and range-limited) rather than glibc libm, with SLEEF only for cosh, tan, erf, pow and similar, so results are not bit-identical to the native baseline. The README numbers come from an older harness: their benchmark names do not appear in the current rapidudf/tests/benchmark.cc, which now runs scalar/vector x native/JIT for trig, Wilson CTR f32/f64, an order rule and fib(20). CPU model and compiler version unstated. Baseline is native C++, not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot. [retier] The wins are Highway SIMD math (detectHost plus dynamic dispatch) against a scalar libm loop built -O2 without -march (SSE2 baseline) that GCC cannot auto-vectorise, not JIT against ahead-of-time code; the Wilson CTR baseline ran in f64 (double literals), so the 10.5x is not like for like (9.3x in the PR #9 rerun). name: sljit
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit) in the pg_jitter shootout
workload: Machine-code generation for PostgreSQL expression evaluation through the pg_jitter sljit backend (PostgreSQL 18.1, 1M-row tables, thresholds forced to 0).
claimed_speedup: pg_jitter BENCHMARKS_v18.md (PostgreSQL 18, ARM64 M1 Pro): execution SUM_int 68.090 vs llvmjit 42.401 ms and GroupBy_5agg 149.033 vs 99.530 ms (sljit slower than llvmjit at run time; slower than the interpreter on 27 of 108 queries, minimum 0.81x on LIKE_3wild). Compile time 0.04-0.46 ms vs llvmjit 17-2043 ms: 220-1,040x, median about 480x without the Wide1K rows (derived from page data); the Wide1K rows (21,000-29,000x) have sljit compiling almost nothing under pg_jitter 0.3.0's deform cap and are not comparable.
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 18.1; C/C++ compiler and build flags for pg_jitter, sljit and PostgreSQL not stated on the page. Benchmark script: tests/bench_comprehensive.sh in vladich/pg_jitter.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB RAM, Darwin 25.2.0 arm64
tradeoffs: Low-level stack-less JIT with a platform-independent API (x86, ARM, RISC-V, s390x, PowerPC, LoongArch, MIPS); you write the code generator yourself (no optimizer); used by PCRE2.
caveats: Indirect evidence: the numbers measure pg_jitter's sljit backend (pg_jitter's own code generator emitting through sljit), not the sljit library alone, and the sljit repo carries no benchmark of its own. pg_jitter's README tells users to build the patched fork vladich/sljit ('bug fixes, extra SIMD opcodes, memory management improvements'), so the measured code may not be upstream zherczeg/sljit. The harness runs llvmjit with jit_inline_above_cost=0 and jit_optimize_above_cost=0 (full LLVM inlining and optimization on every query) while the pg_jitter backends get 500000, which maximizes LLVM's compile time; PostgreSQL's defaults would skip LLVM optimization on cheap queries. With all thresholds at 0, LLVM compile cost dominates the end-to-end totals. Some LIKE/regex wins come from PCRE2 and StringZilla, not sljit codegen. Single machine, ARM64 only (x86_64 results 'TBD'), median of 3 runs, first-party pg_jitter numbers. The baseline is PostgreSQL's LLVM JIT, not one of the category baselines (PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot). [retier] Indirect evidence: a patched vladich/sljit fork (upstream as of February 2026 plus 2 SIMD commits) as a pg_jitter backend, not the library alone; compiler and flags unstated, ARM64 only on a single M1 Pro, and the harness forces LLVM inlining and optimization at cost 0. The Wide1K rows reflect the old deform cap that current pg_jitter source calls incorrect. pg_jitter_sljit.c adds emission time to both generation_counter and emission_counter, so EXPLAIN totals double-count it. Upstream defaults SLJIT_DEBUG=1 and SLJIT_VERBOSE=1; open crash and miscompile issues #376, #366, #271.

name: stryke (strykelang): Perl 5 compatible interpreter with bytecode VM and Cranelift JIT
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1.1774896198 (also perl 5.42.2, Python 3.14.4, Ruby 4.0.2, Julia 1.12.6, Raku)
workload: Eight small scripts (startup, fib, loop, string, hash, array, regex, map_grep) timed end to end with hyperfine, mean of at least 10 runs with 3 warmups, process startup included.
claimed_speedup: README table (stryke v0.7.7, rustc unstated, millisecond workloads including startup): faster than perl 5.42.2 on 7 of 8 rows (startup slower, 3.3 vs 2.3 ms); LuaJIT faster on 5 of 8. The regex row (0.07x vs LuaJIT, 7.1x vs perl) measures a memoised match (the engine runs once for 100,000 identical matches) and is not a regex-speed result; the map_grep, array and fib rows run MapIntMul/GrepIntModEq superinstructions, a native sort_by on presorted input and a fib_like evaluator respectively.
compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, panic abort (from Cargo.toml); rustc version not stated; measured binary reports stryke v0.7.7; LuaJIT build flags not stated
hardware: Apple M5, 18 cores
stars_or_usage: 5 stars; crate strykelang on crates.io (4454 downloads, 956 recent; created 2026-04-19)
tradeoffs: Runs Perl 5 source (a superset with parallel primitives), so it is a Perl runtime rather than a Lua or general JIT; Rust crate, no C API seen; JIT can be switched off with STRYKE_NO_JIT=1.
caveats: First-party numbers from the README benchmark section, produced by bench/run_bench_all.sh. They were measured on stryke v0.7.7, not the current 0.17.59, and the rustc version and LuaJIT build are not stated. Each script finishes in 2-14 ms with process startup included, so the rows mostly measure startup and tiny loops, not steady-state JIT speed. In the loop row stryke's total (3.2 ms) is below its own startup row (3.3 ms), so the loop cost is lost in startup noise. The rows are not like-for-like: in regex, LuaJIT runs Lua patterns, which backtrack from each start position, while stryke uses a regex engine. The array row sorts already-sorted input, which probably favours stryke's native adaptive sort over Lua's quicksort table.sort (reviewer inference, not measured). The fib row hits a fib-shape fast path in vm.rs (sub tagged fib_like, evaluated by fib_like_tail::eval_fib_like_recursive_add with an explicit stack; source comment: 'bench_fib collapses from ~2.7M recursive VM calls to a single while loop'). That path still does the full recursion work, but it measures a specialised evaluator, not general calls or the Cranelift JIT. History: strykelang/bench_fusion.rs held AST-shape matchers for the exact bench_string/hash/array/regex/map_grep/loop scripts that folded them to constants. It was wired into the compiler in 0.1.13-0.1.22 (commit a0e04a9 'fusion', 2026-04-09) and unwired by 0.1.26. The file remains in the tree as dead code, and the v0.7.7 numbers postdate the removal. bench/run_bench.sh (perl only) has a perturbed-source column to catch such matchers, but run_bench_all.sh, which produces the LuaJIT table, does not. The README text claims wins over perl on all 8 rows, but its own table shows stryke slower on startup. LuaJIT wins 5 of 8 rows, and the LuaJIT comparison is one column in a Perl-centred suite. [retier] Workloads take milliseconds and include startup (the loop row total sits below stryke's own startup row); the regex row compares Lua patterns with a regex engine and, in stryke, hits a memo cache after the first match (in v0.7.7 keyed on uninterpolated pattern text, a stale-answer bug later fixed); the array row sorts already-sorted input with native Rust sort_by; the fib row runs a fib-shaped fast path in vm.rs; map_grep runs superinstructions; run_bench.sh's perturbation check only renames variables. bench_fusion.rs folded the exact bench scripts to constants in 0.1.13-0.1.22 (commit a0e04a9), unwired by 0.1.26; the v0.7.7 numbers postdate that. Current crate 0.17.59. Rust.

name: WARP WebAssembly compiler and runtime (wasm-ecosystem/wasm-compiler)
baseline: V8 Liftoff and V8 TurboFan; SpiderMonkey Baseline and Ion
workload: Normalized compilation speed and execution speed of WebAssembly modules from the open-wasm-compiler-benchmark repo (github.com/Schleifner/open-wasm-compiler-benchmark, which returns 404 as of 2026-10-06, so the inputs are not public), WARP's vb_bench versus V8 d8 (Liftoff, TurboFan) and SpiderMonkey js shell (Baseline, Ion) and native clang builds, timed by scripts/benchmark/run_bench.py.
claimed_speedup: README quadrant chart (normalized scores, compilation / execution): WARP 0.8316 / 0.8172; V8 Liftoff 0.747 / 0.4275; V8 TurboFan 0.0423 / 0.8505; SpiderMonkey Baseline 0.8136 / 0.3456; SpiderMonkey Ion 0.099 / 0.8163; native clang 0.5 (comp. speed N/A) / 0.873.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark guide (scripts/benchmark/Readme.md): vb_bench built with clang/clang++, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, -DINTERRUPTION_REQUEST=0 -DEAGER_ALLOCATION=1, VB_ENABLE_DEV_FEATURE=OFF; V8 d8 built with tools/dev/gm.py x64.release and run with --no-wasm-lazy-compilation --liftoff or --no-liftoff --single-threaded; SpiderMonkey built with an optimized mozconfig and run with --wasm-compiler=baseline or ion --cpu-count=1. Compiler, V8 and SpiderMonkey versions not stated.
tradeoffs: Single-pass compiler and runtime aimed at embedded systems (x86_64, aarch64, tricore; aarch32 not implemented), written in C++14 with no external dependencies in production code; 187 kB stripped binary (AArch64, Clang 17, macOS). Compiles ahead of time into an ELF-like artifact that the runtime instantiates.
caveats: Result is a normalized unitless quadrant chart; run_bench.py prints wall-clock means and a score of 10000/geomean, but how the 0-1 chart values were derived is not documented, and native clang's compile score is a placeholder 0.5 ('comp. speed N/A'). CPU model and tool versions are not stated. Benchmark inputs (Schleifner/open-wasm-compiler-benchmark) are not publicly reachable (404). Harness flaws: the compilation benchmark times the whole process with /usr/bin/time -p (10 ms resolution), so d8 and SpiderMonkey js-shell startup and JS harness load are charged to their compile time while WARP runs as a small native binary, which favours WARP; default is a single run per module (-n 1); the 'V8 Liftoff' runs do not pass --no-wasm-tier-up, so hot code may tier up to TurboFan. WARP's execution score (0.8172) is below V8 TurboFan (0.8505) and native clang (0.873) and about equal to SpiderMonkey Ion (0.8163); its win is compile speed at near-optimizing-tier execution speed, and clearly over the single-pass baselines Liftoff (0.4275) and SpiderMonkey Baseline (0.3456). Backing paper (Scheidl, Valent-Blocks, iCCECE 2020) was not opened (IEEE and ResearchGate blocked); a search snippet only says WebAssembly overhead on embedded targets fell from 87% to 21%.

name: WrenJIT
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1 with JIT on (docs/index.html report names LuaJIT 2.1.1785763465; build flags not stated); the report also shows a LuaJIT -joff column
workload: Nine small paired kernels, each written once in Wren and once in Lua (sum, range for, fib, tak, ack, mutual recursion, deep recursion, binary trees, method call); the Wren timer includes JIT warmup and compilation, process startup excluded; best of five self-timed runs.
claimed_speedup: README microbenchmark table, WrenJIT vs LuaJIT time (lower is better): sum 0.641 ms vs 1.092 ms (0.59x), range for 0.074 ms vs 0.584 ms (0.13x), fib(35) 39.4 ms vs 51.9 ms (0.76x), tak 2.224 ms vs 6.361 ms (0.35x), ack(3,7) 0.024 ms vs 1.066 ms (0.02x), mutual recursion 0.098 ms vs 0.321 ms (0.31x), deep recursion 0.625 ms vs 6.724 ms (0.09x), binary trees 8.807 ms vs 19.8 ms (0.45x), method call 0.087 ms vs 0.448 ms (0.19x). Five of these rows do not time equivalent work: range for and method call are computed in closed form by optimizer passes 15-16 (irOptFastForwardRangeSum, irOptFastForwardToggleCounter), ack is replaced by the closed form 2^(n+3)-3 for m=3, mutual recursion by a parity test, and deep recursion is collapsed into a loop, while LuaJIT runs the real loops and calls; binary trees run a hand-written C tree builder and walker. Rows with comparable work: sum 0.59x, fib 0.76x, tak 0.35x. The author's own published report (docs/index.html, ten Benchmarks Game ports) says WrenJIT is faster than LuaJIT on 1 of 10: pidigits 66.4 ms vs 119.8 ms (0.55x); slower on the rest, e.g. nbody 848.4 ms vs 31.8 ms (26.69x slower), regex-redux 19.06x, k-nucleotide 5.68x, fasta 5.25x, binary-trees 4.25x, fannkuch-redux 3.63x, mandelbrot 3.15x, spectral-norm 1.68x, reverse-complement 1.58x.
compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release with a C99 compiler (compiler not named); SLJIT backend; pinned Wren 99d2f0b and sljit d9902b1; LuaJIT build and flags not stated
hardware: Apple M4 Pro
tradeoffs: Only runs Wren programs (a patched Wren VM, patches/0001-wren-jit-hooks.patch). One trace per loop PC, no side traces or trace chaining. Recursion is compiled by recognising complete bytecode shapes and emitting native kernels, not by a general method JIT. Tested on ARM64 and x86-64 only.
caveats: The README calls these 'narrow kernels, not a language-wide victory lap'. Several microbenchmark rows measure benchmark-shaped special cases rather than JIT code doing the same work as LuaJIT: src/jit/wren_jit_recursion.c recognizes exact bytecode shapes and emits Ackermann as the closed form 2^(n+3)-3 (no recursion), mutual even/odd recursion as a single parity test, linear recursion as a loop, and binary-tree make/check through hand-written C (treeMakeFill and a C tree walker); optimizer passes 15-16 in src/jit/wren_jit_opt.c fast-forward range sums and boolean toggle counters in closed form (the report admits these are 'reduced as recurrences instead of paid one iteration at a time'). Outputs are correct and the specializations are guarded, but the 0.02x-0.19x rows say nothing about general Wren code. On the author's ten paired Benchmarks Game ports (docs/index.html; also bench/benchmarksgame_results.json from an earlier run) WrenJIT is slower than LuaJIT on 9 of 10 programs (up to 26.7x slower on nbody) and slower than the plain Wren interpreter on k-nucleotide; only pidigits wins. Programs are separate Wren and Lua ports, self-timed with System.clock/os.clock, best of five, sub-millisecond timings on several rows; Wren timer includes JIT warmup. C compiler not named; LuaJIT build flags not stated. Single author, 4 stars, repo started 2026-02-22. [retier] Claim overstated: ack, range-for, method-call and mutual-recursion benchmarks are closed-form or O(1) replacements (wren_jit_recursion.c, optimization passes 15-16), deep recursion is collapsed to a loop and binary trees run hand-written C; only sum (0.59x), fib (0.76x) and tak (0.35x) compare like work. The fib, linear, Ackermann and Takeuchi shape matchers never check operator symbols or that the call target is the function itself (the README says symbols are validated), so a hot static method with the same bytecode shape gets the wrong native kernel after 50 calls; pass 16 deletes body nodes after the range-sum add without checking the body is otherwise empty; pass 18 is spectral-norm-specific; bench/run_benchmarks.py never compares Wren and Lua outputs. The author's own docs/index.html shows WrenJIT slower than LuaJIT on 9 of 10 Benchmarks Game ports (nbody 26.7x slower) and an earlier run had the JIT slower than the Wren interpreter on fannkuch (11.43 vs 7.12 s), fasta and regex-redux. Compiler and LuaJIT build flags unstated.

name: XS (xs-lang)
baseline: CPython 3.13 and Node 20 (V8), measured in the same README table; the Node column is dominated by Node's own 57 ms process startup
workload: README: two programs run cold from disk with wall time including process startup: hello world (startup) and recursive fib(30); XS shown in --interp, --vm and --jit modes; best of three runs. The repo's benchmarks/run.sh adds sort, mandelbrot, nbody, json, strings, hash and startup ports in XS, Python, JavaScript and Go.
claimed_speedup: README table (wall time including process startup, best of three): fib(30) XS --jit 31 ms vs Node 20 62 ms vs Python 3.13 71 ms (--vm 180 ms, --interp 950 ms); hello world startup XS 3 ms vs Node 57 ms vs Python 15 ms. Subtracting each runtime's hello-world startup, fib(30) compute is about 28 ms for XS --jit vs about 56 ms for CPython (about 2x faster) and about 5 ms for Node (XS about 5x slower than V8) (derived from page data). The committed cross-runtime run (benchmarks/results.json, 2026-05-03, best of 5) shows fib XS --jit 0.038 s vs python3 0.083 s vs node 0.117 s vs go 0.005 s, and mandelbrot XS --jit 0.577 s vs python3 0.338 s vs node 0.112 s, i.e. XS slower than both CPython and Node on mandelbrot.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README table; Makefile default build is gcc -O2 -std=c11, make release is -O3 -flto -DNDEBUG; which build produced the table is not said
hardware: Linux x86-64, AMD Ryzen 7 (exact model not stated)
tradeoffs: A new language shipped as one static binary with compiler, language server, formatter and package manager; compiles to native code, JavaScript or WebAssembly. The JIT compiles only the opcodes in its supported set and falls back to the VM for the rest, and is meant for profiled hotspots.
caveats: The README says 'treat as indicative, not authoritative'. Only one compute benchmark (call-bound recursive fib) is shown, and every timing includes process startup: Node 20's 57 ms startup is almost all of its 62 ms fib(30) time, so the apparent 2x win over Node is a startup artifact and on compute XS --jit is about 5x slower than V8 (derived from page data); the win over CPython (about 2x on fib compute) is real on this one kernel. The README omits the repo's own mandelbrot result (benchmarks/results.json: XS --jit 0.577 s vs CPython 0.338 s vs Node 0.112 s), where XS is slower than both baselines; the other rows in that file (sort, nbody, json, strings, hash) run 1-30 ms and are dominated by Python and Node startup. The reproduction pointer tests/bench_backends.sh only compares XS's own backends (median, fib(28), no Node or Python); the cross-runtime harness is benchmarks/run.sh. In the 2026-04-24 benchmarks/baseline.json the JIT was no faster than the VM (fib 0.155 s vs 0.150 s). CPU model ('AMD Ryzen 7') and compiler/build not stated. XS is its own language, not a drop-in for JavaScript or Python programs, and is unrelated to the Moddable XS JavaScript engine.

name: HHVM
baseline: PHP reference interpreter (Zend Engine), 2014-era version per the OOPSLA 2014 paper (version not seen); HPHPc as a second comparison
workload: Server-side Hack (formerly PHP) programs executed by a JIT virtual machine.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (OOPSLA 2014 paper 'The HipHop Virtual Machine', Adams et al., not opened): 'in sandbox mode HHVM attains a 1.6x speedup over PHP when running real-world applications' (HPHPc could not run these applications; HHVM could not run Drupal); on the paper's benchmark suite HHVM reaches a geometric mean speedup of 2.64x in sandbox mode and 2.79x in production mode, compared to HPHPc's 1.93x (the snippet does not name the base of these ratios). The README itself only says HHVM 'uses a just-in-time (JIT) compilation approach to achieve superior performance'.
license: PHP-3.01 AND Zend-2.0 (core); MIT (Hack typechecker and Hack Standard Library)
tradeoffs: Runs Hack (and, historically, PHP 5/7 code) only; HHVM now targets Hack and PHP support was dropped in later releases (not verified on the pages opened), so any PHP comparison is historical; needs a webserver such as Proxygen or FastCGI.
caveats: Numbers are from search snippets of the OOPSLA 2014 paper (dl.acm.org and the SPLASH page are blocked here); PHP version, hardware and flags unverified. The comparison is against 2014-era PHP; PHP 7 and later changed the interpreter substantially, and the current README describes HHVM as a VM for programs written in Hack, so a Zend-PHP baseline no longer matches what current HHVM runs. Authors are Meta engineers (first-party, peer-reviewed). The Zend-2.0 licence part is not OSI-approved, hence usability mixed. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.

name: LC Scheme BBV JIT (bsaleil/lc)
baseline: Gambit Scheme v4.9.3 and Chez Scheme v9.5.2 (mature AOT Scheme compilers, safe and unsafe modes); also Pycket (February 2019 build, Racket tracing JIT on RPython) for total time
workload: JIT compiler for Scheme on Linux x86-64 using lazy basic-block versioning with interprocedural code specialization (entry and return point tables). Experiments use 38 classic Scheme benchmarks taken from Gambit with Gambit's iteration counts (ack, boyer, browse, compiler, conform, cpstak, deriv, earley, fft, fftrad4, fib, fibfp, mbrot, nbody, nqueens, nucleic, peval, pnpoly, simplex, sum, sumfp, tak, takl and others), driven by tools/benchtimes/run.py; the Gambit and Chez comparison times generated code only (GC and compile time excluded), the Pycket comparison includes JIT compile time.
claimed_speedup: PhD thesis (Saleil 2019, Fig. 6.16, execution time excluding GC and compilation time, 38 benchmarks): average execution time relative to LC is Gambit safe 1.38x, Chez safe 1.27x, Gambit unsafe 1.12x, Chez unsafe 1.09x; LC is faster on more than half of the benchmarks; best case fftrad4 with Gambit at 4.03x (safe) / 3.29x (unsafe) and Chez at 5.10x (safe) / 4.60x (unsafe) of LC's time. Against Pycket (Fig. 6.17, including JIT compile time, excluding GC): LC is 0.87x Pycket's time on average (0.80x with f64vectors), faster on 22 of 38, best nucleic 0.13x, worst fft 3.40x. VMIL 2018 paper (Section 6.3, i7-4870HQ, Gambit v4.8.9 cited): LC optimized generated code 1.47x faster than Gambit on average, faster on 26 of 38; 1.35x faster than Pycket on average (22 of 37 significantly faster); 2.25x over LC naive mode. ECOOP 2017 abstract: 'up to 50% faster' refers to interprocedural versus intraprocedural LC; against Gambit unsafe the generated code ranges from 34% faster (browse) to 390% slower (pnpoly). The README fib(40) timing (0.550 s real) has no baseline.
compiler_and_flags: LC built against the modified Gambit fork (bsaleil/gambit); the Makefile default target compiles LC with gsc -prelude "(declare (not safe))" and config-release.scm (README shows make debug); benchmark runs use --max-versions 5 with interprocedural specialization, tagging and eager flonum unboxing. Gambit v4.9.3: gsc -:m512000 -exe with prefix (declare (standard-bindings) (extended-bindings) (block)), plus (not safe) for unsafe mode. Chez Scheme 9.5.2 single-threaded build: compile-program, optimize-level 2 (safe) or 3 (unsafe), run with scheme --program. The optimize-level and (not safe) settings are stated in the thesis text, not in the committed harness.
hardware: Thesis: Intel Core i7-7700K 4.20 GHz, 16 GB DDR4, GNU/Linux (otherwise unused machine). VMIL 2018 and ECOOP 2017: Intel Core i7-4870HQ, 16 GB DDR3, GNU/Linux; 10 runs per benchmark, min and max dropped, mean of the remaining 8.
stars_or_usage: 33 stars, 1 fork; ECOOP 2017 (artifact-evaluated, DARTS 3.2.14), VMIL 2018, SFPW 2014 and SFPW 2015 papers, and Baptiste Saleil's 2019 Universite de Montreal PhD thesis
tradeoffs: Research JIT, Linux x86-64 only, written in Gambit Scheme and needs a modified Gambit (bsaleil/gambit) fork built first and gsc on PATH at build and run time; the build target is 'make debug'. Specialises by lazy basic-block versioning, so code size and entry-point table memory grow with version limits (the paper tracks code size and table sizes).
caveats: Research JIT, last commit 2019-05-11, abandoned; x86-64 Linux only and needs the author's modified Gambit fork. The averages are modest and mode-dependent: LC skips vector bounds checks, stack-overflow checks and interrupt polling (the thesis cites about 15% polling overhead for Gambit), so the safe-mode leads (1.38x Gambit, 1.27x Chez) partly compare unequal safety, and in unsafe mode the lead shrinks to 1.12x and 1.09x with LC losing on a large minority of benchmarks; the Gambit and Chez times exclude GC and compilation time. VMIL 2018 lists missing features (no first-class continuations, limited eval). The repo commits no timing results; the numbers live in the papers and thesis (PDFs in github.com/bsaleil/bsaleil.github.io/docs; the dagstuhl and schemeworkshop.org copies were EGRESS_BLOCKED). The harness hard-codes the author's /home/bapt paths, has every system except LC5 commented out, and does not set Chez's optimize-level or Gambit's (not safe) mode, which only the thesis states. The ECOOP 2017 'up to 50% faster' figure is LC interprocedural versus LC intraprocedural, not versus Gambit or Chez. [retier] Thesis and VMIL 2018 numbers (i7-7700K, flags stated, harness in tools/benchtimes) give Gambit v4.9.3 1.38x LC's time in safe mode and 1.12x unsafe, Chez 9.5.2 1.27x and 1.09x, but LC's --time measures a warm second in-process run against cold fresh-process baselines, and the committed baseline prefixes use generic arithmetic without the thesis settings; GC and compile time excluded; the ECOOP 'up to 50%' compares LC's own modes. README builds the 2018 stable branch with make debug. Papers reachable only through the author's github.io repo via raw.githubusercontent.com. Abandoned since 2019.

name: quickjs-jit (Longbridge JIT-enabled QuickJS-NG distribution)
language: Rust (with the vendored QuickJS-NG C engine)
baseline: QuickJS-NG interpreter (same runtime with the JIT detached); Bun 1.4.0 (JavaScriptCore) also measured as the external target
workload: 35 JavaScript scenarios (scalar loops, fibonacci, calls, property access, typed arrays, JSON, regexp, collections, exceptions); latency in ms per ten workload calls, median over processes of each process's upper-median of 16 timed batches, paired geometric-mean ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
claimed_speedup: Current README matrix (35 scenarios, Linux x86_64, measured 2026-09-30, revision 8fa2a48 = v0.12.11; QuickJS = the same binary with the JIT detached, QuickJS-NG fd0a0210): versus QuickJS 23 scenarios faster, 7 tied, 5 slower; e.g. scalar-control-flow 49.2x faster (2.13 ms vs 0.0434 ms per ten calls), scalar-expressions 47.4x, fibonacci-iterative 45.8x, quickjs-bitops 42.6x, fibonacci-recursive 27.1x (9.91 ms vs 0.361 ms), float64-dense 22.2x; slower cases collections 0.98x, strings-json 0.96x, json-codec 0.96x, map-set-bigint 0.99x, exceptions-promises-async 0.98x. Versus Bun 1.4.0 all 35 scenarios are slower (closest fibonacci-recursive 0.73x of Bun speed, widest methods-dynamic 0.012x).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98.1 / LLVM 22.1.8, release build (harness built with 'cargo build --release --manifest-path benchmarks/Cargo.toml --bins'); JIT back end is Cranelift 0.116 (jit/Cargo.toml); QuickJS-NG commit fd0a0210b7be00957751871e7e01b8291268fc29 compiled through the sys crate's build.rs with the cc crate's release defaults (C compiler and version not named); Bun 1.4.0 default flags, launched from a .mjs file
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i7-13700KF, Linux 7.2.5 x86_64, CPU 8 pinned, powersave governor (the same README also has an Apple M3 matrix, no CPU pinning)
stars_or_usage: 15 stars, 1 fork (GitHub fork of DelSkayn/rquickjs); published on crates.io as quickjs-jit (latest 0.12.6, 2026-09-03, 110 downloads); the measured 0.12.11 exists only in git
tradeoffs: Experimental tiered JIT on top of QuickJS-NG; the JIT ABI depends on internal QuickJS structure layouts so the runtime, core and sys crates must be the same patch version; consumed as a Rust crate (rquickjs API), so C++ users would have to take the C engine plus JIT sources from the repo directly.
caveats: First-party matrix run on the author's own machine, though the harness, scripts, raw process records, metadata and binary hashes are all in the repo. Not a V8 win: every scenario is slower than Bun (JavaScriptCore) and V8 was not measured. The interpreter control is QuickJS-NG (fd0a0210) in the same binary with the JIT detached, not Bellard's QuickJS. Wins are on scalar and numeric kernels (many 20-50x); string, JSON, collection, regexp and exception scenarios are tied or 1-4% slower. v0.12.11 fixed a 0.12.10 regression in real gpui-shell renders by deferring P2 opcodes, which gave back exceptions-sync (0.21x the speed of 0.12.10) and for-of-array (0.36x) to interpreter speed. The protocol warms 640 calls and polls the JIT after every batch, so embedders that never poll see different tier-up behaviour; the diagnostics table shows compilation still active during timing on some kernels (float64-dense: only 4 of 30 processes quiet, 29 outlier batches; numeric 9 quiet). The JIT is Rust (Cranelift 0.116) over a vendored C engine, outside a strict C++ filter. Development is AI-assisted (AGENTS.md; recent commits co-authored by claude). crates.io has only 0.12.6; the README warns that runtime and core crates must share an exact patch version.

name: Topaz (Ruby on RPython)
baseline: CRuby (MRI) 2.7.7p221 and 3.2.1p31, interpreter without JIT
workload: Thirteen simplified Benchmarks Game style programs (binarytrees, brainfuck, brainfuck2, fannkuchredux, fasta, knucleotide, mandelbrot, matmul, nbody, pidigits, regexdna, revcomp, spectralnorm); best of up to 5 runs, time measured inside the language, in seconds.
claimed_speedup: Faster than CRuby 2.7.7 on 12 of 13 programs (derived from page data): fannkuchredux 0.43 s vs 4.34 s, mandelbrot 1.47 s vs 16.74 s, matmul 1.83 s vs 18.39 s, spectralnorm 1.44 s vs 17.18 s, nbody 5.42 s vs 43.56 s, brainfuck 17.41 s vs 115.31 s, binarytrees 1.97 s vs 6.75 s, fasta 5.29 s vs 18.19 s; smallest win pidigits 7.78 s vs 11.42 s; slower only on revcomp (7.3 s vs 4.2 s). Also faster than the same run's Ruby 3.2.1 interpreter on 12 of 13 (revcomp 7.3 s vs 3.67 s slower).
compiler_and_flags: Topaz translated with rpython -Ojit on PyPy 2.7 v7.3.6 inside Docker (docker/topaz); CRuby built from source with a plain ./configure and make (docker/ruby2); gcc 12.2.0 for the C reference; no extra optimisation flags given
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars (topazproject/topaz); the measured fork kostya/topaz is a fork of it
tradeoffs: Implements Ruby on RPython; the README does not state which Ruby version or how much of CRuby 2.7 or 3.x it covers, so compatibility is unverified. Translation with RPython takes 5-10 minutes and needs a PyPy source tree at tag release-2.4.0 per the upstream README. Memory use is higher than CRuby on allocation heavy runs (binarytrees 63.1 MB vs 44.6 MB Ruby 2.7 in the same table).
caveats: The code measured is not this repository: docker/topaz clones kostya/topaz, a fork by the shootout's own author (8 stars, last commit 2023-01-27) whose README says the original 'is not developed since 2016' and that the fork fixes the build on newer PyPy and speeds up 'some small things for benchmark', e.g. a faster default hash implementation; its commits include 'Optimize hash, by 8 times get/set operations' and 'Make file read operations much faster, by using stream'. Upstream topazproject/topaz (last commit 2022-06-18) would likely be slower on hash- and IO-heavy programs (knucleotide, fasta, revcomp, regexdna). Outputs pass the suite's own check step (Topaz is not on any expected_check_failed list). Baseline is CRuby 2.7.7; the shootout has no YJIT row. Times are measured inside the program, best of up to 5 iterations, so startup is excluded. Topaz implements only part of Ruby, so the programs exercise a small slice of the language. Single benchmark author, one machine, one round (2023-02-28). Found by harvesting a row from a shootout, not from a Topaz-authored claim. RPython/Python project, not C++. [retier] Measured binary is the kostya/topaz fork (unpinned HEAD), tuned 'for benchmark' with an 8x hash path that drops Hash#compare_by_identity semantics (17 rubyspec tags fail) and never compacts deletes; upstream Topaz (abandoned 2022-06-18, last real development 2017, pinned to PyPy 2.4.0) was not measured. kostya/jit-benchmarks takes the best of up to 5 warm in-process iterations while CRuby 2.7.7 finished one brainfuck iteration (115.31 s); revcomp uses 787.5 MB vs CRuby 164.4 MB; no YJIT or CRuby 3.x row.

name: TruffleRuby
baseline: CRuby 4.0.6 (MRI interpreter), also CRuby with --jit (YJIT)
workload: kostya/benchmarks: Brainfuck bench.b, matmul, primes, JSON, base64, run as the same Ruby scripts under each Ruby implementation.
claimed_speedup: Are We Fast Yet 2016 (runtime factor over Java 1.8.0_91): geomean 2.36 vs Node.js 2.89, faster than Node on only 6 of 14 benchmarks, the edge mostly from Node's Bounce outlier. kostya/benchmarks against CRuby 4.0.6: about 16x on bench.b, 12x on Matmul, 2x on Primes, but about 1.9x slower on Base64 and about 10x slower on Json (10.618 s vs 1.031 s); slower than LuaJIT and PyPy on 4 of 6 shared tests (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: TruffleRuby 34.0.1 native and JVM release tarballs vs CRuby 4.0.6 built with CC=clang ./configure --enable-yjit (docker/Dockerfile); scripts run via `truffleruby`, `ruby`, `ruby --jit`.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Docker (Debian forky/sid) per README Environment section; base image and interpreter builds in docker/Dockerfile
tradeoffs: Needs warm-up and much more memory (bench.b: 197.19 + 693.00 MiB vs 12.12 + 0.00 MiB for CRuby in the kostya tables). README offers two configurations: Native (faster startup) and JVM (better peak performance).
caveats: Mixed against every listed baseline. On AWFY the geomean edge over Node.js comes mostly from Node's Bounce outlier, and Node.js has the better median. On kostya/benchmarks TruffleRuby is slower than LuaJIT and PyPy on 4 of the 6 shared tests (mandel.b, Json, Matmul, Primes), with Matmul 5.4x and Json 17x slower than PyPy. Node.js beats it on every kostya test shown. On kostya/jit-benchmarks 2023 it wins about half the time. AWFY numbers date from 2016, and the paper is co-authored by Benoit Daloze, a TruffleRuby developer, so it is peer-reviewed but not independent. JVM mode has high memory use (about 350 MB base RSS on kostya). plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2) lists Ruby only on the proprietary 'Graal EE 23.1.1' build. The README claim ('fastest Ruby implementation', yjit-bench) compares against other Rubies, not the listed baselines. [retier] The kostya Dockerfile downloads truffleruby-34.0.1-linux-amd64 and truffleruby-jvm tarballs, which are Oracle GraalVM builds under the GraalVM Free Terms and Conditions, not the EPL/GPL/LGPL truffleruby-community builds the install guide calls slower, so the numbers do not represent the open-source build; the timed region includes JIT warm-up. Mixed against every listed baseline; clear wins only over other Ruby implementations. The AWFY paper is co-authored by TruffleRuby developer Daloze. Repo now at truffleruby/truffleruby; issue #4093 reports about 159 s vs 43 s on Ruby 4.0 YJIT. Java, not C++.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): smarr/are-we-fast-yet docs/performance.md row 'JRuby+Truffle' and kostya/benchmarks truffleruby rows
kostya/benchmarks README (opened); LangArena README and plb2 README list TruffleRuby as the Ruby contender

verification.tier_reason: The AWFY performance report (suite of the peer-reviewed DLS'16 paper) shows the record's JRuby+Truffle and Node.js values exactly, and kostya/benchmarks (Intel Xeon E-2324G, versions listed, public Docker harness) shows the bench.b numbers exactly, so the evidence stays tier B. The claim is overstated, hence downgrade: TruffleRuby beats Node.js on only 6 of 14 AWFY benchmarks, and beats LuaJIT and PyPy on only 1 of 6 shared kostya/benchmarks tests. The two kostya suites are A-level reproducible but mostly show it slower, so they cannot support an A-tier 'faster' claim.
verification.notes: All quoted numbers check out (AWFY JRuby+Truffle row; kostya bench.b rows and versions), but the record picks the one kostya test where TruffleRuby wins; recorded shortcoming should be 'mostly not faster than LuaJIT/PyPy/V8; wins are against other Ruby implementations'. Metadata checked on github.com: EPL-2.0 OR GPL-2.0-only OR LGPL-2.1-only triple licence, 3.2k stars, not archived, last commit 2026-09-26. The DLS'16 paper PDF (stefan-marr.de) is EGRESS_BLOCKED.
