name: WeavePy
baseline: CPython 3.14.8
workload: 24 in-repo Python benchmark fixtures (deltablue, richards, nbody, fannkuch, fib, spectral_norm, json_bench, pickle_bench, pidigits, etc.) plus a startup fixture, run by the weavepy-bench gate; per-fixture median of the fixture's own timer, interleaved with CPython on the same machine.
claimed_speedup: README (i9-9980HK, CPython 3.14.8 from PATH): geomean 0.50x CPython time over 21 of 24 fixtures (report.rs drops deque_ops, datetime_ops and pickle_bench from the CPython geomean); all 24 rows give 0.53x and about 0.70-0.71x without the sumvm, jitloop and nested_loops micro-loops (derived from page data). The committed macOS-aarch64 baseline of 2026-09-07 showed 2.75x CPython's time.
compiler_and_flags: Release profile in Cargo.toml (opt-level 3, lto = fat, codegen-units 1); the parity doc says only 'release build', so whether tools/pgo_build.py (-Cprofile-generate/-Cprofile-use, trained on the benchmark fixtures at the harness work sizes plus regrtest and an import sweep) was used for the 0.50 run is not stated (PR #82's 0.592 run was PGO). Rust version not stated (rust-toolchain.toml pins 'stable'); CPython 3.14.8 source and build flags not stated. JIT on by default.
hardware: macOS x86-64 development host, Intel Core i9-9980HK
tradeoffs: Python interpreter written in Rust aiming at drop-in CPython 3.14 compatibility, but compatibility is still partial (README tracks conformance against CPython's own test suite); the report says importing large stdlib modules still costs about 2x CPython and peak memory after those imports is about 2x. Needs a Rust toolchain; native JIT tiers.
caveats: Own harness and fixtures on one development laptop (macOS x86-64, i9-9980HK); the CPython 3.14.8 build and its flags are not stated, and neither are the Rust version or whether the measured binary was PGO. The PGO script trains on the very benchmark fixtures at the exact work sizes used for timing, so PGO numbers are fixture-tuned. Fixture timers discard the computed result, so the harness does not check outputs (correctness rests on separate test suites). The README's per-wave history still lists committed baselines of 2.85x CPython's time (slower) on a macOS-aarch64 host, and the September PERFORMANCE.md showed process startup slower than CPython on ARM64 (32.27 ms vs 22.08 ms), so the 0.50 geomean is new (PR #83, 2026-10-05), from a different host, and not reproduced elsewhere; the A/B gates on Linux, macOS ARM64 and Windows compare against main, not CPython. The geomean is dominated by JIT-friendly loop kernels (sumvm, jitloop, nested_loops at 0.05-0.08). Peak memory up to 2-2.5x CPython's. Very new project: 80 commits, single author, 3 stars. [retier] PGO or plain release unstated (PR #83 never mentions PGO; the parity doc says release build), rustc version and CPython build unstated, fixture outputs unchecked, one laptop, 3 stars, unpublished on crates.io (MSRV 1.93); the result swung from 2.75x slower to 0.5x within a month. Rust.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust Python interpreter faster than CPython benchmark startup github' surfaced PR #82 (weavefoundry/weavepy); then opened docs/PERFORMANCE-CPYTHON-PARITY.md, tools/pgo_build.py and Cargo.toml

Small or no win on text tests: fasta 6.81 s vs 8.65 s, knucleotide 8.33 s vs 8.41 s; slower on regexdna 6.1 s vs 5.2 s; brainfuck 165.97 s vs CPython timing out above 190 s. tradeoffs: Needs a build step and a C/C++ compiler; the large speedups require cdef type annotations and C-level constructs, i.e. effectively a different (typed) program. Output can be C++ and linked from C++ code.

Several CPython rows are a single run (binarytrees, nbody). Time is measured inside the program with time.time(), so process start-up and the 0.8-2.6 s Cython+gcc compile time are excluded. Versions are old (Cython 0.29.30, Python 3.10.7, round 1 dated 2023-02-28, not rerun). Cython's own README makes no numeric speed claim. Cython is a Python-to-C compiler rather than an interpreter.

baseline: QuickJS (bellard, version 2026.06.04 in the CI table); V8 and JavaScriptCore are NOT beaten

The composite win comes from three numeric subtests: Richards 11374 vs 1246, Crypto 10633 vs 1170, NavierStokes 21200 vs 2349 (about 9x each, derived from page data); lumen is slower than QuickJS on RayTrace (1925 vs 2408), EarleyBoyer (1808 vs 3217) and Splay (5444 vs 5786). caveats: The README makes no speed claim; the claim here comes only from a third-party engine shootout. On the Ubuntu x86-64 runner lumen scores 444 against QuickJS 1217 and is slower on every subtest; the README says the full set of inline JIT fast paths lives only in the ARM64 backend, while the x86-64 backend is correctness-first with checked per-op helpers. Lumen is not run on Windows in the shootout. It is far behind JIT engines (V8, JavaScriptCore, Node, Bun) on both platforms. name: bc and dc (Gavin Howard)
baseline: GNU bc 1.07.1
workload: bc scripts run through tests/script.sh (add, subtract, multiply, divide), 1234567890^100000, a patched timeconst.bc script and two 100,000,000-iteration loop scripts; best of four runs, wall-clock seconds.
claimed_speedup: With -O2 and no LTO (wall time, GNU bc vs this bc): addition 2.54 s vs 0.88 s, multiplication 7.15 s vs 2.20 s, division 3.36 s vs 1.61 s, power 11.30 s vs 0.73 s, timeconst.bc 16.71 s vs 13.16 s. With -O3 -flto -march=native: power 11.08 s vs 0.71 s, multiplication 7.01 s vs 1.59 s. Slower on a plain for-loop script (16.60 s GNU vs 22.76 s this bc at -O2).
compiler_and_flags: clang 9.0.1; both bc builds compiled with the same flags: -O2 without LTO, then -O3 -flto -march=native, then -O3 -flto.
hardware: x86_64 machine running Gentoo Linux; CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 253 stars, 42 forks, 6,072 commits; per the README it is the system bc in FreeBSD, macOS and Android (AOSP external/bc) and in several Linux distributions, and it is packaged in Fedora
tradeoffs: POSIX bc plus dc in one binary and the bcl C library (callable from C++). Speed comes from packing several decimal digits per hardware integer and Karatsuba multiplication; author says the interpreter loop itself is slightly slower than GNU bc on scripts with little math.
caveats: Numbers are from bc 3.0.0 (2019) against GNU bc 1.07.1, built with clang 9.0.1 on an unnamed x86_64 CPU, best of four runs. The project has had many releases since, and the benchmark scripts' paths (tests/bc/add.bc) no longer exist in the current tree. The wall-clock gains on add/subtract/multiply/divide are inflated by 1.3-2.5 s of sys time in GNU bc's runs (cause not stated on the page). By user time the -O2 gains are 1.42x add, 1.24x subtract, 2.23x multiply, 1.19x divide and 1.22x timeconst.bc, against 2.89x, 2.76x, 3.25x, 2.09x and 1.27x by wall time (all derived from page data). The power test (1234567890^100000) is the clear win at 15.7x user time. The interpreter itself is not faster: at -O2 the 100,000,000-iteration for-loop script is slower (22.76 s vs 16.60 s) and the while-loop script is level (16.98 s vs 17.32 s). The author also found -march=native makes this bc slower. GNU bc is not one of the category baselines (CPython, Lua, Ruby, V8), and bc is a calculator language rather than a general scripting language. The author calls bc complete (no new features) but still actively maintained.

name: Cinder (Meta's CPython fork with method JIT)
baseline: CPython interpreter: the same Cinder build with the JIT disabled (the README calls it stock CPython; the paper did not run a separate stock CPython build)
workload: Python microbenchmarks richards, deltablue, nbody and fannkuch (cinder/3.8 Tools/benchmarks, original untyped plus Static Python typed variants) run with the C++ method-at-a-time Cinder JIT (-X jit, JIT list limited to the benchmark code, with and without shadow frames), versus the same build with the JIT off; README additionally claims gains on unnamed 'Python performance benchmarks'.
claimed_speedup: cinder/3.10 README: the JIT 'can achieve 1.5-4x speed improvements on many Python performance benchmarks'; 'Static Python plus Cinder JIT achieves 18x the performance of stock CPython on a typed version of the Richards benchmark'. Peer-reviewed paper appendix (Programming 2023, Cinder 3.8-era commits, mean of 10 runs, process user time): Cinder JIT with shadow frames on the original untyped benchmarks versus the same Cinder build with the JIT off: richards 3.8x, deltablue 1.9x, nbody 1.6x, fannkuch 1.5x; Static Python + JIT on the hand-optimized typed Richards (T-Max) versus untyped Richards without the JIT 17.7x, and on the simply-typed Richards (T-Min) about 7.2x (all derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Paper: Cinder 'compiled with default configure settings', compiler not named; the cinder/3.10 README says its basic build instructions give a binary without PGO/LTO
hardware: 64-bit CentOS Linux system (paper); CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 3.8k stars; used in production at Meta and Instagram
tradeoffs: Explicitly 'not supported' for outside users (README: Is this supported? Short answer: no); JIT is enabled with -X jit and usually driven by a jit-list file; Static Python needs type annotations; the 3.10 branch is Linux x64 only; the default branch now tracks CPython 3.14 and the JIT ships as the cinderx extension.
caveats: The README numbers sit in the older cinder/3.10 branch (last commit 2024-06-25); the default branch meta/3.14 (last commit 2026-10-06) README says the name cinder is historical and points to facebookincubator/cinderx (MIT, 282 stars, a CPython 3.14+ extension) for the JIT and Static Python, so the JIT code now lives there. Paper timings are from Cinder 3.8 commits d0d071, c9d14c and 144a21 (2022), not the 3.10 branch. The no-JIT baseline is Cinder's own interpreter build, not stock CPython; no CPU model, compiler or PGO/LTO state given. The 18x needs hand-typed Static Python with primitive types (simply typed code gives about 7x); the 1.5-4x JIT range is backed by only four microbenchmarks in the paper. README: 'Is this supported? Short answer: no.' JIT-compiling every called function by default can make programs slower. No comparison with PyPy.

name: cperl
baseline: perl5 releases 5.6.2 to 5.30.0 on the same machine (PerlBench); the README names 'perl5' and 5.14
workload: PerlBench micro-benchmark suite (41 tests: arith, array, call, hash, loop, re, startup, string), scores relative to perl 5.6.2 = 100
claimed_speedup: README: 'about 15%x faster than perl5 overall, more than 2x faster then 5.14' and the least memory measured since 5.6; the STATUS page says 'about 20% faster than perl5 overall'. Neither links a measurement. The project's own PerlBench run (2019-06-14, 41 micro-tests, 5.6.2 = 100, higher is better) gives Average 142.9 for cperl 5.30.0c vs 134.8 for perl 5.30.0 (about 1.06x, derived from page data; cperl wins 26 of 41 tests) and 114.6 vs 102.6 at 5.22 (about 1.12x), but cperl is equal or slower at 5.24 (125.5 vs 127.0), 5.26 (132.4 vs 131.9) and 5.28 (134.7 vs 136.9). Against perl 5.14 (101.9) cperl 5.30 is about 1.40x, not 2x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: cperl 5.30c: pre-release dev build (smoke/relprep b745599, -Dusedevel), BOLT-configured (x86_64-linux-bolt, -Wl,-q, llvm-bolt), clang -O3 -march=native thin LTO, no -fwrapv; perl5 5.30.0: gcc 8.3 -O2; 5.14 built -O1 -g (CONFIG-5.30c.txt and the PerlBench page)
hardware: Linux x86_64 machine ('reini'), Debian kernel 4.19.0-5-amd64; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Diverged fork of perl5 adding types, classes, native compilation hooks and security hardening while keeping CPAN compatibility; not a drop-in for every perl5 release.
caveats: The README's 15% (and the STATUS page's 20%) and '2x faster than 5.14' have no benchmark behind them; the project's own PerlBench page shows about 6% over perl 5.30.0 and cperl slower than or equal to perl5 at 5.24, 5.26 and 5.28. The comparison is confounded: cperl builds used -O3, -march=native and (5.28c/5.30c) clang thin LTO, while perl5 builds used gcc -O2 without -march, and the 5.14 baseline was built at -O1 -g. No CPU model. Archived read-only on 2023-06-01, last commit 2022-07-29; based on old perl5 releases, so it lags current perl5. [retier] The README's '15% faster, 2x vs 5.14' is unbacked; the 2019 PerlBench page gives 5.30c at 142.9 vs perl 5.30 at 134.8 (about 1.06x, partly a perl5 5.30 hash/get regression from 146 to 107), slower or equal at 5.24, 5.26 and 5.28, 1.40x over 5.14 rather than 2x, call tests 0.82-0.87x; a single run with no variance data and no CPU model, with the cperl binary a BOLT-configured clang -O3 -march=native LTO dev build against gcc -O2 perl5. claimed_speedup: After correction: geomean 3-5% faster on pyperformance (issue correction notice; Python 3.14 What's New says 3-5% depending on platform and architecture, baseline Python 3.14 built with Clang 19 without the new interpreter). name: Dino
baseline: Python 3.4.x and Ruby 2.1.x (also PyPy 2.2.x, SpiderMonkey 1.8.x, Scala 2.10.x, OCaml 4.0.x)
workload: Old computer-language-shootout style programs (loop, hash, fact, fib, exceptions, method calls, object creation, sieve, sort, statistics, random, threads, startup, compile) on x86-64, AARCH64, ARM and PPC64; times are relative to Dino's best result = 1.0.
claimed_speedup: 2016 README tables (Dino 0.98, Python 3.4, Ruby 2.1), relative times with plain Dino (no hints) as the fair reference: Loop Python 257 vs Dino 19 (13.5x), Fact 90.4 vs 13.2 (6.8x), Fib 492 vs 112 (4.4x), Method 5.8 vs 1.0, Object 4.4 vs 1.0, Sieve 37.9 vs 1.0, Thread 125 vs 1.0, Hash 2.4 vs 1.0; Ruby 157/25.2/142/1.5/1.4/4.5/43.6/2.2. The 'Dino best' rows for Fact and Fib use !pure result caching and are not comparable. PyPy beats plain Dino on 8 of 14 x86-64 benchmarks (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated.
hardware: x86-64 i5-4670 3.4 GHz Haswell; also AARCH64 (X-Gene), ARM (Exynos 5410 1.6 GHz Cortex-A15), PPC64 (3.5 GHz Power7)
license: GPL-2.0-or-later (DINO interpreter sources; COPYING is GPLv2) and LGPL-2.0-or-later (AMMUNITION library sources; COPYING.LIB is the Library GPL v2)
tradeoffs: Dynamically typed scripting language with an optimizing bytecode interpreter, mark-and-sweep plus mark-and-copy GC, optional function-level JIT through C code generation, type inference, fibers and a C FFI; its own language, not source compatible with Python or Ruby.
caveats: Results are from a 2016 README slide deck (version 0.98 development) on Python 3.4 and Ruby 2.1; numbers are relative to Dino's best run, not seconds. Dino's best row uses JIT, pure-function and inline hints; the plain row is quoted here. PyPy is faster than plain Dino on 8 of 14 benchmarks on x86-64. On AARCH64 Python 2.7.5 was used (Python 3 absent) and Python wins hash (0.5 vs 1.7); on ARM Python beats plain Dino on fact (4.4 vs 18.1) and hash (0.6 vs 1.0); on PPC64 Ruby beats plain Dino on loop (17.6 vs 23.2). The thread benchmark compares Dino green threads with GIL-bound OS threads. The benchmark driver is DINO/compare.tst (shell script, old shootout programs); compiler version and flags for the interpreter build are not stated. The companion arXiv preprint (dino.pdf in dino-lang/implemenation-article, dated 2016/4/5) has a variant table on Python 3.3.x and Ruby 2.0.x with different numbers (e.g. x86-64 loop Python 416, Ruby 237), Fedora Core 21, and GCC 4.9.2 used only for JIT compilation. Author is a GCC maintainer; repo dormant since 2019-11-19. [retier] First-party 2016 tables from DINO/compare.tst: one run per variant, user CPU time only, base taken as the minimum over the plain, -O and hint variants; the Fact and Fib best rows use !pure, which caches pure-function results (preprint section 3.3.2), so the best run does a cache lookup while Python and Ruby run the full recursion. Default build is -Ofast (implies -ffast-math) plus -flto. Python wins fact and hash on ARM, Ruby wins loop on PPC64. Abandoned since 2019-11-19; GPL-2.0-or-later plus LGPL-2.0-or-later.

name: frawk
baseline: gawk 5.1 (Linux) / 5.0.1 (macOS) run with -b, and mawk 1.3.4; one ad-hoc task also against a CPython csv-module script and a Rust csv-crate program (Python version not stated); xsv 0.13.0 and tsv-utils 2.1.1 also compared
workload: AWK-style CSV and TSV processing on 5.2 GB HEPMASS all_train and 8.9 GB TREE_GRM_ESTN files: sum two columns, statistics, select, filter, group by key.
claimed_speedup: Sum two columns, macOS: all_train TSV gawk 10.4 s and mawk 10.8 s vs frawk (LLVM) 3.1 s and parallel frawk 1.7 s; TREE_GRM_ESTN TSV gawk 14.0 s, mawk 42.0 s vs frawk 10.0 s / parallel 3.4 s. Linux: gawk 23.1 s vs frawk 14.7 s on TREE_GRM_ESTN TSV. Statistics (TREE_GRM_ESTN, macOS): gawk 1m13.3s and mawk 1m12.6s vs frawk (LLVM) 12.5 s TSV (about 5.9x vs gawk, derived from page data). On a per-core basis frawk beats mawk and gawk but is slower than tsv-utils wherever tsv-utils ran. Group By Key is a tie with gawk (14.8 s vs 14.8 s on macOS; 22.1 s vs 23.5 s on Linux).
compiler_and_flags: frawk built with use_jemalloc and allow_avx2 features, LLVM and Cranelift backends 'with all optimizations enabled'; mawk on Linux compiled from source with -march=native; gawk invoked with -b; rustc/LLVM versions not stated

caveats: Author's own benchmarks; scripts and raw logs are in info/scripts but rustc/LLVM versions are missing and the numbers date from about 2021 (macOS Big Sur 11.2.1). frawk ties gawk on Group By Key, the Cranelift build is slower than gawk there on macOS, and frawk is slower than tsv-utils per core on every task tsv-utils ran; parallel select/filter does not preserve row order. The CPython comparison is one ad-hoc script, Python version unstated, and frawk's time includes its own compile. The doc asks readers to draw only modest conclusions. gawk and mawk are AWK implementations, not listed category baselines. Building needs nightly Rust by default and LLVM 12 for the LLVM backend; the maintainer noted in 2024 that he has much less time for bug fixes. name: KPHP
baseline: PHP 7.4 with OpCache (Zend micro_bench.php and bench.php); PHP 7.2 for the vk.com page timings
workload: php-src Zend/micro_bench.php and Zend/bench.php (after removing a couple of tests that do not compile), 5 runs each; plus vk.com page generation times and ML-style kernels measured by the authors.
claimed_speedup: micro_bench avg 3.297 s on PHP 7.4 vs 0.460 s on KPHP; bench avg 0.659 s vs 0.119 s ('KPHP is found to be 5-7 times faster'); vk.com/feed 10.1 s vs 0.95 s, vk.com/im 1.25 s vs 0.46 s, vk.com/ads 0.73 s vs 0.20 s (PHP 7.2); neural networks with huge matrices ~8 s vs 0.24 s; deep decision trees ~5 s vs 0.14 s; README: 'when your code fits best practices, it runs 3-10 times faster than PHP'. Companion walk-through page (docs/various-topics/walk-through-php-kphp-cpp.md, quicksort of an int array): PHP 7.4 ~2100 ms vs KPHP ~480 ms (~4x); with the array_swap_int_keys built-in and no wrapper call, PHP 7.4 ~1950 ms vs KPHP ~270 ms (~7x); hand-written C++ with g++ -Os ~220 ms.
compiler_and_flags: g++ on the generated C++ with kphp2cpp.cpp defaults -O2 -ggdb -fsigned-char and -march=sandybridge (the docs' -Os is outdated); PHP 7.4/7.2 baselines without opcache JIT; compiler version and CPU unstated
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler from a limited, strictly typed PHP subset to C++ and then a native binary; no generators, anonymous classes, SPL or XML parsing, no call-by-name; existing PHP code usually needs rewriting to compile; the runtime is C++ and has a fast FFI.
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model or KPHP/compiler version. The Zend micro_bench.php and bench.php had a couple of tests removed and errors corrected before running, and the modified scripts are not published. The doc itself calls the Zend comparison 'absolutely synthetic' and warns it is wrong to say KPHP is always faster (code dominated by C-implemented PHP functions such as strpos or parse_url gains almost nothing). The walk-through shows KPHP dropping to ~940 ms when types degrade to mixed[], and hand-written C++ still about 2x faster than plain KPHP. Baseline is PHP 7.4/7.2, without the PHP 8 JIT, so today's gap is probably smaller. vk.com page timings and ML kernels are not reproducible from public code. KPHP only compiles a restricted, strictly typed PHP subset (no generators, anonymous classes, SPL or XML), so existing code usually needs rewriting. The project website is on github.io (blocked here); pages were read from the repo's docs/ directory. [retier] benchmarks.md has no CPU model, the modified Zend scripts are unpublished and the baseline is PHP 7.4/7.2 without the PHP 8 JIT; the vk.com and ML timings are not reproducible, and only a restricted typed PHP subset compiles. The quicksort walk-through (about 7x) gives KPHP a native array_swap_int_keys while PHP runs a userland polyfill, with unseeded rand(). Open issue #541: binarytrees takes 6.34 s on KPHP against 1.94 s on PHP without JIT and 1.27 s with JIT. Off-baseline (PHP).

name: LLRT (Low Latency Runtime)
baseline: Node.js 20 (V8) on AWS Lambda
workload: AWS Lambda DynamoDB Put function (example/functions/src/v3-lib.mjs), ARM, 128MB: 64 cold starts and 20000 warm starts, percentiles p0-p100 of Lambda-reported Init Duration plus Function Duration and of HTTP round-trip time; results only as two PNG screenshots in the README.
claimed_speedup: README screenshots (2024-01-31): p50 Lambda cold start 64.16 ms vs 1511.93 ms, HTTP round trip 235.61 vs 1719.00 ms against Node 20; not like for like (see caveats). Independent user report, issue #1166: LLRT v0.7.0-beta at 128 MB p50 HTTP 275 ms vs Node 22 at 512 MB 409-681 ms (about 1.5-2.5x). ahaoboy CI v8-v7 throughput: LLRT 972 vs Node 40333 on ubuntu (about 41x lower).
hardware: AWS Lambda ARM, 128MB memory (no CPU model)
tradeoffs: No JIT, so peak compute is far slower than V8 and not recommended for compute-heavy work; partial Node.js API compatibility; ES2023 only; README marks it experimental and for evaluation purposes.
caveats: Only first-party numbers, shown as screenshots committed once on 2024-01-31 ('Add perf screenshots') and never refreshed, so they reflect the launch-era LLRT against Node.js 20, not current versions of either. The win is cold start, where a no-JIT QuickJS runtime with a bundled SDK wins by design; warm p50 HTTP latency is only about 1.4x better (derived from page data) and CPU-heavy code would favor V8's JIT. The load-test harness that produced the tables is not in the repo (benchmarks/ holds the PNGs, fetch-streaming.mjs and a v8-v7 suite). The README calls LLRT experimental and 'intended only for evaluation purposes', and says it is not a drop-in Node.js replacement (many node: modules missing, e.g. http, tls, worker_threads). Written in Rust on QuickJS, so it is a runtime to adopt, not a C++ library. The '2x lower cost' claim has no published numbers. [retier] Cold-start-only win from vendor screenshots never refreshed since 2024-01-31; the LLRT function runs v3-lib.mjs while the Node 20 functions run v3.mjs or v3-mono.mjs (example/infrastructure/src/index.ts), the load generator is not published, and LLRT precompiles the SDK to zstd bytecode and warms TLS by default. Engine is quickjs-ng via rquickjs 0.14 (no JIT): throughput about 41x below Node on ahaoboy CI. Experimental, not Node-compatible.

workload: Eight checksum-verified micro-benchmarks (integer arithmetic, fib(30), dense array ops, string-key table ops, string ops, nested loops, object create and destroy, mixed workload), median of five runs, in milliseconds.

The committed benchmark_summary_latest.json (2026-07-12) has Mobius 1.3x slower than Lua.
compiler_and_flags: buildy.yaml release configuration: -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -flto with -flto -Wl,-O1 at link on Linux (macOS: -O3 -funroll-loops -flto); run_benchmarks.py picks bin/mobius or build/linux-x86_64-release/bin/mobius. Which build produced the README table is not stated.

They predate the README table: the 2026-07-13 and 2026-07-14 commits added intrinsic opcodes and small-string pools (commit 4fdf039 reports 431 ms vs Lua 455 ms), slimmer call frames, table and array op fusions, added type annotations to the Mobius fib benchmark only (f32cde8), and changed the Mobius mixed workload from data:get(i) to data[i] (29a409c). So the README's Lua win is newer than the committed JSON rather than contradicted by it, but the raw output behind the README table is not committed. The Mobius fib script uses typed parameters that the Lua and Python scripts cannot express. name: Pyccel
language: Python (transpiler that emits Fortran or C)
baseline: CPython 3.12 for the dev-branch table (the workflow installs it with actions/setup-python python-version '3.12'); separate tables for pyccel 2.2.3 from PyPI under CPython 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14
workload: 13 numeric kernels (Ackermann, Bellman-Ford, Dijkstra, Euler, midpoint explicit/fixed, RK4, four finite-difference solvers, molecular dynamics, splines); execution time in ms, compilation excluded.
claimed_speedup: pyccel-benchmarks: the devel-branch table (commit 0ccf9ec, timeit best-of, GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest, Python 3.12) gives the headline; the PyPI 2.2.3 tables (pyperf mean) show the GNU C backend much slower (Euler 21.0 vs 6.94 ms, Midpoint Fixed 180 vs 47.4 ms), a release C geomean of about 210x over CPython 3.12 rather than 336x (derived from page data). The GNU C backend is slower than Pythran on 6 of 12 kernels. The Midpoint Fixed row is loop-invariant (humps_deriv depends only on x) and likely collapsed by the Intel compiler (7.24 ms equals its Euler time).
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -mavx -ffast-math added to the pyccel_gnu and pyccel_intel configs (the same flags are added to Pythran); GNU compilers are Ubuntu apt gcc/gfortran and Intel compilers come from the apt intel-oneapi-toolkit, versions not pinned or stated. Dev run used pyccel commit 0ccf9ec3e964e071b933947b75767a052c9692f4, numba 0.66.0, pythran 0.18.1, numpy 2.4.6 (version_specific_results/devel_performance_312_requirements.txt)
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest hosted runner (.github/workflows/run_benchmarks.yml); CPU model not stated and may differ between runs, while builds use -march=native
stars_or_usage: 398 stars; on PyPI (2.2.3 per the PyPI JSON API); JOSS 2023 paper (Pyccel: a Python-to-X transpiler for scientific high-performance computing) cited in the README
tradeoffs: Restricted, statically typed Python subset; emits readable C or Fortran that is compiled and wrapped as a Python extension; supports NumPy and SciPy calls through generated code.
caveats: Numbers come from the Pyccel developers' own benchmark repository (pyccel/pyccel-benchmarks, 5 stars), regenerated by a GitHub Actions workflow on an ubuntu-latest shared runner; CPU model and compiler versions are not stated. Execution times are python3 -m timeit best-of results and exclude compilation; the compile-time table is CPU seconds (rusage user plus system) and lists 0.33 to 8.31 s per kernel across all tools. The CPython column is plain interpreted Python on scalar-loop numeric kernels adapted from Burkardt and Barba examples, so the large ratios do not transfer to code that already runs in NumPy. Pyccel is not the fastest accelerator in its own table: the GNU C backend is slower than Pythran (GNU) on 6 of 12 shared kernels (Dijkstra, FD L Convection, FD NL Convection, FD Poisson, FD Laplace, M-D), and the GNU Fortran backend is slower than Pythran on Dijkstra and M-D. Built with -ffast-math. Pyccel is an ahead-of-time Python-to-C/Fortran transpiler (filed next to Cython, Codon and Nuitka), not an interpreter. The JOSS paper was not opened (host blocked), so no peer-reviewed numbers are used. [retier] Team's own repo run on GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest with CPU and compiler versions unstated; the harness never compares outputs across tools despite -ffast-math and a tolerance-terminated Laplace, and the CPython baseline loops over NumPy elements one by one. Ahead-of-time transpiler for a typed Python subset, filed with Cython, Codon and Nuitka.

name: S6 (DeepMind CPython JIT)
baseline: CPython 3.7 interpreter
workload: Three pyperformance benchmarks modified by DeepMind, in src/benchmarks/: richards.py, raytrace.py, and unpack_sequence_fast.py / unpack_sequence_slow.py. pyperf was removed because it segfaults under S6. Each script runs the plain CPython 3.7 interpreter, then the @s6.jit version, in the same process.
claimed_speedup: Richards: 7x over the default Python 3.7 interpreter at 100 iterations, 9.5x average on internal dev machines; raytrace 3-4.5x; unpack_sequence worst case 0.2x (a 5x slowdown) or 0.97x in a tweaked variant; README headline 'up to 10x over CPython for pure Python benchmarks'.
compiler_and_flags: Public Dockerfile: clang 13 (apt.llvm.org); CPython 3.7 branch built from source with CFLAGS=-fno-omit-frame-pointer and ./configure --enable-shared (no --enable-optimizations/PGO). The build behind the internal-machine numbers is not stated.
hardware: 'internal dev machines' (no CPU model stated)
tradeoffs: Standalone JIT library for CPython 3.7 (strongjit IR lowered to x86 with asmjit); emits x86 machine code via asmjit; calls into C APIs such as NumPy are bottlenecked by C API call time; needs the project's Docker build.
caveats: The repo was archived on 2023-07-05 and holds one Copybara import commit (2022-09-14); DeepMind says it stopped work on S6. The README says most testing used internal or private benchmarks; the public numbers are for three modified pyperformance benchmarks on unnamed hardware. The harness (e.g. src/benchmarks/richards.py) times one wall-clock run of each mode with time.time(), with no repetitions. It ignores the benchmark's own correctness return value, so a wrong-result run would still print a speedup. The S6 timing includes JIT warm-up. The public Dockerfile's baseline CPython is a non-PGO build with frame pointers kept, which is slower than a distribution CPython. On unpack_sequence S6 is 5x slower (0.2x), or 0.97x in the tweaked variant. Only CPython 3.7 is supported, and it is long out of support. Apache-2.0 is in src/LICENSE and in per-file headers (the root build.sh carries the same header); there is no root LICENSE file. [retier] Archived DeepMind research JIT for CPython 3.7 only; the 9.5x Richards figure is on unnamed internal machines with one time.time() run per mode, the Richards result discarded and 50 default iterations against the README's 100. @s6.jit runs at import and calls Initialize(adopt_types=true), swapping tp_setattro to GenericSetAttrUsingClasses and hooking tp_new before the 'Default Python 3.7' baseline is timed, so the baseline is S6-instrumented rather than stock CPython. Dockerfile baseline: clang 13, non-PGO CPython with frame pointers. Last commit 2022-09-14.

name: Shed Skin
language: Python (transpiler) generating C++; runtime library in C++
baseline: CPython 3.14 (headline claim); CPython 3.10.6 and 3.11.0 in the sieve timing
workload: Over 80 non-trivial example programs (more than 25,000 lines) in the examples directory, plus a sieve example with n=100000000 timed against several Python implementations.
claimed_speedup: Typical speedup of 1-100x over CPython 3.14 (average 20x, median 12x) across the examples. Sieve n=100000000: CPython 3.10.6 13.4 s, CPython 3.11.0 11.4 s, Shed Skin 0.9.9 1.9 s (--int32) and 1.8 s (--int32 --nowrap --nobounds), about 6-7x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Shed Skin flags --int32 (and --int32 --nowrap --nobounds) for the sieve runs; C++ compiler, version and optimization flags not stated for either measurement (Shed Skin takes its C++ flags from the FLAGS files in its installation, per docs/documentation.md).
license: GPL-3.0 (compiler); MIT/Expat, BSD-3-Clause and BSL-1.0 for the C++ runtime library; examples individually licensed
tradeoffs: Accepts only a restricted, implicitly statically typed Python 3 subset: about 25 stdlib modules, no external libraries, no nested functions or variable argument counts; depends on the Boehm GC; programs often need refactoring; default integers are int64 (use --int32 for narrower).
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model or compiler version on the page; the examples/ directory has no timing harness or per-program results, so the 1-100x (average 20x, median 12x) figures over CPython 3.14 cannot be checked, and the per-example comparison against CPython 3.10 and PyPy (git tag performance_comparison) is only an image. The sieve table mixes tool versions (CPython 3.10.6/3.11.0, Nuitka 0.6.16, PyPy 3.9 5.8 s, Numba 0.56.4 2.5 s) and the Shed Skin rows used --int32, while Shed Skin now defaults to int64; the README says Numba (int64) would be as fast with 32-bit ints. Only a restricted, implicitly statically typed Python subset compiles, often after substantial refactoring. GPL-3.0 covers the compiler only; the C++ runtime that generated code links is Expat (MIT), with BSD-3-Clause random and BSL-1.0 Boost parts. [retier] README numbers without CPU, compiler or flags; examples/ has no timing harness and the per-example chart is an image only. The README sieve table says n=100000000 but examples/sieve/sieve.py hard-codes n = 10000000 (at v0.9.9, tag performance_comparison and HEAD), and HEAD runs main() 10x timing only the last 5, so the table is not reproducible from the committed example; the sieve rows used --int32. The 'benchmarked by asv' badge points to microtests on one 2015 machine (i5-3320M). Windows 'shedskin build' defaults to --config Debug (the cmake -O2 flag is UNIX-only); fixed-width ints without -fwrapv; dict is std::unordered_map, so iteration order differs from CPython. Restricted Python subset compiled to C++.

name: sjsonnet
baseline: go-jsonnet and google/jsonnet (C++) v0.22.0-rc1 in jrsonnet's docs/benchmarks.adoc; sjsonnet 0.6.2 measured (current 0.7.5)
workload: Evaluating one large production Jsonnet config (staging/runbot-app.jsonnet in the Databricks codebase, about 6.6 MB of output).
claimed_speedup: Independent jrsonnet docs/benchmarks.adoc (Ryzen 9 9950X3D, public nix harness, hyperfine, sjsonnet 0.6.2 Scala Native binary): real-world GraalVM CI 69.6 ms vs go-jsonnet 600.3 ms (about 8.6x) and kube-prometheus 204.6 ms vs 1068.4 ms (about 5.2x), derived from page data; google/jsonnet C++ was not timed on these ('takes longer than an hour'). The rows where sjsonnet trails go-jsonnet (Tail call, Inheritance function recursion, String strips, Big object, manifestJsonEx, manifestTomlEx, parseInt, substr) are in microseconds, about 2.4 ms vs 1.4 ms per process, so they measure startup rather than evaluation. jrsonnet (Rust) is faster on most cases.
compiler_and_flags: Sjsonnet 0.6.2 prebuilt release binaries (Scala Native and GraalVM native-image) wrapped with --max-stack 200000; google/jsonnet built with its own Makefile defaults and go-jsonnet with nixpkgs buildGoModule (nix/cpp-jsonnet.nix, nix/go-jsonnet.nix); compiler versions not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-core (jrsonnet docs/benchmarks.adoc); README 2023 numbers state no hardware
tradeoffs: JVM implementation of the Jsonnet language (Scala); best when kept as a warm long-lived process; startup cost of a cold JVM applies for one-shot use.
caveats: The README's 65x/670x figures are first-party (May 2023, Sjsonnet 0.4.3) on an internal Databricks config that cannot be reproduced, and compare a warm JVM daemon with cold subprocesses for go-jsonnet and google/jsonnet, so they overstate the like-for-like gap. The independent jrsonnet runs (per-process CLI for all) give smaller margins: about 5-9x over go-jsonnet on real-world configs, and the C++ reference was too slow to time on real-world inputs. Sjsonnet is not uniformly faster than go-jsonnet: it is slower on Big object (3756.8 vs 2544.5 ms), Inheritance function recursion (2394.1 vs 1414.3 ms), std.manifestJsonEx (2443.6 vs 1426.9 ms), std.manifestTomlEx (2558.8 vs 1427.7 ms) and std.parseInt (2383.6 vs 1398.2 ms). The Rust implementation jrsonnet beats Sjsonnet on most cases (GraalVM CI 2.0x, kube-prometheus 4.7x per jrsonnet's table; Sjsonnet's own docs/perf-gap-vs-jrsonnet.md, 2026-05-13 on an Apple M3 Pro, still shows kube-prometheus 1.68x behind jrsonnet). The benchmark is run by a competitor; compiler versions for the C++/Go builds are unstated, and the mimir real-world case skipped Sjsonnet (databricks/sjsonnet issue #829). JVM startup adds about 1 s per invocation for the plain JAR (client-server mode cuts it to 0.2-0.3 s per the README). [retier] The README's 65x/670x figures are first-party (May 2023, sjsonnet 0.4.3) on an internal Databricks config that cannot be reproduced (MainBenchmark now points at stdlib.jsonnet) and compare a warm JVM daemon with cold subprocesses. name: Spinel
baseline: CRuby 4.0.4 (MRI interpreter) and CRuby 4.0.4 with --yjit
workload: 28 benchmarks in the repository's benchmark/ directory (mandelbrot, fib, matmul, nqueens, sieve, binary_trees, json_parse, ao_render and others), compiled ahead of time to native executables by Spinel versus the same scripts run by CRuby.
claimed_speedup: 'Geometric mean: ~8.5x faster than Ruby 4.0.4 with --yjit across the 28 benchmarks (~15.2x against the interpreter)'. Examples vs YJIT: mandelbrot 18 ms vs 938 ms (53.6x), matmul 6.1 ms vs 201 ms (32.9x), binary_trees 2.7 ms vs 13 ms (4.7x), json_parse 28 ms vs 133 ms (4.7x), csv_process 95 ms vs 396 ms (4.2x).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3 builds the generated C; the README does not list flags, but Spinel's cc driver defaults to -O2 (src/main.c opt_level "2", Makefile COPT ?= -O2) plus -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -ffp-contract=off. CRuby 4.0.4 (revision b89eb1bc) run with --disable-gems, and with --yjit for the JIT column; each cell is the mean of five wall-clock runs under `perf stat -r 5`, measured 2026-09-17 on spinel 74c8e0a4.
hardware: '32-core Linux box' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: An ahead-of-time compiler for a Ruby subset (see the README Supported Ruby Features section), not a drop-in interpreter: it does whole-program type inference, emits C and invokes the system cc. Compiled binaries start in about 0.8 ms.
caveats: First-party numbers with only a core count for hardware; no timing script is checked in (make bench is a pass/fail output check against CRuby), so the perf stat runs are not reproducible from the repo as-is. Sub-10 ms cells are dominated by process startup (about 0.8 ms per binary; README says those ratios are lower bounds). The README itself warns the fib row (44.6x vs YJIT) reflects the C compiler folding a pure call tree at build time, not per-call speed. YJIT is essentially identical to the interpreter on mandelbrot, nqueens, matmul, partial_sums and sieve, so the largest multiples there are against an un-accelerated baseline. Spinel compiles a Ruby subset (whole-program type inference, no eval or dynamic metaprogramming), so the benchmarks are programs inside that subset. The geometric means (8.5x vs YJIT, 15.2x vs interpreter) reproduce from the 28 table rows (derived from page data).

name: Janet
baseline: CPython
workload: Computer Language Benchmarks Game programs, single-threaded idiomatic versions: fannkuch n=10, binarytrees depth 21, knucleotide on a 25M-line input, nbody 5,000,000 steps, reverse-complement on a 100M input, pidigits 10000 digits (Python uses built-in big ints), regexredux on a 5M input. Timed by runbench.janet as user+system CPU seconds from /usr/bin/time, one run each; only the exit code is checked, not the output.
claimed_speedup: Mixed, not an across-the-board win. README FAQ (qualitative only): programs 'tend to be a bit faster than they would be in a language like Python', VM 'about the same speed as most interpreted languages without a JIT compiler', 'YMMV'. Independent run (MikeBeller/janet-benchmarksgame, Janet 1.14.1 vs Python 3.8, user+sys seconds): Janet faster on binarytrees 71.63 vs 110.94 s (1.55x), knucleotide 137.59 vs 164.44 s (1.20x), nbody 17.53 vs 37.77 s (2.15x); slower on fannkuch 5.04 vs 4.83 s, reverse-complement 35.78 vs 7.37 s (4.9x slower), pidigits 5.98 vs 3.92 s, regexredux 15.86 vs 13.51 s. Geometric mean over the seven: Janet about 1.12x slower than CPython (derived from page data). Lua 5.4 beat Janet on fannkuch, knucleotide, nbody and reverse-complement.
compiler_and_flags: Janet 1.14.1 built with CFLAGS='-fPIC -O2 -flto' (C compiler not named); Python 3.8 from Anaconda (prebuilt binary); Lua 5.4.
hardware: Intel Core i5-7500 @ 3.40GHz, 4 cores, hyperthreading disabled
stars_or_usage: 4.4k stars; single-file amalgamation (janet.c + janet.h) for embedding in C and C++
tradeoffs: Lisp-like language with its own syntax, a stop-the-world GC, boxed 8-byte values; threads have isolated heaps; PEG engine built in.
caveats: No first-party numbers: the README FAQ's 'a bit faster than Python' is hedged and qualitative, and the same FAQ says tight critical loops should be written in C or C++. The only Janet-versus-CPython timings found are a small independent repo (16 stars, last commit 2022-04-04, no license file) from 2021 on Janet 1.14.1 and Python 3.8: Janet won 3 of 7 benchmarks (pure-interpreter object and float work: binarytrees, nbody, knucleotide) and lost 4 where Python's C-implemented builtins do the work (bytes.translate, re, big ints), for a geometric mean about 1.12x slower (derived from page data). Versions are dated: CPython 3.11+ is substantially faster than 3.8 and Janet has had many releases since, so current standing is unmeasured. Single run per benchmark, no output validation.

Developer notes in TODO.md (measured 2026-10-05) time Shed Skin's sieve and ant example programs under tpy and Shed Skin, and a JSON parse of a 15 MB, 20K-record dataset; scripts/perf/generator_frames.py compares generator forms inside tpy only.

name: Djinni (Snapchat fork of dropbox/djinni)
baseline: original dropbox/djinni generated JNI string conversion (Java to C++ string passing); the README names no baseline explicitly
workload: Passing strings between Java and C++ through Djinni-generated JNI glue; the README's 'Modifications' list gives one line and no benchmark, string sizes, device or version.
claimed_speedup: 'Speed up string passing between Java and C++ (about 5-10x faster depending on string size)'.
stars_or_usage: 238 stars (Snapchat/djinni); dropbox/djinni has 2.9k stars and is archived
tradeoffs: Cross-language binding generator (C++ with Java/JNI, Objective-C and WASM/TypeScript), not a scripting engine. The fork switched the build from sbt/gyp to Bazel, added array<>, outcome<>, future<> and protocol generation, and removed CppProxy finalizers. The djinni.xlcpp.dev documentation site named in the lead belongs to the separate cross-language-cpp djinni-generator and support-lib, whose README has no performance claim.
caveats: First-party one-line claim with no baseline version, string sizes, device or method. The repo has an Android perftest app (perftest/, djinni_perf_benchmark.djinni) whose README shows example output for the fork alone (argString 16/128/4096/16384: 4,622/4,893/24,407/109,606 ns average; returnString same sizes: 5,285/5,605/57,891/230,499 ns) but no run of the original Dropbox code and no device or Android/NDK version, so the 5-10x figure cannot be checked from it. Code reading: the original dropbox/djinni support-lib/jni/djinni_support.cpp converts strings with miniutf-derived handwritten UTF-8/UTF-16 code that substitutes U+FFFD for invalid sequences and unpaired surrogates; the Snapchat fork's jniStringFromUTF8/jniUTF8FromString now use std::wstring_convert with std::codecvt_utf8_utf16, which is deprecated since C++17 and removed in C++26, and which throws std::range_error on invalid input instead of substituting (a behavior change for malformed UTF-8 or lone surrogates; inferred from the standard, not tested). A search snippet of Snap's engineering post (eng.snap.com, blocked here) said a 16 KB string took more than 2 ms through the original handwritten conversion on a fairly fast device; not verified. dropbox/djinni itself makes no performance claim, so only the fork's string-passing change has evidence. The 'array<> is an order of magnitude faster than list<>' line compares two Djinni types; the perftest example output supports it (argListInt 128: 353,718 ns vs argArrayInt 128: 8,210 ns, about 43x, derived from page data), but argArrayRecord is declared as list<RecordSixInt> in djinni_perf_benchmark.djinni, so the 'ArrayRecord' rows actually measure list<>.

name: Software Architecture with C++ 2E: binary search (std::ranges::lower_bound) versus linear scan (std::ranges::find) in a sorted vector
baseline: std::ranges::find (linear scan) on a sorted std::vector<int>
workload: Google Benchmark of std::ranges::lower_bound against std::ranges::find on a sorted std::vector<int> holding 0..n-1: main_1 and main_2 look up the constant value 2137 in 10M elements; main_3 looks up 2137 in sizes 1e3 to 1e7 (x10 steps); main_4 looks up needles n/8, n/2, n-1 (last element) and n+1 (absent, larger than every element) in vectors of 1e3, 1e5 and 1e7 elements. The same benchmark also exists as Catch2 and nanobench/doctest variants.
claimed_speedup: Book sample run (relayed via seed lead, not on a repo page): binary search 24.2 ns versus linear search 471 ns for the fixed needle 2137 in a 10M-element vector, so the about 19x (derived) compares a 2,138-element linear scan that stops at index 2137 with a 24-probe binary search, not a full 10M scan; with the needle at the end of 10M elements (main_4) about 24 ns versus 2.8 ms, about 117,000x (derived).
compiler_and_flags: Repo README for Chapter13 requires a Conan profile of GCC 15, gnu20, libstdc++11 and a CMake Release build (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, so CMake's default GCC Release flags, normally -O3 -DNDEBUG, which the repo does not spell out); targets set cxx_std_20 (Google Benchmark 1.9.4 via Conan, benchmark_1..4) or cxx_std_23 (Catch2 3.12.0 and nanobench 4.3.11 variants). The compiler and flags of the book's actual run are not stated.
hardware: Book run reported only as a 20-thread 2022 MHz CPU with 48 KiB L1d and 24 MiB L3 (Google Benchmark context block, relayed via lead); no CPU model.
stars_or_usage: 74 stars, 22 forks; Packt companion repository of the book Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed.
tradeoffs: Binary search needs sorted input and random access (O(log n) versus O(n)); for tiny vectors a linear scan can win because of branch prediction and cache locality, which the 1000-element points in benchmark_3 and benchmark_4 are meant to show. Not a library: a std algorithm choice.
caveats: The printed numbers are the book's own sample run, relayed through the seed lead; they are not on any repo page (the repo carries the benchmark source only, no result files), so they could not be checked against a page. The comparison is an algorithmic-complexity truism (logarithmic versus linear on sorted data), not a faster implementation of the same algorithm; the speedup grows with n by construction. Both sides are the C++ standard library, so the stdlib under test (libstdc++ per the repo's GCC 15 Conan profile) is not stated for the book's run. Each benchmark repeats the same needle on the same vector, so the about 23 probes of the binary search stay in cache and the 24 ns figure is a warm-cache best case; a random-needle lookup in a 40 MB array would be bound by cache misses. Tier C: first-party book run, compiler, flags and CPU model are unstated (the Google Benchmark context block reports only 20 threads at 2022 MHz, 48 KiB L1d, 24 MiB L3) and the repo holds code only. In the Google Benchmark and Catch2 variants the vector is built outside the timed region; the nanobench_doctest variant builds the vector inside the timed lambda (main_4), so it times construction as well as the search. The same benchmark is written three times (Google Benchmark, Catch2, nanobench with doctest) and only the Google Benchmark numbers are given in the book. Repo files opened: Chapter13/microbenchmarking/benchmark/main_1..4.cpp and CMakeLists.txt, catch2/main_4.cpp, nanobench_doctest/main_4.cpp, Chapter13/conanfile.py, CMakeLists.txt and README.md. [retier] Enricher: main_1..3 fix the needle at 2137, so for n >= 1e4 std::ranges::find always stops at index 2137 and the linear series is flat from 1e4 to 1e7; the earlier caveat that the speedup grows with n holds only for main_4. Every iteration repeats the same needle (warm cache and a repeating branch pattern); main_4's needle is int64_t against a vector<int>, and the Catch2 variant narrows a size_t needle to int. The repo's CI builds only Chapter10/customer; Chapter13 is never CI-built.
